Scaramucci says Europe’s Trump strategy is off the Mark https://www.politico.eu/article/mark-rutte-mark-carney-donald-trump-anthony-scaramucci-white-house-strategy-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:32:19 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9247566 European leaders are using the wrong strategy to deal with U.S. President Donald Trump, according to Anthony Scaramucci, who briefly served as the White House’s communications director during Trump’s first term.

“You have to be firm with him. He doesn’t respect people that aren’t. I think you have got to wait him out,” Scaramucci told WELT AM SONNTAG, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

Scaramucci described two ways of handling Trump: the Carney approach and the Rutte approach.

“There’s two models of behavior: one is [NATO Secretary-General] Mark Rutte and one is [Canadian Prime Minister] Mark Carney. I think Mark Carney is handling him better. The Canadian people are with him, even if it causes some level of economic hardship,” Scaramucci said.

“Rutte, on the other hand, is making a big mistake. Because when you equivocate or flatter him, when you act in the manner that Mark Rutte has acted, all you’re doing is losing his respect. You’re not gaining anything,” he added.

Rutte has often lauded the U.S. president: “I just like the man. I think what he is doing for NATO is great news,” the military alliance chief said in an interview with POLITICO this summer.

Europe has seemingly yielded to Trump’s wishes on numerous occasions. The EU-U.S. trade deal was criticized as playing in Washington’s favor, while European allies agreed to a 5% of GDP spending target by 2035 at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, matching Trump’s headline demand.

Carney, by contrast, has been more unwilling to bow to Trump’s pressure. He walked away from U.S. trade talks, saying Ottawa could not accept the offer or the demands — and promised to match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.

In the interview, Scaramucci also lambasted members of Trump’s own Republican Party. “That is the other side of this story: the cowardice of the political servants that are supposed to check Donald Trump, the members of the Republican Senate caucus and the House caucus,” he said.

He added that lawmakers had failed to speak out against Trump’s decision to waive key provisions of the Russian sanctions law championed by the late South Carolina senator, Lindsey Graham.

“They’ve done nothing to speak out against that or to rebuke Trump, even though they could override him,” he said. “This is a case study in what you would call the strong arm tactics. People that believe in authoritarianism operate with levels of intimidation. That’s what Trump has done.”

]]> en Russian citizen faces spying charges in Poland after photographing railways https://www.politico.eu/article/russian-citizen-detained-in-poland-over-espionage/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:35:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9247353 A Russian citizen was charged with espionage in Poland after he was caught taking photographs of the country’s railway infrastructure, police in Lower Silesia said Friday.

Authorities said officers patrolling after a football match in Świdnica, south-western Poland, stumbled upon the 55-year-old Russian national as he was taking photographs of passing trains at an unguarded railway crossing.

“Everything indicates that the photos he took could be used against the security of the state,” the regional police authority wrote in a press release.

Police found a large amount of evidence suggesting that the man took pictures of strategic infrastructure systematically. “There were photographs of various places and important communication facilities, not only in Poland,” Łukasz Dutkowiak, a spokesperson for the Lower Silesian police, told Radio Wrocław.

Prosecutors are now investigating “activities for foreign intelligence against the Republic of Poland,” the regional authority added.

Poland has faced multiple sabotage attacks against its military and railway infrastructure over the past year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Ukrainian nationals of “cooperating with Russian services” after a November 2025 attack damaged a rail line close to the Polish-Ukrainian border.

Fires broke out at a drone-components plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna and an aircraft-parts facility in Lublin in late August. In September, a Starlink communications station was set on fire near Warsaw.

“Russia does not even have to cross our border,” Tusk said after the September attacks. “It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet.”

European officials have pointed to an escalation of sabotage attacks from Russia over the past few months, as President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv. 

]]> en Unrest in France is nightmare fuel for Macron’s heirs https://www.politico.eu/article/unrest-in-france-is-nightmare-fuel-for-emmanuel-macron-heirs/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:48:37 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9233906 PARIS — France’s center-right presidential candidates are bracing for more doom and gloom ahead of another tense day of protests Saturday, as polls suggest the combined effect of massive marches and the connected violence is fueling their rivals on both ends of the political spectrum.

Five polls, including one commissioned by POLITICO, conducted in the aftermath of the unrest in France on Oct. 17 — when hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets while violence and looting broke out across the country — have all shown the same thing: The potential successors from President Emmanuel Macron’s coalition would be eliminated in the first round.

Both Marine Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left have been able to capitalize on the movement: the former “by presenting herself as a candidate who guarantees law and order,” and the latter acting as a “hero and herald of protest,” said Gaël Sliman, the head of French polling firm Odoxa.

They are facing a divided field of mainstream candidates on the center and center-right, including two former prime ministers under Macron in Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister. These candidates have struggled to settle on a common message in response to the crisis — let alone agree on who the best candidate would be to avoid their nightmare scenario of a runoff between Mélenchon and Le Pen.

‘Out of ideas’

Three officials supporting centrist and conservative candidates told POLITICO that they were concerned the events of the past few weeks would cause lasting damage to their campaigns.

“It’s definitely going to kill us,” said one campaign official who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “We cannot be the solution anymore, only the problem.”

A Philippe supporter went as far as suggesting his champion was ill-equipped for the moment. “It’s exactly what he doesn’t need,” the supporter said last week, drawing parallels between the protests and the 2018–2019 Yellow Vest movement under Philippe’s premiership. “He doesn’t know how to do this. He’s not empathetic, and he’s not pretending to be.”

“Honestly, I don’t know how we’re going to get through this. Things are tough, and we’re out of ideas,” a centrist MP said.

The protests have taken place two Saturdays in a row and are expected to continue in the weeks to come. High school students are demanding better learning conditions while the wider public are protesting the cost-of-living crisis. The movement has been marred by scenes of vandalism and looting, especially on Oct. 17, when Macron’s government appeared to have underestimated both the scale of the protests and the potential for violent unrest.

In the following days, the government and center-right candidates focused on attacking Mélenchon and his party, France Unbowed, for fanning the flames that led to dramatic scenes of violence and looting. The strategy may have further dented his image among voters who already oppose him, polls suggest. But it did little to weaken his particularly young voter base.

“There is a kind of synergy between the social movement and France Unbowed,” a party strategist said. “This leads participants to see Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s impending victory as a logical conclusion.”

Le Pen, meanwhile, pushed her “protective vision” while her deputy Jordan Bardella said a far-right victory was “the only solution to allow the return of order and return of authority.”

As things stand, Le Pen is leading the race by a double-digit margin, while Mélenchon appears best placed to take second place and qualify for a runoff.

‘Muddled and hazardous’

Centrists and conservatives have been hindered by their persisting inability to agree on a single candidacy to take Macron’s mantle.

Attal, the candidate for Macron’s Renaissance party, made a surprise pitch for a “large primary of democrats” Wednesday, in a bid to narrow down the field of candidates against the far left and the far right.

Such a primary could see him face Philippe and Retailleau as well as David Lisnard, the mayor of Cannes running as an outsider on a conservative, small-state platform.

But Attal’s proposal was swiftly dismissed by rival campaigns. Laurent Marcangeli, who leads Philippe’s Horizons party in the National Assembly, called it “muddled and hazardous” Wednesday evening. “Without Philippe, there’s no primary,” a Retailleau backer said.

Despite these rebuffs, Attal on Thursday kept pushing for a contest to avoid the “cataclysm” of a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff. “Our country wouldn’t recover from this,” he told public broadcaster France 5.

]]> en Former US ambassadors: America must stand with Ukraine https://www.politico.eu/article/former-united-states-ambassadors-say-america-must-stand-with-ukraine/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:28:44 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9242865 The United States cannot credibly defend freedom around the world while treating the survival of a democracy under attack as a bargaining chip.

Russia’s war against Ukraine is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a test of whether democratic nations will defend the principles that sustain their freedom — or allow an authoritarian aggressor to destroy these principles through military force, terror and economic coercion.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was unlawful. Its conduct has included attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and in March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. All grave allegations that demand accountability.

As Ukraine continues to fight for its survival, current U.S. policy raises a fundamental question: Does Washington understand what is at stake?

If Moscow succeeds in subjugating Ukraine, other authoritarian leaders will also ask whether military conquest can succeed. Can U.S. commitments be trusted? Will democratic nations stand together when the price becomes politically inconvenient?

Ukraine’s defense is not charity. It is a strategic investment in American and European security, Washington’s credibility and the deterrence of future conflicts.

The U.S. emerged from World War II understanding that an international order based on sovereignty, freedom and rule of law serves its interests. And successive Republican and Democratic administrations recognized that unchecked authoritarian expansion threatens both American security and the independence of its allies.

That understanding must guide U.S. policy toward Russia today.

Diplomacy is essential. Negotiations to end the war should be pursued seriously. But peace cannot mean rewarding aggression, compelling Ukraine to surrender its sovereignty or giving Moscow time to rearm for another invasion.

Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it.

Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion.

On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided.

The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained.

The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law.

This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives.

If Washington weakens its own pressure without obtaining meaningful concessions, it risks surrendering leverage while leaving Russia’s aggression unresolved. Every source of revenue helping Moscow sustain its military campaign has consequences for Ukrainian civilians, who bear them in destroyed homes, shattered families and lost lives.

U.S. policy should not make it easier for Russia to finance a war Washington says it wants to end.

American history has a bipartisan tradition of leadership that combines the defense of freedom with strategic judgment.

Harry Truman understood U.S. security depended on resisting authoritarian expansion. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, John F. Kennedy demonstrated that strength and diplomacy are not opposites. Ronald Reagan understood freedom must be defended against those who seek to suppress it. And George H. W. Bush knew sovereignty and alliances are essential to an international order where nations cannot redraw borders by force.

Though from different eras, the leadership of these presidents reflected a common principle: American security is strengthened when the U.S. combines military strength, alliances, diplomacy and a commitment to the independence of free nations.

A policy that pressures Ukraine more than Russia, offers Moscow economic relief without substantial concessions or asks Ukrainians to accept an insecure future is not a strategy for lasting peace. It risks rewarding aggression and inviting further conflict.

And above all, Ukraine’s future should not be decided over the heads of Ukrainians.

Democratic institutions can be attacked and dismantled far faster than they can be rebuilt. Ukraine’s struggle is therefore about more than one war. It is about whether the democratic world will remain a community of nations bound by common principles or become a collection of states left to negotiate individually with authoritarian regimes.

History will not judge U.S. policy solely by the immediate cost of weapons, energy or sanctions. It will judge whether America stood by a nation fighting for survival, upheld the principles it asks others to respect and helped prevent future wars by demonstrating that aggression does not pay.

Adrian Zuckerman is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2019-2021); Mark Gitenstein is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2009-2012) and to the EU (2022-2025); Ron Gidwitz is a former U.S. ambassador to Belgium (2018-2021) and acting U.S. ambassador to the EU (2020-2021); Jim Gilmore is a former U.S. ambassador to the OSCE (2019-2021); Kathleen Kavalec is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2023-2025); Jim Rosapepe is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (1998-2001).

]]> en Streeting insists Burnham won’t make ‘arbitrary’ welfare cuts https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-budget-streeting-insists-burnham-will-not-make-arbitrary-welfare-cuts/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 10:43:30 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9246888 LONDON — Andy Burnham will avoid making “arbitrary” cuts to Britain’s rising social security budget, a top Cabinet minister said Friday, as he defended days of mixed government messaging on welfare.

Defense Secretary Wes Streeting accused Labour’s opponents — and the Keir Starmer government he served in as health secretary — of not properly thinking through plans to reduce the welfare bill, leading to a collapse in political support.

Streeting told the BBC Today program: “I saw it, frankly, after the last general election, when we went too far too fast with an arbitrary figure to cut welfare and when people saw the detail of what that meant for disabled people in our country, the very same people who were saying we need to cut the welfare bill were saying ‘but not like that’.”

He said: “What I do understand from experience, and I’ve seen this experience borne out under both Conservative and Labour governments, is that when you put in place arbitrary targets to cut welfare without a thought-through plan to do so sustainably and responsibly, the plans fall apart.”

Spending on U.K. health and disability-related benefits has increased sharply since the Covid pandemic, with the bill for working-age disability benefits in England and Wales increasing from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026.

Former Health Secretary Alan Milburn is leading a report into how to help the estimated one million young people not in employment or education. It is due to be published in November, and the government is also waiting on minister Stephen Timms to make recommendations on disability benefit reform.

A previous bid to reduce welfare under Starmer was scrapped after a revolt among Labour MPs. The row was seen as deeply damaging to Starmer’s authority and a sign that the leadership had lost touch with rank-and-file MPs.

Streeting’s comments came after an extended back-and-forth between ministers and journalists Thursday over whether Burnham’s government will lower welfare spending before the next general election.

Healey was asked by the BBC Thursday whether cuts to the welfare bill would be made before the next election.”There will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we’ll do that in a Labour way,” he said.

But Treasury officials tried to clarify that Healey had not put a date on reductions, with the chancellor telling Channel 4 News shortly afterwards: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”

Streeting said of welfare Friday: “We all agree we’ve got to bring it down, we’ve just got to do it in the right way.”

Tories leapt on the confusion yesterday to say Labour were “confused, unserious, and [had] no plan.”

Deputy Conservative Chairman Matt Vickers told GB News Friday morning that Healey had given “no answers” on welfare. He added: “The government’s priorities are completely wrong. We need to get in there, sort the ballooning welfare bill, and protect this country properly.”

]]> en Economy minister warns France could ‘hit the wall’ as new figures show GDP contraction https://www.politico.eu/article/economy-minister-roland-lescure-warns-france-could-hit-the-wall-as-new-figures-show-gdp-contraction/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 10:19:54 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9246861 PARIS — France’s economy shrunk by 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, according to fresh estimates from national statistics agency Insee, pushing the country closer to recession and further complicating the government’s efforts to stave off a debt-driven financial crisis.

Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Friday that this summer’s extreme heat and spiking energy prices were responsible for the negative growth.

In an interview with Franceinfo, he said the new figures give added urgency for lawmakers to pass the 2027 budget proposed by the government, which aims to bring the deficit down to 5% of gross domestic product next year with €43 billion in savings.

“If we don’t have the budget adjustment we put in the budget, we will hit the wall,” Lescure said.

But France’s fragmented parliament failed to pass budgets before the new year in both 2024 and 2025, and the spring 2027 presidential election may further complicate efforts to seek compromise this time around. That could force Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to push through the budget using a constitutional backdoor that bypasses a parliamentary vote, but it would expose the minority government to potential motions of no confidence.

Lescure insisted that adopting a budget for next year was key to “reassure markets” and relaunch growth in the last quarter of the year. The French economy contracted by 0.1% in the first quarter of 2026 and recorded no growth in the three months that followed.

That anemic growth will likely complicate the government’s pledge to bring the deficit down to 5.4% of GDP this year, as the target was based on the assumption the economy would grow by 0.5% in 2026.

“The French economy is at a standstill,” Lescure said. “It has to restart.”

“In the course of terrorist attacks on the civil infrastructure of our region and country, the vile enemy from Kyiv launched a record number of drones. There were no casualties, which is the most important thing,” Samara Governor Viacheslav Fedorischev said in a statement on Russian state messaging app Max.

Russian air defense forces shot down 1,043 Ukrainian drones over Samara, and 18 other Russian regions overnight, Moscow’s Ministry of Defense reported Friday.

Fedorischev asked locals not to reveal what was struck, but independent Russian media channel Astra reported a fire at the local oil refinery, which produces jet fuel for the Russian army. Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery can produce about 8.8 million metric tons of oil per year, according to Russian oil company Rosneft.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Kyiv had agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump. The unofficial halt is expected, according to the report, to last until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. Ukraine had paused drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for 72 hours when Trump announced an energy ceasefire earlier this month. But the Kremlin kept bombarding Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

“That didn’t help. There was all kinds of rhetoric, and no one thanked us for those three days,” Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv earlier this week.

As of Friday morning, Ukraine has not taken responsibility for the latest strike — though there was some trolling from the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.

“Little drone, how did you end up there? The Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery welcomes guests from Ukraine,” Ukrainian defense company Fire Point — which produces long-range drones used by Kyiv to bomb targets in Russia — said in a morning Telegram post.

Russia also attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and more than 100 drones overnight, killing one person in Kyiv and leaving 350,000 people without electricity in Dnipro.

A massive fire broke out.]]>
  • Confirmed Ukrainian military losses have exceeded 220,000, while the share of missing personnel is rising.
  • Ukraine lost thousands of personnel both during the Kursk region operation and in the battle for Krynky.
  • Following an unofficial pause, Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian refineries — and with considerable success.
  • Ukraine claims to have hit another two Russian Su-34 aircraft. Russia has suffered too many such losses over the past two months.
  • Videos of the day: a report on a soldier who operates drones with his chin; a welcome for Ukraine’s ombudsman in Oleshky.

    • In Ukraine Battlefield update, we report fairly regularly on the enormous losses suffered by Russian soldiers. The Ukrainian command publishes them daily. This figure is probably inflated, but it shows a trend. And that trend shows that October is already the bloodiest month since the start of the full-scale invasion.

    Verified figures are also published by the independent Russian outlets Mediazona and the Russian BBC. The problem is that they can only verify these figures retrospectively, while the Russian state is placing ever more obstacles in their way as they seek information about deaths.

    As Dima Treshchanin wrote, the author of the project, they are currently working on deaths from the summer of 2025.

    However, we devote less attention to Ukrainian military losses. Unfortunately, these are also high.

    However, when independent analysts examined its data, they found it credible. Each entry links to a source of information on a Ukrainian website, mostly an obituary, and the analysts did not find many duplicates either.

    Ukrainian losses are tracked by the UA Losses project. It is an anonymous website and its background is a mystery. Ukrainian authorities describe it as propaganda and have blocked access to its website in Ukraine.

    UA Losses has updated its data in recent days.

    ]]>         Culture groups ‘on their knees’ after 30% funding cut proposed in EU’s next budget https://euobserver.com/245996/culture-groups-on-their-knees-after-30-funding-cut-proposed-in-next-eus-budget/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:05:12 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245996 Culture, media and rights groups demand that European capitals oppose a 30 percent cut to €8.6bn proposed for AgoraEU in the EU's next long-term budget. “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP.]]> “Thirty percent, we don’t consent” chants echoed across Schuman roundabout in the Brussels European quarter this week, as culture, media and journalist workers demanded that national leaders halt plans to reduce cash for culture in a protest on Thursday (29 October).

    Representatives from European rights forums, culture groups and a journalism federation gathered in a bid to keep enough money flowing to their organisations.

    “There’s a very grim future if we continue with these cuts,” said Rhys Nugent of Culture Action Europe, one of the protest’s organisers. “These sectors are already on their knees.”

    The demonstration came after EU leaders discussed giving less money than previously proposed to AgoraEU, an umbrella for culture, media, democracy and rights initiatives, within the EU’s 2028-2034 budget.

    30% less for culture

    Reacting to the EU Commission’s proposal to give AgoraEU €8.6bn under the long-term budget, the EU parliament’s budget committee asked to ramp this up to €10.7bn.

    But national capitals have not agreed to either proposal.

    Instead, the Irish presidency of Council presented a plan earlier this month (October 10) to allocate €5.3bn for AgoraEU –  representing a 30 percent cut to the commission’s proposal. It was responding to pressures for frugality from some member states.

    National capitals are yet to finalise a budget agreement.

    Read more

    Pressure mounts on EU leaders to strike a budget deal by December

    “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP and chair of parliament’s culture and education committee.

    “If this goes through, people will wake up one day and ask: why are my rights not protected? Why has that film festival disappeared? Where has my local publisher gone?” she said.

    “These cuts will save only a tiny percent of the EU budget but cause massive damage to these sectors,” added the German lawmaker. 

    What could be chopped?

    AgoraEU is a new umbrella for Creative Europe and Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV).

    Protest organiser Nugent said Creative Europe “funds everything from small theatrical productions to large cooperation around Europe.”

    He pointed to Flow, an Oscar-winning film, Europa Cinemas, and Culture Moves Europe as examples of the types of bodies that could be affected by a lack of EU funding.

    More than 400,000 emails exchanged by AfD members between March 2013 and September 2026, effectively covering the party’s entire history, have appeared online.

    They were published by hackers from the Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) organisation, who obtained 284 gigabytes of data, including minutes from meetings of the party leadership, payslips, strategic documents, membership lists and donors’ names.

    AfD and its enemies

    According to the Correctiv website, the material also includes election campaign plans, for example for the 2025 parliamentary election. Their authors describe how to reach potential voter groups. They describe the governing parties at the time as enemies.

    It is unclear yet whether all the emails are genuine, but the party has confirmed the leak. German media outlets with access to them estimate that assessing the information could take months.

    It is already clear that the emails offer an insight into how Germany’s currently strongest political party operates and how it approaches certain issues, including neo-Nazism.

    The media are gradually uncovering messages that are uncomfortable for AfD’s leading figures, including its co-chair Alice Weidel.

    One of the most striking findings is that in private she was not as radical as she liked to portray herself in public. And, according to German media, the difference is considerable.

    The leaked emails also suggest how the German party sought to forge closer ties with the US conservative Maga movement and president Donald Trump, whom it saw as a potential ally.

    In foreign policy, they also point to deeper links with Russia than had previously been known.

    Thousands of emails could also play a role in a potential ban on the party, which is not yet decided upon but is being debated in Berlin.

    So what have they revealed?

    What had not previously been known about relations with Russia

I will not go back there.”

    The 25 year old Nigerian man is one of many rescued by the German NGO SOS Humanity on Tuesday (27 October) to have escaped living hell in Libya, at the hands of a regime paid by the EU to keep migrants away from its borders.

    “I was in prison for one year, for no reason,” said Sulaiman, whose name has been changed to preserve his anonymity. “Any time in the morning they come to distribute food, there are beatings. No one lets you go without a beating,” he told EUobserver.

    Every day he’d subsist on one small slice of bread in “a cage for 100 people, where there are all skeletons,” he described with tears in his eyes. 

    Sulaiman had tried to leave Libya twice before on small boats, but each time he’d been pulled back to land by violent militias, one of whom he described to be an ‘official’ authority. 

    Data from the International Organisation for migration (IOM) and the UN found over 200,000 people to have been illegally intercepted in the central Mediterranean and returned to Libya since 2016. 

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    And like many other search and rescue organisations, SOS Humanity’s own work has been significantly impeded by Libyan groups – whether they be the so-called Libyan coast guard or paramilitary groups known for hijacking small migrant boats in open sea to rob everyone on board and pull them back to illegal detention facilities.

    Men, women, families with children, and unaccompanied minors alike are kept in prisons until they can pay their way out.

    “I lied, and told my family I was in Tunisia,” a young boy from Sudan told EUobserver. 

    “I knew my mother couldn’t take it, knowing what would be happening to me in Libya,” he said, after having been rescued by SOS Humanity alongside 27 others in the early hours of Tuesday. He is one of 10 children aboard traveling alone.

    ]]>         Listen: Why is the EU introducing a new €2 charge on parcels? https://euobserver.com/245922/listen-why-is-the-eu-introducing-a-new-e2-charge-on-parcels/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:36:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245922 From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.

    So why is the EU doing this, and what difference will it make? Let’s start with what’s changing.

    From this Sunday, there will be a €2 tax on each product category contained in a parcel coming from outside the EU. This ads up to the €3 tax on small parcels introduced in June this year. So for a parcel of less than €150, you can already count a €5 charge, and that’s if your parcel contains just one category of item.

    Say you order four different garments from the Chinese platform Shein. The total charge comes to €20.

    Officially, it’s the sellers who are supposed to pay, not consumers. But in practice, they pass the cost on to customers one way or another.

    So why this second charge? The €3 charge adopted in June was meant to tackle the flood of small parcels coming from companies like Temu and Shein.

    Parcels of very low value, often just a few euros. And that’s not an exaggeration. According to Kristian Vanderwaeren, Belgium’s head of customs, the average value of a parcel before the charge was around €5. And that’s an average, so imagine the number of parcels worth less than €5 that literally come from the other side of the world.

    Read more

    Listen: Who will benefit from the new €3 tax on small parcels?

    Until now, parcels worth less than €150 were exempt from customs duties. That was a big hole in customs revenue. And at the same time, customs officers had more and more parcels to process. Hence the €3 levy.

    Now the new charge is different. It applies to all parcels, not just the smallest ones. Its goal is to raise revenue to cover the cost of checks. Because if the EU wants to fight fraud and make sure products on the market are safe, customs controls have to increase. And that takes time, and therefore money.

    We don’t know yet exactly how much the new tax will bring in revenues. What we know, even if the situation is not comparable, is what the €3 tax is starting to bring.

    Between June and September, the €3 charge brought in €364mln for Belgian customs. In just three months.

    Belgium is a major entry point for parcels bound for the EU, through the port of Antwerp and Liège airport. So we cannot duplicate that figure for other EU countries.

    Read more

    EU ‘open’ to curbs on imports of Chinese chemicals and machinery, after hybrid-car deal

    Still, over a full year, the two charges combined, on top of standard customs duties, should raise a significant amount. We can therefore imagine that countries outside the EU are not happy, especially China.

    Beijing describes the measure as protectionist. It also argues that the cost will largely be passed on to European consumers, which means, in its view, that the EU is shooting itself in the foot.

    But that is, to some extent, exactly what Europeans are hoping for. If Chinese products become more expensive, they become less attractive.

    Business groups agree. Comeos, the Belgian federation for trade and services, welcomed the charge as a response to unfair competition.

    Think about an everyday product worth less than €100. There is usually a big price gap between the Chinese version and the one made in Europe. When that gap is somewhere between €5 and €20, the charge can tip the balance. It may push you to buy local, or not to buy at all. In both case, this means less money getting out of the EU.

    And there are already signs it’s working. Since the €3 charge came in in June, the volume of small parcels arriving at Liège airport has dropped by 60 percent.

    The European consumer organisation BEUC has also welcomed the move, saying more border controls mean safer products.

    Something that is not immediately visible for citizens, but which has its importance.

In Switzerland, the Swiss armed forces rejected Palantir’s offers nine times. The military’s conclusion was that it was technically impossible to guarantee that  sensitive national data would not reach American intelligence services.]]> I moved to Poland from London with my Polish husband, and we are raising our two-year-old  son here. My son will grow up and live his entire life within the digital infrastructure that the government is building today. The fact that I was not born in Poland does not mean I don’t care about its future, as a mother, I have an obligation to fight for my son’s rights as a Polish  citizen. 

    Recently, I saw that the Polish Ministry of National Defence has signed a  Letter of Intent with the American analytics company Palantir Technologies.

    Having lived  through what happened in the United Kingdom when our government signed similar agreements, I believe that Polish people deserve to know what happens when public systems are handed over to a foreign defence contractor.

    Among the company’s founding investors was In-Q-Tel, the CIA’s venture capital arm. 

    Read more

    Public money for Palantir, pennies back in tax: EU procurement is failing Europe

    In London, I was part of a campaign group fighting against Palantir’s contract with our National Health Service (NHS).

    Under that agreement, the US defence contractor gained deep access to NHS data systems, including mental health records, reproductive health data, and medication history.

    Heavily redacted contracts

    Over 100 pages of the contract remain heavily redacted and hidden from the public. Because Palantir is an American corporation, citizens cannot easily hold them to account or use basic data access requests in the way they could with an EU-based company.

    In the UK, two parliamentary committees and the British Medical Association are calling on the government to exit the contract before the break clause in  2027. 

    Poland is not the first European country Palantir has approached, but other allied nations  have already drawn the line.

    In Switzerland, the Swiss armed forces rejected Palantir’s offers nine times. The military’s conclusion was that it was technically impossible to guarantee that  sensitive national data would not reach American intelligence services.

    When a Swiss  investigative outlet reported on this, Palantir sued them and lost on 22 of 23 counts. In Germany, the Bundeswehr explicitly excluded Palantir from a military cloud procurement on  grounds of data sovereignty, with senior military officials stating that granting external  industry employees’ access to the national database was completely unacceptable. 

    Poland is now preparing to deepen its cooperation with a company that the Swiss and German militaries both rejected on security and sovereignty grounds.

    It is our children who  will have to face the long-term consequences of today’s decisions. I have seen what happens when people in the United Kingdom did not ask questions until it was too late, and I cannot stay silent and watch exactly the same thing happen in Poland.

    If you care about data sovereignty, public transparency, and protecting the next generation,  join us at the public protest against Palantir’s contracts in Poland, organised by Nasze Dane, on 8 November at Plac Konstytucji in Warsaw at 3pm.

    The phraseology, made during von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech, surprised many EU diplomats who claimed that they had not been consulted.

    It was also never clear precisely what this would mean.

    The idea of Canada having representatives or observer status in the EU institutions always sounded fanciful.     The draft communique circulated ahead of the summit talks of “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.” 

    Von der Leyen appeared not to have read the memo. 

    Officials would “start discussing how to make Canada the first associate member of the EU,” she said on arrival in Montreal, adding that “our ambition is to build the closest partnership we have ever had with a non-European country”. 

    Yet this is a dispute over language rather than substance. The EU and Mark Carney’s Canada see each other as their closest ally. Both have been repeatedly threatened with hefty trade tariffs by Donald Trump’s White House and the consequences of Trump’s foreign policy adventures in the Middle East and the Arctic. Carney’s remarks at the World Economic Forum in January that ‘middle’ powers should club together to avoid being squeezed between China and the US were aimed at the EU.  

    Read more

    Commission officials may blench at the comparison, but the EU is a collection of middle ranking and small states. And it is yet to act like a world power on the political stage.

    ]]>         What is ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ – and how is it distorting Europe’s online democracy? https://euobserver.com/245695/what-is-coordinated-inauthentic-behaviour-and-how-is-it-distorting-europes-online-democracy/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:07:30 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245695 From Serbia's election to wider foreign information manipulation campaigns, coordinated networks can manufacture the appearance of online political support and become more powerful when their content is amplified by the mainstream media.]]> If you have come across messages such as “what Europe needs is a peaceful continent” on Facebook or X, you may have encountered coordinated inauthentic behaviour (CIB).

    CIB is a manipulative communication tactic that uses a combination of authentic, fake and duplicated social media accounts to operate as an adversarial network across platforms such as X, Facebook or Bluesky.

    By coordinating their activity, these accounts can amplify particular messages and create an online impression that may not reflect the reality of public opinion.

    The tactic spread massively during Covid.

    In a paper entitled ‘Coordinated inauthentic behavior: An innovative manipulation tactic to amplify Covid-19 anti-vaccine communication outreach via social media’, Monica Murero wrote that such operations could be “one of the greatest threats to freedom of expression and democracy in our society”.

    But this distortion becomes particularly visible during elections.

    Indeed, with political momentum, spreading messages and content online can influence how voters perceive the strength of an incumbent government and the prospects of its opposition.

    Manufacturing political dominance

    The latest example is Serbia.

    Ahead of parliamentary elections in Serbia, the Balkan Free Media Initiative (BFMI), in collaboration with Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub, investigated how coordinated networks promoted former Serbian PM and president Aleksandar Vučić while undermining independent media.

    “CIB corrupts the public signal that democracies rely on to understand themselves,” head of research at BFMI Vanesa Valcheva told EUobserver.

    The findings point to a broader problem for democratic debate: online visibility can be manipulated to sustain an image of political dominance, even when the picture on the ground appears different.

    “Incumbents often try to look unbeatable to discourage opposition voters, reassure their supporters, and show outside partners that things are unlikely to change,” Valcheva said.

    Before the rise of these coordinated online operations, the digital space offered dissent more room to breathe.

    But nowadays, CIB networks can undermine the online space by repeatedly circulating messages that support a particular political interest and make it appear more widely shared than it is.

    And indeed, Vučić dominated the space on X and Facebook while the streets suggested otherwise.

    Read more

    Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll

    ]]>         Middlemen raked in billions of forints from Szijjártó’s Covid ventilator deals (Day 170 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/245711/middlemen-raked-in-billions-of-forints-from-szijjartos-covid-ventilator-deals-day-170-of-the-tisza-government/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:39:37 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245711 Hungarian prime minister befriends Czech counterpart Andrej Babiš while EU Commission and Council presidents Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa come to Budapest to celebrate the anniversary of the 1956 Revolution. ]]> More than a year ago, we launched our Hungary Briefing series, a weekly roundup of news from Hungary’s election campaign. The series continues, covering developments following the historic election and the actions of the Tisza government. This week’s topics:

    • The great Covid scam.
    • Former minister kept €25m in cash at home.
    • Closer ties with the Czech Republic.
    • Mixed results for the revolution’s anniversary commemorations.
    • Poll of the week: Tisza supporters lean liberal.

    The Covid scam

    Shortly after the Covid pandemic broke out in the spring of 2020, the Orbán government purchased almost 17,000 ventilators for 300 billion forints, equivalent to €860m at the exchange rate at the time.

    The machines were imported from China through various foreign intermediary companies. Viktor Orbán later said he had consulted mathematicians about how many ventilators Hungarian hospitals would need under the worst-case scenarios.

    They did not save lives

    Yet most of these machines never reached hospitals — and even if they had, they would not have been able to save lives. György Velkey, a state secretary in the Tisza government, wrote on Facebook, citing a 2020 military medical report, that only around half the machines had been classified as usable. The remaining half were either recommended for hospital use “only with serious compromises” or not recommended at all.

    Many of the machines are still gathering dust in warehouses.

    In 2023, former opposition MP Tímea Szabó showed what 12,000 unopened ventilators looked like in a warehouse in Gödöllő. The Hungarian state was paying 80 million forints, or approximately €200,000, a month just to store them.

    The middlemen cashed in

    And that is not all: the companies contracted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, headed by Péter Szijjártó, made a fortune from procuring the machines. Further details emerged after a raid on Tuesday(27 Ocober) by the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV).

    NAV detained three people, while an international arrest warrant was issued for the suspected leader of the criminal organisation. He is believed to be in Indonesia — and the news outlet 444 discovered that he operates a Ferris wheel in Bali.

    “Acting as part of a criminal organisation, the perpetrators who sold ventilators and medical masks to state bodies during the Covid-19 pandemic laundered more than three billion forints [approximately €7.5m] in profits, then deprived the state treasury of 660 million forints [approximately €1.7m] by evading tax,” NAV said.

    Footage recorded during the raid also reveals the luxury in which the suspects lived. As 444 notes, this may be only part of the story: other companies may also have been involved in the overpriced procurement deals. There is no word yet on whether the authorities are investigating any responsibility Szijjártó or Orbán may bear in the case.

    Presented as a success story

    The Orbán government tried to portray its pandemic response as a success story. In early 2025, it released a short film entitled How We Defeated the Covid Pandemic.

    Read more

    How extending Covid funds could be a key bargaining chip in EU budget fight

    Almost 49,000 people died in the pandemic in Hungary. According to international statistics, the country had the world’s fifth-highest death toll per million inhabitants.

    Former minister kept €25m in cash

    Hungarian authorities accuse Miklós Seszták, who served as development minister in the Orbán government between 2014 and 2018 and was re-elected to parliament this year, of accepting at least 11 billion forints, or approximately €27.5m, in bribes. On Wednesday (28 October), a court extended his pre-trial detention until the end of January.

    Its ruling revealed an important detail in the corruption case.

    During a search of Seszták’s home, investigators found an empty safe in which, according to the court, he had kept nine billion forints in cash — approximately €25m at the current exchange rate. He had arranged for the money to be hidden before he was questioned.

    As 444 calculated, that amount of cash would be extremely heavy: 450,000 banknotes with a face value of 20,000 forints could weigh 450kg.

    They did not know where to put the cash

    Commenting on the news, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi wrote that “in principle, this is entirely consistent with what several colleagues and I have long been hearing from sources with inside knowledge of the NER” — the political and economic system built around Orbán.

    According to Panyi, as early as the 2010s, one of the major problems facing people within the Orbán regime was how to store the vast amounts of cash generated by corruption. They could not deposit it in a bank without having to explain where it came from.

The question that will outlast the result is not who wins, but whether the winner is willing to say no to prime minister Rumen Radev.

    Radev spent nine years as president with Iliana Yotova as his vice-president.

    He resigned in January to enter party politics and the office passed to her automatically; she has never been elected to it.

    In April his Progressive Bulgaria coalition won 131 of parliament’s 240 seats, and it now backs her for a full term.

    In the first round she led Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, by fewer than three points. Turnout was 22 percent – the lowest on record.

    Read more

    [Interview] Bulgaria’s presidential election becomes a test of Rumen Radev’s grip on power

    The presidency’s power to say no

    An elected majority is legitimate; so is cooperation between government and president. The constitutional risk begins where cooperation becomes an expectation of loyalty. An institution can keep every legal power and still lose the will to use it against political allies.

    In Bulgaria those powers are modest but real.

    A president can send a law back, and parliament must debate and vote on it again in public. Radev’s majority can pass it a second time with 121 votes, but the second vote is on the record.

    A president can also refer a law to the Constitutional Court, commands the armed forces, and chairs the Consultative Council on National Security, where the state assesses threats to itself.

    None of this can stop a determined majority. All of it can force one to explain itself.

    Black Sea test came late

    Meanwhile, since the start of October, at least seven merchant ships have been hit by drones off the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts.

    Both governments suspect Russian involvement, although responsibility has not been conclusively established; more than two dozen sailors are dead or missing.

    Read more

    EU unlikely to send Black Sea naval mission to repel Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian grain ships, despite Kallas’ support

    The first strike in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone came on 6 October. By then Yotova had been president for nine months without once convening the security council. She convened it the next day, after the opposition demanded it in public.

    It condemned the attacks and endorsed better surveillance and counter-drone defences: the right decisions, taken after the pressure rather than before the risk.

    Her legislative record points the same way.

    Yotova knows how to use a veto: in February she returned an Electoral Code amendment that limited the number of polling stations in countries outside the EU, calling it unconstitutional.

    That parliament was not Radev’s. Against his majority the test came in July, with the 2026 budget. The reformist and conservative opposition, the Podkrepa trade union and a petition with more than 32,000 signatures asked her to return it. Y

    Yotova argued that a veto would deepen financial uncertainty and promulgated the budget. On 20 October, the Constitutional Court upheld the budget as a whole but struck down two provisions inserted through it. The challenge came from MPs and the ombudsman, not the presidency.

    Nato dispute

    One policy dispute between the candidates concerns Article 4 of the Nato treaty. Gyurov wants Bulgaria to request consultations with its allies. Yotova initially opposed invoking it, but later acknowledged that coordinated action with other allies remained an option.

    Radev ruled it out on the day of the first attack because the ships were struck outside Bulgarian territorial waters. Yet Article 4 does not require an attack on national territory; it applies whenever an ally considers its security threatened. Whether to invoke it is a political choice. Territorial eligibility is not the obstacle.

    The test of an independent presidency is not whether it agrees with the government on Article 4. It is whether it would demand a public account of what the state knew, what it did and what went wrong, and publish it even when it embarrasses the people who put it in office.

    The European Commission’s rule-of-law report in July noted that most of Bulgaria’s regulators had their mandates renewed without becoming any more independent. A renewed mandate is not proof of oversight. Neither is a convened council.

    The same test applies to Gyurov, an independent nominated by the reformist parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, who told CNN on 23 October that Bulgaria needs a counterweight to its government. A counterweight that only ever pushes against Radev is a faction, not an institution. A president elected by the opposition would have to challenge the opposition too.

    EU leaders condemned the attacks at their 15–16 October summit, and Nato has announced additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones.

    Both are entitled to a clear account of what Bulgaria saw, when it acted and what failed.

    Brussels, for its part, should judge institutional independence not by formal procedures, but by whether those institutions are willing to challenge those in power. The question to ask is simpler: when did it last contradict the government?

    Radev has a mandate to govern. The next president will hold a separate one: to question, to return, to refer and, when necessary, to refuse.

    Europe does not need a Bulgaria that pretends it never makes mistakes. It needs one that can find and correct them before its sailors, its neighbours and its allies pay for them.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/29/binance-crypto-exchange-hack</link>
      <description><p>Cryptocurrency exchange scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far, and says it will cover losses</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/30/crypto-heist-binance-who-did-it-are-investments-safe">Q&amp;A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/30/tell-us-have-you-been-affected-by-the-binance-hack">Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/30/uk-house-price-growth-crypto-industry-6bn-binance-hack-eurozone-france-gdp-latest-news-updates">Business live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p>The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by an industry-record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.</p><p>Binance has scrambled to freeze the affected assets, with about $3bn located so far. The company gave no update on the other $3.3bn as Binance’s co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/29/binance-crypto-exchange-hack">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Government corruption a top issue for US midterm voters, exclusive poll finds</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/30/government-corruption-us-midterm-poll</link>
      <description><p>Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday Americans</p><p>Government corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.</p><p>Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem, according to the survey.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/30/government-corruption-us-midterm-poll">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>The ex-presidential candidate tells Democrats to prosecute corruption and bring real change for the working class</p><p>A corporate plutocracy. A broken healthcare system.       <description><p>Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom</p><p>The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.</p><p>Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/29/delta-uber-ftc-pricing</link>
      <description><p>Regulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or service </p><p>The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is demanding some of the US’s biggest airlines, ride-share companies and retailers divulge how they are using algorithms and loyalty programs to target customers and drivers with different prices and wages.</p><p>Nine companies – Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart – were named in the inquiry, which comes after <a href="https://www.consumerreports.org/money/questionable-business-practices/instacart-ai-pricing-experiment-inflating-grocery-bills-a1142182490/">investigations</a> and lawsuits alleging consumers are charged different prices based on their buying histories and drivers <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/uber-drivers-claim-personal-data-used-to-manipulate-fares/">paid different fares</a> based on their personal histories.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/29/delta-uber-ftc-pricing">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/european-central-bank-chief-christine-lagarde-to-step-down-nine-months-early</link>
      <description><p>Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairs</p><p>Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.</p><p>Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/european-central-bank-chief-christine-lagarde-to-step-down-nine-months-early">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/28/fed-interest-rates-midterms</link>

      <title>The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires</link>
      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1011492107">proposed that</a> rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.</p><p>They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis</p><ul><li><p>Follow our <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/live/2026/oct/28/inflation-abs-labor-anthony-albanese-parliament-greens-david-shoebridge-one-nation-ntwnfb">Australian politics live blog</a> for latest updates</p></li><li><p>Get our <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/email-newsletters?CMP=cvau_sfl">daily political email</a>, <a href="https://app.adjust.com/w4u7jx3">free app</a> or <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/series/full-story?CMP=cvau_sfl">daily news podcast</a></p></li></ul><p>Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with a key gauge that strips out volatile prices also elevated, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week.</p><p>The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred measure of consumer prices, called underlying inflation, came in at an annual 3.6% to September.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/28/inflation-rate-australia-2026-number-data-consumer-price-index-cpi-release">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 30 Oct 2026 14:46:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Unions warn of further strike date in November if talks fail to yield new public pay deal]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/30/unions-warn-of-further-strike-date-in-november-if-no-deal-is-agreed-at-pay-talks/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/30/unions-warn-of-further-strike-date-in-november-if-no-deal-is-agreed-at-pay-talks/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:36:14 +0000A second national public services strike will be scheduled for Wednesday November 11th if no deal between the Government and trade unions on a new pay agreement is reached before or over the weekend.

In a message sent to public service unions on Friday, Kevin Callinan, general secretary of Fórsa and chair of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions’ public services committee, said the 19 unions it encompasses should meet on Monday to get an update on the talks and, if no agreement has been reached by then, to discuss taking further action.

In the message, he says the strike, which would again close the State’s schools and severely affect health, local authority and other services, would allow for demonstrations in Dublin and other big urban centres by more than 300,000 staff affected.

The move comes as talks continue between the two sides at the Workplace Relations Commission.

In a separate update to the 100,000 members of his own union, Callinan said the talks had been “lengthy and at times heated” and that while a deal remains possible “the Government has yet to put forward a credible offer, and it remains to be seen whether it will do so”.

He said it remains unclear if an agreement can be reached over the coming days.

Referencing the prospect of another one day stoppage, Callinan told members: “If we fail to reach an acceptable agreement by the weekend, it leaves unions with no alternative but to escalate the action.”

Senior officials from the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform as well as the four union leaders participating in the main negotiations arrived for the latest session at 10am on Friday.

There had been some optimism that an agreement could be reached if the two sides pushed through the night on Thursday, but in the end it was concluded that their respective conditions were not close enough to continue past about 10pm.

Sources close to the process, which has been ongoing for two weeks, still believe a deal is possible, even probable, over the next 24 hours. However, several of the key areas under discussion have yet to be concluded despite significant progress having been made.

Arrangements for a second national strike on November 11th have to be put in place early next week as seven days’ notice must be given.

In health, the required notice period is generally three weeks but the unions believe they are covered by the original notice of action served last month and the continuing work-to-rule.

The potential for another national stoppage may be viewed by the Government side as an attempt by the unions to leverage their power as the talks enter what one source described as their “crunch period”.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Nasdaq tumbles at open as Amazon, Intel add to AI spending woes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/30/nasdaq-tumbles-at-open-as-amazon-intel-add-to-ai-spending-woes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/30/nasdaq-tumbles-at-open-as-amazon-intel-add-to-ai-spending-woes/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:46:03 +0000The ‌Nasdaq opened at its ‌lowest level in more than two ​months on Friday, after Amazon’s aggressive artificial intelligence (AI) spending ​plan and Intel’s ⁠cash burn warning intensified ‌investor concerns ‌about ​escalating costs of AI ⁠infrastructure ​buildout and the ​return timeline.

The Dow ‌Jones Industrial Average ​rose 0.08 per cent. The S&P 500 rose 1.16 per cent, while ⁠the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.26 per cent.

Before trading even began, the big names in tech were all plummeting down the index.

Intel ‌tumbled 25 per cent in premarket trading on a bleak outlook, deepening a broader retreat in technology stocks as investors grew increasingly ‌wary of weakening PC demand and the vast spending required to build out AI infrastructure.

The forecast underscores the challenges facing ​chief executive Lip-Bu Tan’s turnaround effort, with Intel still grappling with a prolonged PC market slump even as it invests heavily in AI and manufacturing expansion.

Semiconductor stocks, including Advanced Micro Devices, Arm Holdings, Qualcomm, Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron, fell between 2 per cent and 9 per cent ​in premarket trading.

“The market is in a sell first, ask questions later mood right now, and Intel’s warning has given ⁠investors an easy excuse to take some money off the table across chip stocks,” said Matt ‌Britzman, ‌senior ​equity analyst, Hargreaves Lansdown.

The sell-off spread to server makers, reflecting investor caution towards companies tied to the semiconductor and AI infrastructure supply chain.

Shares of server makers ⁠Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Super ​Micro Computer fell between 6 per cent and 12 per cent in ​pre-market trading. – Reuters

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[Are extended warranties worth the money?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/30/are-extended-warranties-worth-the-money/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/30/are-extended-warranties-worth-the-money/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:51:21 +0000You’ve just bought yourself a new washing machine with so many different spin cycles you could choose a different one for every day of the month. Or maybe it’s a fancy new TV, with a 4K display, an AI assistant and a screen that covers half your sittingroom wall.

The shop assistant scans your item and next comes the inevitable question: “Would you like to buy another three years of cover for your new [insert product]?”

The washing machine has just set you back €650 and the TV a cool €1,399. The money you’ve spent should ensure both are still in decent working condition several years later.

But what if something were to go wrong? Perhaps the extra couple of hundred euro for enhanced insurance would be worth the investment?

The nightmare scenario of the washing machine or TV going kaput a week after the warranty expires flashes through your mind.

But what would you really be paying for, and how much better is it than the protection you already have under consumer law?

The first thing to know is you have very robust rights as a consumer in Ireland, and indeed throughout the EU.

If a fault emerges with a product within 30 days of buying or receiving it, you are entitled to cancel your purchase. Under your “short-term right to terminate a sales contract”, you can opt for a repair or, if you prefer, a replacement.

Your legal position is particularly strong during the first year of ownership, but your rights in relation to faulty goods can extend for up to six years if the product – such as a washing machine or TV – could reasonably be expected to last that long.

It is important to note that your contract is with the retailer, not the manufacturer, and it is the retailer’s responsibility to remedy faulty products.

Consumer law does not, however, cover ordinary wear and tear, or products that were misused or accidentally damaged.

Serious problems, if they arise, still have to be dealt with. For the first year, the law is generally on your side and assumes the fault was already there when you bought the product.

After that, the onus shifts to you to show the problem was inherent in the product rather than caused by wear and tear, misuse or accidental damage.

And this is where extended warranties or appliance insurance might begin to offer something extra.

There are, broadly speaking, two types of cover you’re likely to be offered.

Extended warranties usually offer additional repair or replacement cover, sometimes extending beyond the manufacturer’s guarantee.

Insurance policies, on the other hand, offer wider protection and that can include things such as accidental damage. Naturally, this can be more expensive, and protections can vary hugely so pay close attention to the details.

For something more robust such as a washing machine, you might decide breakdown cover is enough if accidental damage is less of a concern.

Our €1,399 4K TV, though, can easily be knocked from its stand, or the screen could get a whack from a sweeping brush or two kids playing catch. This is where an insurance policy might be an option.

Retailer Currys offers “tech insurance” for TVs in different price categories, ranging from €200 to more than €3,000.

For our €1,399 TV the cost would be €180 for a three-year package, and €280 for five years. Monthly payment plans are also on offer if you prefer to spread the cost.

For that, Currys promises to fix the TV within 14 working days and if they don’t meet that deadline, or they’re unable to repair the item, they’ll offer a replacement.

Their website says there is no limit to repairs and if the TV suffers repeated problems, you can seek a new one.

Similar plans are in place for laptops, tablets, cameras, home-cinema set-ups and satellite equipment.

Harvey Norman’s Product Care offers similar cover in two-, three- and four-year plans. It includes things such as “food spoilage cover”, which pays for up to €500 worth of food if a fridge or freezer fails.

Similarly, it offers cover of up to €150 for laundry expenses if your washer or dryer is out of service for more than 10 days after you notify it of the fault.

Are these plans worth it? That’s probably a question only you can answer.

As with any type of insurance, some people are risk-averse and will draw comfort from knowing an unexpected fault or accident will be dealt with. Others might decide they are better off keeping the money in their pocket and taking on the risk themselves.

The price of the appliance matters, but so, too, does your ability to absorb the loss if forced to buy a new item.

Replacing a TV that cost less than €500 might be irritating but manageable, particularly with second-hand options available. Having to find €1,399 – or north of €2,000 for a super high-spec telly – is a completely different story.

You might also want to consider your own track record.

Are you very careful, or are you living in a busy household with children and pets where accidents are more likely to happen?

And before buying any extra protection, make sure to check what it covers.

Currys’ policy, for example, covers sudden accidental damage and mechanical or electrical breakdown. It does not, understandably, extend to cosmetic damage, misuse, neglect or damage during severe weather.

Ultimately, the decision whether to buy will be a combination of your risk appetite, how much the product costs and whether your household budget could absorb the sudden shock of a full replacement.
