]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Breaking down the bill: where does the money you pay for electricity actually go?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/breaking-down-the-bill-where-does-the-money-you-pay-for-electricity-actually-go/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/breaking-down-the-bill-where-does-the-money-you-pay-for-electricity-actually-go/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Irish people pay more for their power than most other Europeans. But no matter how you weigh it, the actual electricity accounts for a far smaller share of your electricity bill than you think.

All in, electricity here costs families around 40 cent a kilowatt hour, the unit in which it sells to domestic customers. That is roughly the energy needed for a typical load in your washing machine. The EU average is 29 cent. Germany is the nearest to us at more than 38 cent.

But that 40 cent ends up going in multiple directions. Energy think-tank Trifecta Ireland estimates that costs other than the actual electricity consume 55 per cent of what Irish homes and industries pay every year.

Those costs range from the money required to get that electricity from power plants to customers to incentives for businesses to build those generators in the first place.

Consultancy Aurora Energy Research calculates that of the €1,583 that an average urban household paid in the 12 months to October 2025, €597, or 32 per cent, covered the price of the electricity, with two-thirds of the total going on associated costs.

Aurora bases its assessment on a home consuming 4,200 kilowatt hours a year, which is what the industry says a typical household uses over 12 months. Those figures pre-date price increases of between 8 and 11 per cent, depending on the supplier, which began to bite this summer. They will have pushed that €1,583 average past €1,700.

Surges in the price of natural gas, which is used to generate half of our electricity, was responsible for those hikes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine has pushed gas prices higher as supply tightens.

But the other costs are creeping up also. Last year, regulators approved plans by national grid operator, Eirgrid, and ESB Networks to spend up to €18.9 billion between now and 2030 on improving the systems that get electricity from power plants to customers. That increase could add up to €1.75 a month to household bills.

More recently, industry watchdog, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilties (CRU), confirmed that emergency generators installed as a backstop against short-term electricity shortages would remain in place up to February 2029. Customers will pay €229 million for this. That scheme will have cost those bill payers €1.44 billion by 2029.

Liberalised

Over the last quarter of a century, the Republic has liberalised its electricity market, merged it with Northern Ireland’s, introduced increasing amounts of wind and solar as it shoulders a large part of meeting the State’s climate targets and shut ageing power plants, all while expecting it to meet increasing demand from economic and population growth.

The policies and strategies meant to deal with all of that have left the State with an increasingly complex system, says Conall Bolger, chief executive of Trifecta Ireland.

“The system we have now wasn’t planned, it sort of evolved rather than being planned, and it’s become unwieldy,” he explains. “We tried to make it do something that it wasn’t built to do.”

Part of the problem is the national grid itself. Stephanie Unsworth, Aurora analyst and author of the consultancy’s recent report on affordability, points out it was built “back in the sixties and seventies”. “Everything then ran on oil and gas,” she says.

At that time, it was a question of connecting power plants, that ran constantly, to where there was demand. It was not designed to link remotely located wind farms than run intermittently to distant cities and towns.

Alongside this, University College Cork academic Paul Deane told the launch of Trifecta’s report this month, electricity is distributed to customers through a large network of copper wire strung on timber poles. This is a legacy issue, according to Deane, who noted that there is enough copper wire in the Irish system to run four times around the globe.

The upshot is that national grid operator Eirgrid is often forced to tell power plants not to supply electricity, even when it is available, as bottlenecks in the system mean it cannot reach customers.

Wind farms, including those in Northern Ireland, are worst hit. This is a double whammy for consumers as alternative suppliers must switch on or increase output even though their power may be more expensive than that of the company unable to operate. Customers pay for this through something called “imperfection charges”, which the CRU says came to €790 million over the last 12 months.

Eirgrid says it is using new technologies to increase its use of renewables and to store power. Following initial trials, it has begun using “dynamic line rating” which allows more effective use of the grid. The State company points out that a planned €18.9 billion investment, approved last year, will tackle many of the problems.

Customers also face a bill of €550 million to support gas-fired power stations when they are on standby to back up renewables, but not supplying electricity, and so not earning money. These “capacity payments” are an incentive to encourage developers to build these plants in the first place.

Unsworth notes that many of the extra charges are the price customers pay as they foot the bill for integrating renewables into a system designed for fossil fuel. He does agree that the plans by Eirgrid and ESB Networks to invest in the system over the next four years should help.

Trifecta, funded by the family of industry veteran, Eddie O’Connor, focuses on providing affordable, secure and clean electricity. Its report, What Can Move the Needle on Bills Before 2030?, assesses ways of cutting costs to the consumer in the shorter term.

Its CEO, Bolger believes that we need to step back and look at all elements of the system in their entirety. He argues that the needs of consumers got lost while government and State agencies increasingly added complexity to the system. But cutting bills in the absence of a major overhaul remains challenging.

Deane told the Trifecta launch that, in some cases, cutting €10 from bills could require spending of €100 million on the system.

Trifecta proposes 17 smaller measures that it says should add up to greater savings. They focus on more efficient use of the grid that takes more account of customers’ needs. More electrification of heat and transport should help, the organisation says. This is because many of the “non-electric” costs are fixed, so spreading the burden across more customers cuts individual burdens.

Unsworth agrees that more electrification is part of the solution, but with a different emphasis. Instead of focusing on “crazy” renewables targets, she advocates building power plants to meet demand while incentivising electrification, which would still allow the Republic to meet its climate targets. Aurora calculates that taking this alternative approach would cost consumers 20 per cent less by 2035 than if we continue with our current mix of strategies.

How your electricity bill adds up

Generation: This is the cost of producing the electricity we use. It is generated by burning natural gas, or by wind and solar farms, along with contributions from other sources, including imports and hydroelectric power.

This amounts to a lower portion of bills than most people assume. A recent report by Trifecta Ireland calculates it at 45 per cent across the board. A breakdown of charges for a typical home by consultancy Aurora Energy Research shows it came to €597 out of a total annual average bill of €1,583, or around 38 per cent, in the 12 months to October 2025.

Network: This is the cost of getting electricity from power plants to homes and businesses. Basically, it goes through two stages. The national grid takes the electricity direct from power stations, and the distribution network takes it from the national grid and transmits it to customers’ premises. This cost is itemised as a standing charge on electricity bills, generally coming to around one-third of the total.

Aurora calculates that this cost its typical home €443 last year. Energy industry overseer, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is currently reviewing how these costs are allocated across electricity customers.

Public Service Obligation (PSO): This pays for schemes that guarantee prices for power produced by renewable power plants. Two account for most of this charge. The first is the Renewable Energy Feed-in Tariff, which guarantees older onshore wind farms €72 or €75 per mega-watt hour for their electricity. If the market price falls below that figure, customers make up the difference through the PSO levy. If the market price is higher, the renewable power companies keep any surplus.

The second is the Renewable Energy Support Scheme, which pays wind and solar farms prices agreed at various auctions. Customers make up the difference if the market price falls short but get a rebate if the market price tops the guaranteed amounts.

The CRU recently set the PSO at €6.12 for each household in total for the coming 12 months, a sharp reduction on what they paid between October 2025 and this month. The charge is itemised on domestic bills.

Imperfection charge: This is one of two big items not set out on your bill. It is the cost of bottlenecks on the national grid that prevent it from transmitting electricity generated in one place to where the customers are located. In this situation, national grid operator, Eirgrid, instructs the power plant to reduce output. The market compensates the supplier for this. At the same time, the grid may have to instruct other companies whose electricity can reach those customers to step in. Those companies are also paid for their power.

Industry organisations have been highlighting this problem for a while. Most often, it hits wind farms in the west or other locations far from the greater Dublin area, where demand for electricity is greatest.

One significant bottleneck is the continued absence of a planned high-capacity power line between counties Meath and Tyrone. This prevents wind farms and other suppliers in the North from getting their electricity to the South. All electricity customers share this cost. Overall, CRU approved €790.24 million for imperfection charges over the last 12 months. Aurora calculates that it added €67 to individual bills last year.

Capacity payments: These are incentives to suppliers to build gas-fired power plants. Wind and solar power are not available all the time so our system needs gas plants that can be switched on or off quickly to back them up.

Admittedly, the US had a bear market in 2022 without a recession. It was relatively short and shallow, making it an excellent buying opportunity. Portfolio managers at top hedge funds in London often have non-compete clauses requiring them to sit out of the market for as long as 18 months to two years before they can join a rival, while an analyst might have to wait a year.

Citadel, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, successfully lobbied last year for legislation in its home state of Florida to allow non-compete agreements lasting up to four years.

While highly paid fund managers often appreciate the chance to take time off and travel or spend time with their family, such lengthy non-compete periods can make top performers less attractive to other employers, limiting the opportunities to seek out better and higher-paid roles.

Workers are usually unpaid during the period in the UK at least, and their skills may fall behind those of their peers, particularly in fast-growing sectors.

Burnham said the clauses “stunt innovation and trap workers” because these “prevent the best really being energised and bringing that dynamism to the economy”.

The UK’s tech sector has criticised non-competes for making it harder for them to hire. More than 20 start-up founders recently wrote to Burnham to ask him to “ban lengthy post-termination restrictions”.

Alan Chang, founder of the $5 billion (€4.5 billion) energy start-up Fuse and co-signatory of the letter, says his company’s progress has been slowed because of the delay in hiring caused by non-competes and other employment restrictions.

Chang says his chief technology officer, Greg Wilk, was originally subject to an 18-month non-compete clause. This was reduced to six months of gardening leave – which differs from a non-compete period as the person remains a paid employee – before he joined Fuse because he was changing industry.

But Chang says the wait was still too long. “Let’s say [Wilk joined in] one month rather than six ... I think our share price [would] be worth a lot more ... And rather than us being in two markets, we [would be] in four markets.”

Jacomo Corbo, founder of $2.4 billion start-up PhysicsX, says he is currently negotiating a 15-month non-compete agreement to hire an employee, an experience that has made him consider recruiting more in the US where restrictions are less prevalent.

“In Europe ... on the whole, you find that these long notice periods and gardening leave are very prevalent,” he says. “The lack of liquidity means you end up refocusing a lot of that hiring on US hires.”

Edward Hughes, who had a three-month gardening leave after leaving Google DeepMind to co-found London-based artificial intelligence (AI) start-up Inherent, which co-ordinated the letter to Burnham, says restrictions risk leaving fast-growing companies a “generation” behind their Californian competitors.

People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers. What makes a great one?

“It’s a little bit like you buy your great striker and the Premier League season starts and all the other teams are playing and ... your striker is sat on the bench instead,” he says.

Burnham did not give full details of the reform he is planning, but said the aim was to free up hiring for innovative companies, including in the AI sector.

The UK is an outlier in having relatively few constraints on employers’ use of non-competes, although they must show a clause is reasonable to enforce it in court. Elsewhere, efforts to curb the use of non-competes have had mixed results: a long-standing ban in California has not stopped some employers writing the clauses into contracts, even though these cannot be upheld by law.

Spain can fine employers that use them wrongly; France requires companies to continue paying staff part of their salary during non-compete periods. Australia plans to limit their use to high earners.

Shivchand Jhinku, an employment partner at law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer in Sydney, says an unintended consequence of restricting non-competes in Australia may be to benefit bigger companies that have more ways to compete for staff, such as the ability to pay more and offer better perks.

“Smaller businesses and start-ups, which often rely on non-competes as the only practical mechanism to protect their investment in key employees, may be less able to compete for talent,” he says.

Lawyers predict the curbing of non-competes in the UK may lead employers to use other tools to protect their intellectual property and delay the departure of employees. In their letter to Burnham, the tech founders also argued for the restriction of “extended notice periods and gardening leave”.

Another downside to non-competes is that disputes over the terms often result in costly and stressful legal contests.

Citadel, for example, this year launched a lawsuit against its former portfolio manager Daniel Shatz, who left to join UK rival Marshall Wace.

London-based quant trader Couture was sued by Jump Trading in 2023 after telling the Chicago-headquartered firm he was joining rival Verition Fund Management. He had already served a 12-month notice period after resigning, but his contract also included an extra non-compete period of up to a year, which Jump insisted he respected.

The 41-year-old reached a confidential settlement with Jump that allowed him to continue working at Verition, but only after he had spent almost £1 million (€1.2 million) on lawyers to defend himself in court. “It was a huge stress,” he says. “Anxiety for the whole family went through the roof.”

Couture still believes non-compete clauses can play a valuable role, but thinks they should have a time limit placed on them by law. “The fact that UK law does not express up to what point they are reasonable makes it a matter to be determined by a judge, where individuals have to face deep-pocketed companies,” he says.

“I think non-competes are perfectly fine, up to a year ... After a certain point, whatever remains in people’s memory is skill and experience and not precise enough to amount to confidential information.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

This tool was created in 2022 to prevent fragmentation in the euro zone bond markets, but it comes with conditions and has never been used so far. Tweaking the TPI conditionality to make France eligible may be politically toxic in other countries.

Ideally, verbal intervention would suffice. The question is whether proverbial constructive ambiguity can work in France’s case – a communication strategy the ECB has long relied on to signal willingness to intervene while preserving flexibility.

These trade-offs come at a time when heads of state and government will need to agree on a large package of nominations for the bank’s executive board in coming months.

Bank president Christine Lagarde has now announced her departure. This will allow governments to decide on all executive board replacements before the French election. The changeover will inevitably raise questions about the direction of policy under the next leadership.

In that context, Klaas Knot’s self-described approach of “principled pragmatism” looks particularly relevant. The former president of the Dutch central bank and a contender for the top job argued that the European Central Bank would need to keep acting decisively to preserve monetary transmission in the future without becoming a substitute for fiscal or political action.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, the former governor of the Bank of Spain, is another strong candidate with the credentials and experience to run the ECB.

Both have been in charge during previous economic and fiscal crises. Whoever gets the job will need to strike the right balance between principles and pragmatism in the next one. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

His 14 years on the ​ECB’s rate-setting governing council can be characterised by two distinct periods: increasingly open hostility to then ECB president Mario Draghi’s stimulus measures and perfect harmony with Christine Lagarde, who succeeded Draghi in 2019.

Considered a pragmatic policy hawk, Knot joined in a period of upheaval as the euro zone suffered a series of financial and debt crises that threatened to rip it apart. He had initially expressed reservations about Draghi’s “whatever it takes” pledge to preserve the euro ​but came around, unlike his German colleague, and eventually called it a pivotal moment.

However, he came into open conflict with Draghi in the following years when the ECB unleashed a massive stimulus effort to rekindle inflation during ⁠a decade it undershot the 2 per cent target.

The criticism was initially reserved for private discussion but came fully into the open in late 2019 when Draghi pushed through a ‌new ‌stimulus ​scheme, despite the opposition of a third of policymakers, an unprecedented rift for a collegial body that usually decides matters unanimously.

Under Lagarde, Knot came back into the fold, even if he was an early advocate for tighter policy in response to the historic 2022 inflation ⁠surge.

From 2021, Knot also served as chairman of the Financial Stability Board, ​a global body responsible for monitoring financial stress and devising policy recommendations.

Pablo Hernandez de Cos: Considered a moderate policy dove, de Cos (55) has been heading the Bank for International Settlements, the global umbrella group of central banks, since 2025.

He also served one six-year term as ‌the Bank of Spain governor from 2018 to 2024, a tumultuous ​period that started with ultra-low inflation, followed by the pandemic and a historic interest rate hike cycle to tame runaway inflation.

De Cos also served as the Bank of ⁠Spain’s chief economist, taking the rare step of moving from staff to ⁠a policymaking role, a reflection of his success ​in elevating the profile of research at the bank.

Colleagues describe him as a pragmatic economist, possibly even a swing voter, who always brings a wealth of evidence and data to back his points, avoids dogma, and is known for being a team player.

Earlier this year when some of the world’s top central bankers openly backed Jerome Powell, then the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, against political pressures, de Cos was said to be a key coordinator of the process.

De Cos also gained an international profile when he served as the chairman of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, the most important global forum dedicated to monitoring and harmonising banking rules.

Joachim Nagel: The head of the Bundesbank since 2022, Nagel (60) has fundamentally altered Germany’s relationship with the ECB.

While his predecessor, Jens Weidmann, was in open ‌conflict with Mario Draghi’s ECB for years, ⁠Nagel has toned down the rhetoric and rejoined the fold, even if he remains a moderate hawk.

Colleagues say Nagel, also a PhD economist, clearly expresses his red lines but can compromise on other issues and he is not known to have opposed any key policy decision during his tenure, a big change ‌from the hostility of his predecessors.

He has also supported the creation of the European Deposit Insurance Scheme, a project Berlin has long opposed, fearing that the German taxpayer would have to pay for the financial irresponsibility ​of others.

Nagel has fiercely defended the ECB’s independence, pushed back on political criticism of the bank, and recently argued that some ​of the proposals of the far-right AfD party were self-defeating and could scare away investors.

A member of Germany’s Social Democratic Party, Nagel previously held senior roles at the Bank for International Settlements and the KfW Group.

Although politically in the context of the ECB, Germany and its Bundesbank is a pivotal player, of the three, he is seen as the least likely winner. – Reuters

]]>The Washington Post<![CDATA[Farewell to ‘aeroplane mode’: Flying loses its status as the last internet black hole]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/29/easyjet-internet-in-flight-wifi-starlink-elon-musk-aer-lingus-ryanair-short-haul/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/29/easyjet-internet-in-flight-wifi-starlink-elon-musk-aer-lingus-ryanair-short-haul/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:00:01 +0000Back in 1997, an episode of Seinfeld introduced the world to a unique approach to long-haul travel. David Puddy, played by Patrick Warburton, the boyfriend of Elaine Benes (Julia Louis Dreyfus), decided he would just stare at the back of the seat in front of him for the whole flight.

No television, no movies, no headphones, no books, not even a nap. He was going to sit upright, eyes-open, and stare straight ahead for what was meant to be a very long trip.

Although this was wild even to contemplate almost three decades ago, it isn’t viewed in quite so simple a light today.

Is airplane mode really just a setting on your phone? That’s the philosophical question that has moved to the foreground in recent days.

On Monday, EasyJet announced it would install Elon Musk’s Starlink internet across its fleet during the first half of next year, with roll-out completed in 2028.

Aer Lingus already offers Starlink on its transatlantic flights with plans eventually to extend it to European flights.

The jump from wifi of any standard on a plane being impressive to high speed being the norm has come about rather quickly.

Aer Lingus has begun its free in-flight wifi. Bang goes a rare oasis of tranquillity

Airline wifi has, for most of the 20 years it has been available, been somewhat of a joke. Typically it has been considered slow, expensive and definitely not reliable. Yet that’s far too broad an assumption.

Even back in 2019, I recall an Air France trip back from China where I was overjoyed that the quality was good enough to watch Dublin beat Mayo in the All Ireland semi-final. Still, that was definitely the exception, not the norm.

With Starlink’s satellites orbiting around 550 kilometres above ground, they are shortening the journey that was previously needed for signals to reach planes.

With the Aer Lingus transatlantic fleet as an example, the speeds promised exceed 500Mbps. When it comes to connectivity quality, that’s absolutely stellar stuff.

With EasyJet, well it’s essentially the same service only focused squarely on short-haul. That is rather new as plane wifi has thus far almost exclusively been targeted at long-haul by carriers in Europe.

It is a huge step for wifi to go from being an available extra service towards it being expected on all journeys in the not-too-distant future. It’s heavenly to some of you and no doubt a nightmare to others.

That’s because the last acceptable excuse for being unreachable is disappearing. An aeroplane is one of the few places where you have outright immunity from checking emails or messages. That’s from everyone in your life, although, for most of us, the first thing to come to mind is work.

“I’m 35,000 feet above ground embracing the engineering miracle of mechanised flight” won’t necessarily be considered a good enough excuse any more.

Yet the benefits are substantial. That game I watched back in 2019 was exactly what I needed. I’d just spent a couple of hours in Hong Kong airport interviewing protesters and it was emotionally moving and draining. Being able to decompress by watching Con O’Callaghan and Paul Mannion run riot was the best possible thing for me at the time.

There’s also the matter of parents travelling with children. As a child-free person, I was surprised by how popular YouTube premium is with parents. Several have told me it’s the last subscription they would consider giving up. For them it is a reliable way to make sure their kids have access to their favourite videos while travelling. Getting that access on planes only adds to that support for parents.

Connectivity doesn’t have to be about productivity. An employer who expects you to stay connected with work when you’re on a plane probably has a lot more wrong with them than just that.

Smart bosses know that rest matters. Even remotely intelligent ones know that flights are tiring in and of themselves, so it’s not like you’re getting a net productivity benefit by irking staff while they’re strapped to a seat high above the ground.

Retaining the ability to disconnect should not come down to whether there actually is a connection.

Not everyone agrees with the move to connect and that includes airlines. For the foreseeable future, Ryanair is not going to embrace Starlink.

Michael O’Leary has said plainly that he felt the cost/benefit analysis just did not compute for his airline.

Still, where it is an option, it’s important that people remember that an option means they have a choice.

Warburton has jokingly apologised for his character kicking off the unfortunately named “rawdogging” trend. This, however, is not a choice of extremes. Those who feel the need to stare at the back of a chair still can, while, in the near future, those who want optimal connectivity will have it.

Everything in between is also on the table and a matter of free will. You can just watch a movie on the screen, follow the map or listen to something downloaded on your phone. You’ll simply have more choices as to what you can do.

If your concern is not being able to disconnect, then you really shouldn’t blame the airline. Instead, ask who or what in your work or personal life makes you feel the need to be always on. Then address that deeper issue, which is beyond Aer Lingus’ or EasyJet’s pay grade.

The reader has availed of the tax-free Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP), now paid at €400 a month, for accommodating a Ukrainian family in her holiday home.

There were 16,300 people hosting 38,300 Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection as of October 11th, according to the Department of Justice.

Occupants under the ARP scheme are regarded as licensees rather than tenants, says Shane O’Dea, a senior solicitor at Amorys Solicitors.

“Hosting under the ARP is not a formal landlord/tenant relationship, so they have no landlord/tenant rights at the moment,” says O’Dea.

If no additional payments were made to the landlord by their ARP occupant, then no tenancy existed under the Residential Tenancies Act, says the Residential Tenancies Board.

The reader says she would be happy for her Ukrainian friends to continue living in her holiday home after the ARP scheme ends in March. She would plan to charge a modest rent but this would constitute a tenancy, which, according to RTB rules, would begin from the date that rent became payable by a tenant.

New private rental sector tenancy rules mean the reader would be restricted in how she could end that tenancy.

Tenancies created since March 1st this year are subject to rolling six-year tenancies of minimum duration.

A landlord can end a new tenancy in the first six months for any reason, says the RTB. But after six months, they must have specific reasons to do so.

“If a tenant has been renting a property for six months and they haven’t received a valid notice of termination, a landlord can only end the tenancy during the six years on very limited grounds,” says O’Dea.

The specific conditions are linked to how many tenancies the landlord has.

All landlords can end a tenancy during the six years if the tenant doesn’t meet their obligations, such as paying rent.

Small landlords – those with between with one and three tenancies – can avail of additional grounds for ending a tenancy. These are if they need to sell due to financial hardship or if they or a close family member, such as a spouse, civil partner, parent, parent-in-law or child, wants to use the property as a primary residence.

Using the property as a holiday home is not one of the reasons under which a tenancy can be ended.

He said a £10 billion black hole in the UK defence investment plan would be filled by extra 1 per cent per year spending cuts by other departments.

Britain is a nation increasingly convinced it must prepare for a future war with Russia, for which its rickety armed forces are unprepared. The debate is usually pitched in Westminster as an imperative to cut welfare spending to fund new military equipment.

Healey kicked this can further down the road until his next spending review, which is unlikely to be before next autumn. He said the UK government wanted time to first consider reports it had commissioned on youth unemployment and disability payments, which are due next month.

In her two budget since Labour’s election win in 2024, Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves backloaded departmental spending cuts, with the worst of the pain not due to land until nearer the end of the current UK parliament in 2028 and 2029.

Healey left Reeves’ plan untouched in his budget speech on Wednesday, which further fed the early election rumours among Westminster observers unconvinced he would really be prepared to implement austerity in the run-up to a scheduled election.

Meanwhile, he persevered with a swathe of baffling, small measures, such as reduced tariffs on certain canned vegetable goods.

“The prime minister came to power promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism and instead we got 4p off gherkins,” said Badenoch.

]]>House of Commons<![CDATA[Fed holds US interest rates ahead of midterm elections]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/fed-holds-us-interest-rates-ahead-of-midterm-elections/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/fed-holds-us-interest-rates-ahead-of-midterm-elections/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:53:52 +0000The US Federal Reserve has kept interest rates on hold days before midterm elections even as the surge in fuel prices sparked by the Iran war reverberates across the world’s biggest economy.

Most of the rate-setters on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee of the US’s central bank on Wednesday said they needed “more information” before deciding what to do “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to their 2 per cent goal, after holding the federal funds rate within a range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent.

The decision to hold came after a 10-to-two vote, with two members favouring a quarter point rise in rates.

The committee acknowledged economic activity was “expanding at a strong pace”, signalling mounting concern the economy is in danger of overheating from the AI boom.

The decision, which was widely expected by Wall Street, comes despite fresh evidence that inflation is accelerating and spreading across the economy.

While the Fed says it does not take politics into account in its decisions, some economists said rate-setters would be reluctant to raise rates with the critical election that will determine control of Congress looming next Tuesday.

Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz and inflation in the US rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.

The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress.

Before Wednesday’s announcement, senior Fed officials hinted they were willing to wait and see what happened to price pressures before raising interest rates again.

The central bank increased rates for the first time in more than three years in September in an attempt to contain inflation. The decision defied Donald Trump’s attempts to press the central bank into drastically lowering rates.

Wall Street stocks slightly pared gains after the decision which shifts the probability of a rate hike to the Fed’s next monetary policy meeting in December.

“The Fed didn’t throw any curveballs,” said ​Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group in Omaha. “Likely ⁠the pressure will be to do one more hike in December, as inflation is ‌still ‌potentially ​an issue.”

Financial markets ⁠are pricing in an 86 per cent likelihood ⁠of a 25-basis-point rate ​hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, up from 78.3 per cent on Tuesday, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026 / Reuters / Guardian service

]]>Saul Loeb<![CDATA[Brothers at loggerheads over decision to appoint director to building firm they own ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/brothers-at-loggerheads-over-decision-to-appoint-director-to-building-firm-they-own/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/brothers-at-loggerheads-over-decision-to-appoint-director-to-building-firm-they-own/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:42:09 +0000A dispute has broken out between the brothers who own the successful Glenman Corporation building company over the appointment of a third director to their two-man board, the High Court heard.

The two sides are already due in court in December for hearing of a shareholder oppression case.

Judge Brian Cregan on Wednesday granted an interim injunction to Micheál Conneally, one of the two owner-directors of Glenman, preventing his brother and majority shareholder, Albert Conneally, from appointing a third director.

The application was made by counsel Gary McCarthy on an ex parte, or one side only represented, basis.

Glenman Corporation Ltd was set up 33 years ago by the Conneallys, who built up a thriving building, contracting and civil engineering business in Ireland and Britain.

They initially worked on upgrading pubs, restaurants and churches, before developing housing projects and becoming one of the leading builders of schools in the 1990s and 2000s.

Albert holds 60 per cent of the shares and Micheál the other 40 per cent.

Differences arose between the brothers, and in 2023 Micheál brought shareholder oppression proceedings against his brother. Albert sought to have the case heard “in camera”, or in private, but this was rejected by the High Court in April 2024.

A hearing of the dispute began in October last year after mediation failed to produce a resolution. The hearing was adjourned to facilitate further mediation efforts, Micheál’s solicitor Peter Boyle said in an affidavit. These also failed to produce a resolution, and the case is now listed for hearing at the start of December.

Last Friday, Boyle said, Micheál received an email stating Albert wished to appoint a third director, David Issott, to the board. Under Section 194 of the Companies Act 2014, a majority shareholder can appoint a new director without having to convene a general meeting, the court heard.

Correspondence followed, and in one letter from Albert’s lawyers to Micheál’s lawyer, the suggestion that the appointment of Issott was an attempt to usurp Micheál’s rights was rejected.

“The prolonged inability to agree on matters of management, to put matters neutrally, has produced a structural impasse which is detrimental to the company,” the letter said.

It also said Micheál should “not be permitted to hold the company to ransom” during the proceedings by making a claim that the appointment of an independent and external director is somehow inappropriate.

Boyle said no opportunity had been given to Micheál to consider Issott’s nomination.

He also said Micheál had overseen the growth of UK business to the extent that it is now the only profitable arm. Albert, he said, had meanwhile overseen the demise of the Irish arm.

According to figures produced on behalf of Albert, turnover in the UK for 2025 was €32 million, while in Ireland it was €2.7 million.

Boyle said it was intolerable that Albert should continue to act in this manner, especially with the hearing of the oppression proceedings just four weeks away. The existing deadlock is likely to be addressed by that hearing, he said.

The judge said he was satisfied to grant the interim injunction restraining Albert and the company from proceeding to appoint a third director.

He said the case could return next week.

]]>Iryna Melnyk<![CDATA[PTSB attacks Axis in court over effort to disrupt Bawag’s €1.6bn takeover ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/ptsb-share-price-was-of-utmost-importance-in-ministers-decision-on-16bn-takeover-offer/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/ptsb-share-price-was-of-utmost-importance-in-ministers-decision-on-16bn-takeover-offer/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:29:52 +0000PTSB has in court attacked the approach of advisory group Axis, cofounded by former Bank of Scotland Ireland chief Mark Duffy, to try to disrupt the lender’s takeover by Austrian banking group Bawag.

Axis Capital is “nowhere near a position to make an offer” to rival the €1.6 billion offer from Bawag, the High Court has heard.

There was “no certainty’ that the firm’s offer of €3.20 a share, higher than Bawag’s €2.97 a share proposal, “can actually be made”, Kelley Smith, counsel for PTSB, told Judge Michael Quinn on the second day of legal proceedings to approve the proposed acquisition of the bank.

“Axis is a €100 micro-company,” she said, pointing to financial accounts for the year ended May 2026 that “showed €100 on its balance sheet”. Axis was cofounded by Duffy and Lutz Hartmann, a Frankfurt-based international lawyer.

“The company has no track record in M&A [mergers and acquisitions] transactions and, we would say, lacks the resources to actually implement an offer. We now see that, actually, it is not an offerer but it intends to be some form of arranger,” Smith said.

“Axis have waxed and waned on what they’d like the court to do,” Smith continued, and “the court should discourage such approaches” that “seek to disrupt” proceedings.

Duffy asked for “one minute” of Judge Quinn’s time.

“What has struck me since yesterday, particularly over the past few minutes, is that everyone is talking about the Bawag offer. There is at least one other offer – that comes from Axis,” he said.

The offer “is not speculative” and is supported by “one of the most esteemed investment banks in the world. We have a credible route to funding”, Duffy said. “And we are credible people, we have done many transactions in Ireland and globally”.

“We want access to information and limited time to consider this information,” he said in reference to the announcement last week that Axis Capital would seek an adjournment of up to six weeks.

Earlier in proceedings, the court heard from Des Carville, head of the shareholding and financial advisory division at the Department of Finance, on what led to Minister for Finance Simon Harris using the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in PTSB to support Bawag’s offer.

Share price was “of utmost importance”, Carville said, as it was “our primary driver to maximise value for the Irish taxpayer” when considering the State’s exit of its stake in the Irish banking sector.

Piotr Skoczylas, the managing director of Scotchstone Capital, which owns a less than 1 per cent stake in PTSB and is one of three shareholders objecting to the deal, asked Carville a series of questions on what formed “part of the Minister’s overall assessment to support the Bawag’s recommended cash offer”.

Small PTSB shareholders ‘paying for Minister’s exit’ in €1.6bn takeover deal, court hears

These included commercial matters, such as the bank’s branch footprint, and the Minister’s views of Bawag’s approach to the deal – for example, meeting trade union representatives.

Carville said these issues were not the Minister’s primary considerations. “Price was the first and foremost consideration,” he said. “Other points are secondary points; they flow from the transaction.

“It was a consequence of the offer by Bawag [that] the proposed transaction afforded the Minister the opportunity to exit his last remaining stake” in the bank, Carville said. “It was not a major part” of the Minister’s decision, he added, but “a small part of it”.

“We have resisted pressure from banks to sell shares” at times when the price on offer was not optimal, he said, and “it has taken us 13 years” to get to a point of satisfaction with a PTSB takeover bid.

“If price was not important to us, I would not have spent 13 years of my time working on this,” he said.

]]><![CDATA[Healey keeps bond markets onside in first UK budget ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/uk-to-hike-taxes-on-banks-to-pay-for-energy-bill-cuts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/uk-to-hike-taxes-on-banks-to-pay-for-energy-bill-cuts/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:05:35 +0000British prime minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government succeeded in keeping skittish bond markets onside with its first budget, which raised taxes on banks and gambling to pay for cost of living measures such as cuts to energy bills.

After creeping up for months, Britain’s cost of borrowing on international markets fell slightly after the budget on Wednesday, the first delivered by John Healey who has replaced Rachel Reeves as chancellor of the exchequer.

As he rose to his feet in the house of commons, Healey insisted his inaugural budget would be “built on fiscal discipline”, echoing language previously used by Reeves.

He mostly delayed big decisions around cutting Britain’s ballooning welfare bill and funding investment in its decrepit armed forces. Healey did, however, increase Britain’s “fiscal headroom” buffer to £15 billion (€17.7 billion), which reassured bond traders who had been worried about rises in inflation and spending against a backdrop of weak growth in Britain.

Healey also said he would stick to his predecessor’s “fiscal rules” that have proved popular with City traders, including eschewing borrowing for day-to-day spending and ensuring UK debt falls when measured against the size of the economy.

“[The point of] today was to really avoid a Liz Truss ‌moment,” said Mike Bell, head of market strategy at BlueBay Asset Management.

“[Healey] has been successful. The headroom came in line with expectations. It doesn’t give gilt investors anything to panic about in the near term, which was the goal.”

The Office of Budget Responsibility (OBR), Britain’s statutory fiscal watchdog, predicted UK economic growth would fall to 1 per cent next year from 1.2 per cent this year, before rising to 1.8 per cent by 2029, on the back of the budget. It predicted growth would slip to 1.6 per cent within a further two years, however, as the “drag” effect of higher taxes weighed.

Since former prime minister Keir Starmer was ousted over the summer, Healey and Burnham have focused on modest cost-of-living measures to give people “breathing space”, while delaying big fiscal decisions.

The flagship measure of Healey’s budget was a £2.6 billion scheme to lodge a £100 cash payment directly into the bank accounts of 20 million households, ostensibly to help pay rising fuel bills. The cash will be paid into all bank accounts that pay the first four bands of UK council tax, which excludes those with so-called “trophy homes”.

Healey also extended VAT cuts on electricity and a freeze on fuel duty.

The measures will be paid for by others including a rise in a levy on bank profits. The levy, which is paid on profits above a certain threshold and is due in addition to normal corporation tax, will be doubled to 6 per cent for 15 months from January, raising £1.2 billion.

Healey also announced higher taxes on gaming machines, savers and rental income, while suggesting that multiannual cuts in the budgets of all other government departments would be used to fund a £10 billion black hole in British military spending.

“We know who we are, we know where we are going,” said Healey of Britain’s economy.

Opposition Tories, meanwhile, criticised the budget as “not bold enough”.

]]>House of Commons/UK Parliament<![CDATA[Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump.

The irony is that it won’t be the racist rhetoric, his role in the Capitol riots, or the self-sabotaging tariffs that remove the Teflon, but something entirely more mundane: gas prices.

They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war. The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.

Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.

The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.

More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.

The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

What are the US midterms? A visual guide

This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.

Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.

“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.

To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.

But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.

But Trump can’t help himself.

US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. It had been expected to fall to the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent by the end of 2025, paving the way for growth-affirming interest rate cuts.

But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.

This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]>Jacquelyn Martin<![CDATA[More than time: watchmaker Nomadic secures top cross-border award]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/more-than-time-watchmaker-nomadic-secures-top-cross-border-award/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/more-than-time-watchmaker-nomadic-secures-top-cross-border-award/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:13:28 +0000Peter McAuley learned that watches are about more than telling the time when he lost a watch left to him by a much-loved uncle deep beneath the waters of a Fermanagh lake during a day’s kayaking.

On Wednesday, Nomadic Watches, the Belfast watchmaker run by McAuley and his wife, Jane, won the €150,000 gold award in this year’s North-South Business Cooperation Awards run by Greek-Cypriot billionaire, Stelios Haji-Ioannou.

“I was always interested in watches. My dad had always got nice watches, and my uncle. When my uncle died, he left me a nice Tag Heuer, and I would wear it for everything.

“I wore it on a kayaking trip in County Fermanagh. When I got back, the watch had fallen off my wrist in the water, and it was gone forever. That was when I realised that watches are about more than telling the time,” says McAuley.

Beginning with models costing £1,000 and upwards, each Nomadic watch has “a little piece of either Belfast history or Irish history weaved into them”, says McAuley, speaking at the awards ceremony in Castle Leslie in Glaslough, Co. Monaghan.

“A lot of the watches, which have a Swiss-made mechanical movement, have a yellow second hand that represents the Harland & Wolff cranes in the shipyards in Belfast,” he goes on

Founded in 2021, Nomadic next month opens a shop in Dublin city centre in partnership with Weirs: “We met them at an awards ceremony last year, and told them everything about what we were doing.

“They loved it. They put our watches into their store on Grafton Street last Christmas and they performed exceptionally well, and from there, the partnership’s just grown and grown,” McAuley goes on.

In its Belfast store, the public see watchmakers at work behind a glass wall: “Just last weekend, we had a guy from California who flew in specifically just to come and see our watchmaking.”

The award is “a tremendous milestone” for the five-year-old Belfast watchmaker and helping to expand plans to create a brand rooted in storytelling, design and the industrial spirit of Belfast”, McAuley went on

Now in its second year, the cross-Border awards, which offer €500,000 in prizes to budding businesses, attracted “excellent” applications, Haji-Ioannou, who is deeply involved in every element of the competition, told The Irish Times.

Paying tribute to Nomadic, Haji-Ioannou said: “How difficult is that to wake up one morning and say, ‘I’m going to start watchmaking, I’m going to compete with the Swiss who been doing it for 200, 300 years.’ It’s incredible.”

The Greek-Cypriot began to offer cross-border awards in Cyprus: “We haven’t, touch wood, had any objections here which was always my worry at the beginning, that people would say, ‘Why are you doing this? You’re Greek, you shouldn’t be here.’ ”

The best way to ensure good cross-border relationships in Ireland, but also everywhere else, is where people do business with each other every day, learning to understand each other, he went on.

The decision to present the awards in Castle Leslie was deliberate, he said, since “this part of the world, especially in Monaghan, is the best way to understand the peace dividend from the Good Friday Agreement”.

Stephen Dallas, the chief executive of Co-operation Ireland, a partner on the awards, said this year’s winners “are a powerful example of what can be achieved when entrepreneurs see opportunity across the whole island”.

The two silver awards worth €100,000 each went to Marteye, a technology company that enables farmers interact with 120 marts across Ireland and Britain, and Langtry Lane and Dae Ice Cream.

The €25,000 bronze awards went to Trident Project Engineering; ADHD Now and Duality Healthcare, Rep-Tec; X-Lite Beverages, Chimac and StreatSchool, which supports entrepreneurs building mobile food businesses.

]]><![CDATA[Glenisk co-owner Vincent Cleary on rebuilding the company after it burned to the ground]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/podcasts/inside-business/glenisk-co-owner-vincent-cleary-on-rebuilding-the-company-after-it-burned-to-the-ground/https://www.irishtimes.com/podcasts/inside-business/glenisk-co-owner-vincent-cleary-on-rebuilding-the-company-after-it-burned-to-the-ground/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:13:43 +0000In the first half of this week’s Inside Business, host Ciarán Hancock will be talking to Vincent Cleary, co-owner of Offaly-based organic yoghurt maker Glenisk.

Vincent is co-owner of the business with his brother Brian, a company that was set up in 1995 by their father Jack.

Glenisk had a near death experience in 2021 when its manufacturing plant, warehouse and offices burned to the ground. Vincent explains how it has bounced back from that devastating moment.

Plus, a couple of years ago, streaming giant Netflix looked untouchable. It had emerged from the pandemic with record subscriber numbers, was cracking down on password sharing and introducing advertising on its platform.

But things have changed. This year the share price has tanked, and it is now laying off staff and rethinking its strategy.

Ian Curran of The Irish Times has been covering the story and joined Ciarán on the line to outline what has gone wrong for Netflix over the past 12 months.

Produced by John Casey with JJ Vernon on sound.

The Left, a junior partner in Poland’s ruling coalition, has proposed a bill to abolish the Church Fund, which provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy. It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund.

However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted.

📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️

Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️

✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr

— Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found.

In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025

An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained.

Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law.

“I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”.

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.

A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.

Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries.

Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.

She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.

Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.

Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.

Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.

Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany, while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.

Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026

Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań.

Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average.

Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20.

 

Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.”

Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia.

“I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports.

“We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”.

Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry.

He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition.

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion.

The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections.

— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026

As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges.

Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read.

In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges.

Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hanukkah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”.

 

Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups.

Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison.

In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month.

 

The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher.

Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”.

For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term.

In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”.

Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%.

If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition.

Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand.

In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023

The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.

Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026

In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition.

However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:32:30 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 ‘Tech carnage’: AI stocks plunge as investors spooked by gloomy earnings https://www.cityam.com/tech-carnage-ai-stocks-plunge-as-investors-spooked-by-gloomy-earnings/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:55:26 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473328

The global tech sell-off deepened on Friday after a string of heavily disappointing earnings revived fears over the pace and scale of AI spending.

The Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 2.2 per cent at the open on Friday after a $500bn rout in Google-owner Alphabet’s shares on Thursday. Roughly $3 trillion has been wiped off the tech-heavy index since its peak on 6 October.

Chipmaker Intel’s gloomy forecast of lower than expected revenue driven by a persistent PC market slump and supply chain issues, had a chilling effect, as shares plunged more than 28 per cent on market open.

Investors were also spooked by Amazon’s results following market close on Thursday, as the e-commerce giant recorded weaker than expected sales and gave a lacklustre outlook for its retail operation.

Amazon’s shares tumbled 2.7 per cent, which analysts said showed investors are expecting a “bleak Christmas period ahead”.

Neil Wilson, UK investor strategist at Saxo, said the sell-off showed “tech carnage as October wraps up”, as all stocks with exposure to AI went into “meltdown”.

Fellow Magnificent Seven companies, Microsoft and Nvidia also slipped 1.9 per cent and 3.5 per cent respectively.

Shadows cast over Asia

The sell of on Thursday seeped into Asia, with Deutsche Bank analyst Jim Reid saying the US rout “exacerbated” losses across the region.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent, with losses led by Fujitsu which plummeted 16.2 per cent to 3,622 yen (£17.1), and electronics firm Ividen which declined 15.2 per cent.

OpenAI investor Soft Bank slipped six per cent, taking its losses to 48 per cent from its June peak.

South Korea’s blue-chip index fell 3.4 per cent, as its heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell three per cent and 1.5 per cent respectively.

FTSE rides high

Despite Amsterdam-listed chipmaker ASML falling 5.7 per cent, Europe’s wide-spread lack of exposure to technology leaders allowed it to dodge the AI fallout.

In particular, the FTSE 100 was hailed an “island of tranquility” by Wilson, after the index climbed 0.3 per cent in early trading. Since January, the index has gained eight per cent.

Wilson said: “The FTSE 100 looks like an island of tranquillity amid all the carnage in tech. It’s often been the outperformer when the global market leaders- tech- turns south. Valuations remain compelling and earnings growth is good.

 The FTSE 100 remains a safe bet, fundamentally anchored by old-economy sectors that deliver tangible returns. It might not be flashy but it’s reliable.”

But London Stock Exchange’s few tech stocks on the AIM market were not immune to the global problem. Raspberry Pi tumbled 4.6 per cent 555p, while Computacenter shed 3.4 per cent.
