TWO-TIME Breeders’ Cup winner and current Godolphin work rider, Kieren Fallon, believes that Notable Speech is a “dream ride” in the Breeders’ Cup Mile, but won’t be rooting for the Godolphin horse on Saturday night.

Speaking to Bets And Horses ahead of the 2026 Breeders’ Cup from Keeneland, Fallon said: “The fast ground will suit a lot of the European horses, especially Notable Speech. He’s in great form. I’d say he’s the soundest horse Charlie [Appleby] has ever trained, in every way. He’s never had problems with his wind, he doesn’t bleed, I don’t even think he’s ever taken a false step. Royal Ascot is the only blip in his copybook and going uphill seems to be the only thing he doesn’t like.

“He does so well in Canada because it is a beautiful, flat turf track. It’s perfectly level and it’s always good ground. Canada isn’t as tough a place to go as the rest of North America and I don’t know why more trainers don’t send horses there. The prize money is brilliant, they look after you really well and the tracks are always in great condition.

“Notable Speech obviously has no problem running anywhere – he travels for fun. He’s a dream ride for anyone because you can put him where you want. He has a good draw in the Breeders’ Cup Mile and he should get a nice run into the race.

“That said, I don’t want him to win. I want Lake Forest to win because my son Cieren rides him.

“I don’t think Lake Forest is far behind Notable Speech. He was behind him at York and on paper he isn’t as good, but the gap is smaller than some people think. You need a lot of luck in running round there and you won’t be given an inch at the Breeders’ Cup. If Notable Speech gets the run, he wins. However, if there’s any blips, I think Lake Forest will be there to pounce.”

It will take a high-class performance to derail Notable Speech’s bid to become the first back-to-back winner of the Mile since Wise Dan 13 years ago, and Fallon puts the five-year-old level with Modern Games as the best Godolphin milers of all-time.

“He’d have to be up there with Modern Games,” said Fallon. “Modern Games was a beautiful, compact, genuine miler and Notable Speech is the same. I couldn’t find anything between them, and it’d be a very close race between the two of them.”

Notable Speech will be accompanied at Keeneland by stablemate El Cordobes, who is set to line up in the Breeders’ Cup Turf, and Fallon believes he can outrun his odds.

“At 25/1 now, I think El Cordobes is overpriced,” Fallon said. “He went to Belmont a couple of weeks ago and he was heavy when he went over there. His work rider is a really good judge and he expects him to come on a lot for that run. He might not be good enough to beat the likes of Diamond Necklace, but he’s certainly up to running a big race.”

Both the Grade One Breeders’ Cup Mile (8.20pm) and Grade One Breeders’ Cup Turf (9.26pm) will be live on ITV on Saturday evening.

The Breeders’ Cup action from Keeneland begins on Friday, with five races live on ITV from 6.55pm, while on Saturday a card of nine Grade Ones begins at 5.10pm.

The High Court has upheld the media watchdog Ofcom’s powers to harvest retroactive safety data from tech giants. The High Court has upheld the media watchdog Ofcom’s powers to harvest retroactive safety data from tech giants.

In February, Ofcom issued formal information notices to major tech platforms, including Meta, Tiktok, and X, requiring them to share detailed data on content and user exposure to harmful material under the Online Safety Act.

Meta, Tiktok, and X jointly challenged Ofcom with a judicial review case at London’s High Court.

The court rolled the platforms’ legal challenges into one case, in which they challenged the notices on several legal grounds, largely arguing the watchdog unlawfully circumvented the act’s specific transparency framework.

The Online Safety Act was designed to tackle the risks to users, including children, of encountering harmful content online. It provided Ofcom with extensive powers, including the ability to fine non-compliant platforms up to £18m or 10 per cent of their qualifying global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

On Friday, the High Court refused permission for the tech platforms’ claims, in the first judicial review proceedings to test Ofcom’s new powers.

Lord Justice Singh and Justice Collins Rice found that Ofcom’s information-gathering powers served a distinct regulatory purpose and that the individual notices did not legally trigger the threshold for an overarching impact assessment.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “We welcome the High Court’s decision to dismiss the challenges brought by Meta, X and Tiktok against our efforts to gather information from them.

“Under the Online Safety Act, Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that’s been unaccountable for more than 20 years.

“Gathering information from companies is fundamental to our ability to do our job of assessing compliance with their duties, and we’ll continue to use our powers to create a safer life online for people in the UK,” they added.

A Tiktok spokesperson said: “We are considering this judgment.”

“We’re disappointed with the court’s decision, but we and others across industry pursued this challenge because information-gathering of this scale goes beyond what is necessary or proportionate. We remain committed to working with Ofcom and are reviewing the judgement in full,” a Meta spokesperson said.

X was also approached for comment.

Earlier this month, Meta appeared in the High Court, challenging how Ofcom calculates fees and fines under the UK’s online safety law, arguing the methods are disproportionate and unlawful. While in August, Tiktok lost in the Court of Appeal to overturn a £12.7m fine from the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) for illegally processing the data of over 1.4m children under the age of 13.

Law firm Gibson Dunn is set to snap up a team of almost 40 private funds lawyers in London from Weil, Gotshal, and Manges, as the storied US law firm prepares to wind down after nearly a century. Gibson Dunn, the law firm which led on the UK side of Space X’s $75bn stock market [...]]]>

Law firm Gibson Dunn is set to snap up a team of almost 40 private funds lawyers in London from Weil, Gotshal, and Manges, as the storied US law firm prepares to wind down after nearly a century.

Gibson Dunn, the law firm which led on the UK side of Space X’s $75bn stock market listing, had been in ongoing talks to acquire Weil’s entire private funds team for over a year, according to a source with knowledge on the matter, prior to the recent collapse of Weil.

The move comes after US legal powerhouse Weil told partners on Wednesday the firm should be wound down after 95-years.

The wind down is expected to be at the centre of a partnership vote in the coming days. If given the go ahead, it would put thousands of jobs at risk, including 50 partners, 200 solicitors, and roughly 120 business services staff at its London office, which has operated since 1996.

Gibson Dunn’s move to poach the team, which is one of the largest lateral moves for a law firm in London in recent years, comes as part of a longer term plan to build out its private funds practice in London as part of a long-term investment plan, the source said.

The team set to join Gibson Dunn includes ten partners, led by co-heads James Bromley and James Sargent. Los-Angles founded Gibson Dunn’s London office boasts 265 lawyers, and has over 2,200 lawyers globally.

Weil’s downfall came after an exodus of its top talent globally over the past year and the departure of some of its top-billing partners. The length of talks between Gibson Dunn and Weil’s funds group suggest the team had been weighing an exit long before the company’s ultimate decision to dissolve.

Gibson Dunn declined to comment. Weil was contacted for comment.

Weil’s ‘Titanic situation’ rocks London lawyers

On Thursday, a former partner at Weil told City AM the unravelling of Weil is “a Titanic situation.”

“This is probably the worst succession planning in legal history,” the former partner said. “I’m shocked about this…It’s crazy to me this is the path they chose.”

The City’s legal professional body, the City of London Law Society, confirmed on Thursday it is on standby to support Weil Gotshal and Manges trainees as they are forced to find new jobs.

]]> 2473228Rosie Harris-Davison Rosie Harris-Davison Fiat Multiplina is a four-seater reported to cost £14k https://www.cityam.com/fiat-multiplina-is-a-four-seater-reported-to-cost-14k/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:24:23 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2472866

Fiat has taken the much-loved 1956 Multipla, squeezed it down to about the size of an original 500 and made it electric, and if the price lands where the early estimates point, it could be the cheapest way to get four people across town without waiting for a bus. Fiat’s new Multiplina is a four-seat [...]]]>

Fiat has taken the much-loved 1956 Multipla, squeezed it down to about the size of an original 500 and made it electric, and if the price lands where the early estimates point, it could be the cheapest way to get four people across town without waiting for a bus.

Fiat’s new Multiplina is a four-seat electric car about three metres long, with a claimed top speed of 55mph, and it’s due on sale in 2028. Fiat hasn’t put a price on it yet, but Auto Express reckons it’ll come in at around £14,000, which would slot it between the £8,995 Topolino and the £18,995 Fiat 500 Hybrid. The catch is that it’s classed as a heavy quadricycle, which comes with much lighter rules than a normal car, and Fiat hasn’t said whether it’ll build one with the steering wheel on the right for British buyers.

We’ll admit our first reaction was a grin, because it looks like something you’d see parked outside a café in Turin in 1960, but the more we read about it the more it looks like a clever bit of thinking from a brand that knows small cars better than almost anyone.

Fiat Multiplina price and specs

The £14,000 figure is an estimate, so treat it as a guide. Italy’s Il Sole 24 Ore thinks it could sit closer to Topolino money, with options taking it to about €12,000, so the real number could be lower still, and either way it would be one of the cheapest four-seaters you could buy new.

Underneath, it uses a stretched version of the Topolino’s platform with a bigger battery (Fiat hasn’t said how big). That’s what lets it move up a class to the heavy quadricycle rules, which cap top speed at the 55mph Fiat claims, against the Topolino’s 28mph. Fiat hasn’t given a range, but it should comfortably beat the 46 miles the Topolino manages, and the concept has two doors, four seats and little windows that hinge outwards.

What is the Fiat Multiplina based on?

The name and the shape come from the Fiat 600 Multipla of 1956, a tiny people carrier with a flat, upright nose that could seat six in about 3.5 metres and stayed in production until 1967, with around 240,000 sold, according to Autocar. The Multiplina borrows the vertical front, the round headlights and the bubble-shaped profile, and it was first shown as the Quattrolino earlier this year (it was renamed, Auto Express says, because Audi owns the rights to “quattro”).

Most people in Britain will think of a different Multipla, the bug-eyed 1998 MPV with three seats across the front that became a bit of a national joke. Fiat says this one draws on the 1950s original, so don’t expect any of that car’s odd styling, though we suspect the shared name will do Fiat no harm at all when it comes to getting people talking.

Fiat boss Olivier François calls it “the missing link” between the Topolino and a normal city car, speaking to CAR magazine, and that’s a fair way to describe it.

Is the Fiat Multiplina coming to the UK?

Nothing is confirmed yet. What we do know is that Fiat only opened UK orders for the Topolino this summer, at £8,995, which suggests it thinks there’s a market here for tiny electric cars, though it has also said some Topolino versions won’t come to Britain, so there are no guarantees.

Is the Fiat Multiplina a good city car?

Regit’s motoring reporter Tim Barnes-Clay hasn’t driven it (it’s still a concept), but he’s already sold on the idea.

​“I get excited about driving anything wacky and wonderful, and the Multiplina is both,” he says. “Fiat has always been at its best when it builds small cars with a sense of humour, and if this arrives at around £14,000 I’d happily have one as a London runabout, as long as Fiat can show me it’ll look after the people inside.”

For London, it makes a lot of sense on paper. You get four seats in something short enough to squeeze into the gaps that most hatchbacks drive straight past, and 55mph is plenty when so much of inner London is now limited to 20mph. Where we’d be less keen is on a fast dual carriageway with lorries thundering past, because a three-metre quadricycle is going to feel very small out there.

The bigger worry is safety. Quadricycles aren’t held to the same crash-test rules as normal cars, and Fiat hasn’t said anything yet about what protection the Multiplina will offer, which is the first thing we’d want to know before putting three passengers in it.

It also has a rival from France. Citroën’s revived 2CV is due around 2028 for similar money, and if that turns up as a full car you can take on the motorway, it’ll be the obvious one to compare this with.

What we like

●       Four seats in a car about three metres long

●       An expected price around £14,000, well under a Fiat 500 Hybrid

●       A top speed of 55mph, so it can keep up on faster town roads

●       Styling that will make people smile

What worries us

●       No UK plans or right-hand drive confirmed yet

●       Quadricycle crash-test rules are much lighter than a normal car’s

●       No range figure yet, and it’s two years away

Verdict

If Fiat brings the Multiplina to Britain at close to £14,000, it’ll be the most charming way we can think of to move four people around a city, and for a London household that wants a second car for the school run and the shops, we can see the appeal. But it’s a quadricycle, and until we know how it protects the people inside, and whether Citroën’s 2CV arrives as a proper car for similar money, we’d hold off getting excited and keep an eye on both.

If the Multiplina has you wondering whether the family’s second car is still earning its parking space, get a free valuation with Regit and see what it’s worth before 2028 comes round.

]]> 2472866Jodie Chay-O'Neil Jodie Chay-O'Neil ​2026 BMW i7 review: is it worth £109,320? https://www.cityam.com/2026-bmw-i7-review-is-it-worth-109320/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:23:32 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2472444

BMW’s facelifted i7 now goes up to 452 miles between charges and rides with all the calm you’d hope for at £109,320. Tim Barnes-Clay took it to Epsom Downs and calls it a heart-over-head choice, though the company car tax bill gives the head a surprisingly strong argument too. The BMW i7 is a seriously [...]]]>

BMW’s facelifted i7 now goes up to 452 miles between charges and rides with all the calm you’d hope for at £109,320. Tim Barnes-Clay took it to Epsom Downs and calls it a heart-over-head choice, though the company car tax bill gives the head a surprisingly strong argument too.

The BMW i7 is a seriously luxurious electric saloon, but with the i7 50 xDrive M Sport costing £109,320, it needs to be more than a comfortable way to travel. The 2026 facelift brings a bigger battery, faster charging and a redesigned digital cockpit, lifting the range to as much as 452 miles (up from 388), while the ride remains exceptionally refined.

For me it’s worth the money because it makes you feel special behind the wheel, and as a BMW lover I’d call it a heart-over-head choice that says you’ve made it. The head gets a say too, though, because at 4% benefit-in-kind a higher-rate taxpayer pays about £1,750 a year to run one as a company car.

BMW i7 price and specs


The 2026 facelift is what BMW calls its most extensive model update ever, with new battery cells, faster charging, a new face and the iDrive X dashboard.

The fully electric i7 is the one to have if you want limousine comfort without a petrol or diesel engine. Prices start at £104,230 for the i7 50 xDrive, rising to £109,320 for the M Sport version I tested. The i7 60 xDrive (from £120,335) and the range-topping M70 xDrive (£164,420) sit higher in the line-up, with the M70 aimed at buyers who want a lot more performance.

Even the entry-level car comes generously equipped. Standard features include a 17.9-inch central touchscreen, a 14.6-inch screen for the front passenger, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, satellite navigation, heated seats, adaptive air suspension and four-zone climate control.

M Sport adds a more assertive body kit, darker exterior trim, an M steering wheel, upgraded brakes and 20-inch alloy wheels. Move further up the range and the equipment can include doors that open and close automatically, rear window blinds, a panoramic glass roof with illuminated details and rear-seat entertainment.

The options list can get expensive very quickly. My test car didn’t have any options fitted, but I can see the temptation, because once you’ve spent north of £100,000 another couple of thousand pounds doesn’t feel like much. Personally I think less is more, so I wouldn’t add anything.

BMW i7 design and dashboard

The i7 is enormous, and it looks it. The facelift brings a slimmer, more upright kidney grille, new vertical headlight units, a reshaped bonnet and longer tail-lights. I love the way it looks and think it’s an improvement on the last model, and if you want to make an impression in the company car park, its dignified presence will do the job.

The rear is more restrained, with longer tail-lights and a clean tailgate, but the overall effect is still imposing, which is part of the appeal if you want your luxury saloon to stand apart from more conventional executive cars.

Inside, BMW has created a cabin that feels suitably special. The materials and build quality impress, the seats give the sort of comfort you’d expect from a flagship, and there’s plenty of adjustment in the driving position, so longer journeys feel less demanding.

The updated infotainment system is responsive, with sharp graphics and a more modern interface. BMW’s Panoramic Vision display runs along the base of the windscreen from pillar to pillar, alongside a 3D head-up display, so you don’t have to rely on the central touchscreen for everything.

BMW’s decision to remove the iDrive rotary controller, which the 7 Series had until this facelift, is disappointing, though. The touchscreen is capable, but a physical controller is easier to use when you’re concentrating on the road. My hand reached for it briefly out of muscle memory, but I’d adapted within five minutes behind the wheel.

The optional rear theatre screen is one of the i7’s most extravagant features. At 31.3 inches, it folds down from the ceiling to entertain rear passengers, and other options include touch-sensitive controls in the rear doors, a Bowers & Wilkins sound system and lounge-style seating with a footrest. They’re impressive, but they only make sense if you regularly carry passengers who’ll use them.

BMW i7 performance and driving experience

The i7 has the sort of performance that makes a car weighing the best part of three tonnes feel surprisingly effortless.

The i7 50 xDrive produces 455hp and accelerates from 0 to 62mph in 5.5 seconds. The i7 60 xDrive raises output to 544hp and cuts that time to 4.8 seconds, while the 680hp M70 xDrive does the sprint in just 3.8 seconds.

The way it delivers that performance matters just as much as the figures. Acceleration is smooth and instant, with none of the gear changes you get with a combustion engine, and the i7 gathers speed without making a fuss, which suits its luxurious character.

Its size and weight mean it will never feel like a small sports saloon through tight corners, but the handling is more composed than you might expect. There’s plenty of grip, the body stays controlled and the steering gains useful weight as the road gets more demanding.

The real highlight, though, is the ride. Adaptive air suspension helps the i7 glide over uneven surfaces, and the cabin stays impressively quiet at motorway speeds. I drove it around Epsom Downs and the racecourse in Surrey, where it looked perfectly at home, and it wafted along beautifully, though like the horses up the road it could break into a gallop whenever I asked.

Optional active roll stabilisation improves body control further, but it’s frustrating that such a desirable feature isn’t standard across the range.

BMW has also worked on the smoothness of braking and energy recuperation. In a large electric car, the transition from regenerative braking to coming to a halt makes a noticeable difference to passenger comfort, and the i7’s refined behaviour helps keep the feeling that everything happens with minimal effort.

Driver assistance does a lot of the heavy lifting on long trips. Driving Assistant Plus is standard, and I particularly liked the way it keeps the car centred in its lane, which could make a real difference if your concentration dips for a second or two.

BMW i7 interior and boot space

Space is one of the i7’s strongest selling points. There’s loads of room in the front, rear passengers get generous legroom and headroom, and the electrically adjustable driving position makes it easy to get comfortable.

Rear-seat comfort is particularly impressive. Depending on the specification, the back can have reclining seats, a footrest and entertainment that turn it into a very relaxing place to spend time.

Visibility is reasonable for a car of this size, although the thick rear pillars restrict the view behind. Parking sensors and a 360-degree camera help when manoeuvring, but the i7’s sheer size still demands attention in multi-storey car parks and narrow streets.

The boot holds 500 litres, with extra storage under the floor. A ski hatch lets longer items through to the cabin, but the rear seats don’t fold, so if you regularly carry bulky things you’ll find that limiting.

Cabin storage is useful, with door bins, cupholders and a central storage compartment. A powered glovebox adds to the sense of occasion, and there’s an optional fridge if you want to take the luxury theme further.

BMW i7 range and charging

The 2026 i7 has a new battery built from BMW’s Gen6 round cells, with 112.5kWh of usable capacity. BMW quotes up to 452 miles of WLTP range for the i7 50 xDrive, up to 451 miles for the i7 60 xDrive and up to 426 miles for the M70 xDrive, against up to 388 miles before the facelift.

My drive was on a warm day on A and B roads, and although I didn’t go far, I was averaging 3.3 miles per kWh, which points to a more realistic 370 miles or so. That’s still a very usable range for a car of this size.

DC charging is rated at up to 250kW, up from 195kW before the facelift, and BMW quotes 28 minutes for a 10 to 80 per cent charge under the right conditions. That makes a big difference when you’re using a high-power public charger on a long trip.

At home, overnight charging is the most convenient option if you have off-street parking and can fit a wallbox. On a typical 7kW home charger, filling the battery from empty takes around 16 to 17 hours, so an overnight top-up is easy but a full charge from flat isn’t. The i7 can take up to 22kW on AC, which helps at faster workplace and destination chargers.

Home charging is generally much cheaper than relying on public rapid chargers, but tariffs vary, and a car of this size and weight uses a lot of energy over long distances.

BMW i7 as a company car

This is where the i7 makes most sense. Because it produces no tailpipe CO2, it sits in the 4% benefit-in-kind band for 2026/27, rising to 5% in 2027/28. On the £109,320 M Sport before options, that’s a taxable benefit of about £4,370, so a basic-rate taxpayer pays around £875 a year and a higher-rate taxpayer around £1,750. A petrol or diesel limousine at the same price would sit in the top 37% band, which would mean a bill of more than £16,000 a year for a higher-rate taxpayer.

That said, a BMW is a driver’s car, and I’d argue there’s little point having one as your company car if you only ever sit in the back. That would be like buying a mansion and never living in it, and anyone chauffeured around in an i7 would soon be jealous enough to want the wheel for themselves.

Private buyers have a different sum to do. Electric cars pay vehicle tax now, at £10 in the first year and £200 after that, and because the i7 costs more than £50,000 it also pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement from its second year to its sixth, which makes £640 a year.

BMW’s warranty runs for three years with unlimited mileage, and the battery is covered separately for eight years or 100,000 miles.

What we like

1. Excellent ride comfort. The i7 feels calm and refined over long distances, with impressive isolation from road and wind noise.

2. A luxurious interior. Spacious seating, high-quality materials and clever technology make the cabin a lovely place to spend time.

3. Strong performance. Even the i7 50 xDrive has ample acceleration, and the more powerful versions are exceptionally quick.

4. Improved electric range. Up to 452 miles, up from 388 before the facelift, with 28-minute rapid charging.

5. Low company car tax. At 4% BIK it costs a higher-rate taxpayer about £1,750 a year.

What worries us

1. The price. The i7 costs more than £100,000 before you add any of the more extravagant options.

2. The missing rotary controller. The touchscreen works well, but losing a familiar physical control is a step backwards for some tasks.

3. Its size. The spacious cabin comes with considerable exterior dimensions, which make parking and manoeuvring harder work.

4. Real-world range. I was seeing about 370 miles on a warm day, well short of the official 452.

The i7’s six-figure price means it pays the Expensive Car Supplement for five years, and if you’d like to know what your own car costs to tax, Regit’s free car tax checker will tell you.

Is the BMW i7 worth it?

The BMW i7 is an exceptionally accomplished luxury electric saloon. It combines a refined ride, strong performance, generous passenger space and an interior packed with technology, and the 2026 facelift brings real improvements to its range and charging.

Its price is the biggest obstacle, especially when the options list can add so much to the bill. The loss of the iDrive rotary controller is another disappointment, and its imposing size won’t suit every driver.

If you want a luxurious electric car that covers long distances in comfort and looks after its passengers, the i7 deserves serious consideration, and the i7 50 xDrive M Sport is the one I’d buy, because it’s quick enough that you don’t need the much more expensive M70.

It’s best for the company car driver who wants a limousine but still wants to drive it, and for them it’s hard to think of a better place to spend £109,320, especially with a 4% tax bill to help justify it.

It speaks to Prem Rugby’s ambition that its chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor is jetting off to the United States to drum up investment and sponsorship for the English game, as reported by City AM earlier this week.

It suggests the league – unlike many other top-flight union competitions – is actively seeking to go beyond its traditional market in order to attract financial support. Being backed by a major American insurance firm in Gallagher is one thing, but finding a US bank partner and further private investment into the league’s 10 teams would be a tonic for a sport still in need of as much help as it can get.

But I hope that Massie-Taylor, who was previously commercial chief at the Rugby Football Union, uses his trip to see just how US sports are able to commercialise, develop and sweat their assets, because that will be the difference between Prem Rugby truly turning a corner and repeating past mistakes.

Over 10 years ago the NFL launched an investment fund called 32 Equity, using a start-up contribution of $1m from each of the league’s main owners. By late 2026, it has raised more than $250m and had stakes in the likes of merchandise giant Fanatics – having purchased a three per cent stake at a $3bn valuation in 2017, the firm is now worth $30bn – and Genius Sports, the company behind VAR in the Premier League.

Stateside lessons

It is a smart way of keeping owners on the straight and narrow, incentivising them with investments into firms that directly work with the NFL, like Fanatics. Assuming you could persuade the Prem Rugby owners – whose wealth generally ranges from the billions at Bristol Bears and Newcastle Red Bulls down to the low tens of millions elsewhere in the league – to part with some cash, it could go into buying stakes in catering firms, sports AI organisations and kit/streetwear suppliers which could then service the league.

The NFL is a smart, rather large, cookie and Massie-Taylor should look beyond the bright lights of Manhattan’s banking district or the wider East Coast business front on his trip. US sports are great at turning their athletes into their own brands which transcend the field or the court and, while meetings with Matchroom suggest Prem Rugby is well on its way there, it is about getting players to invest and build portfolios. For all of the cheating that was revealed at Saracens at the end of the last decade, at least a number of players have gone on to have stakes in or ownership of successful businesses.

When David Beckham joined Jonny Wilkinson (or more likely the other way around) for an Adidas advert in 2003, the world was Wilko’s oyster. The star of England World Cup win could have gone on to be the most commercial figure the sport had ever seen, but he chose not to. Massie-Taylor must encourage his roster of players to build their appeal beyond the game; and that means more than Henry Pollock doing the cover of Men’s Health and being named one of Tatler’s 200 “hottest young eligibles”.

Play Video

Prem Rugby opportunities

Adidas once paid for the entire Newcastle team – including yours truly – to go on a pre-season tour to Japan because they wanted Wilkinson for brand promotion. Five weeks in the Far East was an incredible experience for me as a youngster, but there was one snag for the apparel brand, who undoubtedly forked out tens of thousands: Wilko got appendicitis on the first day and was forced to fly home.

Rugby needs brands – like Red Bull with, ironically, Newcastle again – to trust the growth potential in the sport and it looks like that may need to come from the US, given its own incentives to develop rugby ahead of their World Cup hosting duties in 2031 and 2033.

I commend Massie-Taylor on his growth agenda. But he needs to go beyond the surface and delve into just how sports Stateside have made themselves commercial, and fan-loved, behemoths.

Haldane was held up by some in Andy Burnham’s camp as one of three economic heavyweights helping shape the Prime Minister’s plans for government, though his involvement never evolved into a formal role. Now, the president of the British Chambers of Commerce, he has since issued a string of rebukes over what he sees as the government’s unwillingness to tackle Britain’s perilous fiscal situation or unleash the private sector in its pursuit for growth.

Speaking to the Political Thinking podcast, Haldane said the UK had been given a temporary reprieve by the fact the “markets’ spotlight is not on us”.

“It’s focused across the Channel,” he added. “France is ablaze when it comes to concerns about their debt and deficits […] Nonetheless it wouldn’t take much for that for that searchlight to cross the Channel onto our shores, and that’s why I wanted the Chancellor to put more insurance in place – to guard against that fire spreading across the Channel.

The former Bank of England official gave Healey’s maiden fiscal event a four out of 10, on the grounds it failed to make sufficient inroads into protecting the public finances. “I think this is around a four,” he said, adding: “John Healey plainly [on Wednesday] had sworn the Hippocratic oath before he gave his speech. Healey avoids bond market backlash in Budget

The Treasury was approached for comment.

So, my time is almost up with the Renault 5. I had quietly hoped that Renault’s press office would forget to ask for it back, but no such luck. After four months as our do-it-all family car, we’re obliged to say au revoir. 

Production of the reborn R5 started in October 2024 and, two years later, there’s still a buzz around this French supermini. Even friends and relatives with zero interest in cars seem intrigued by it. Several of them made comments along the lines of “I don’t like electric cars, but I’d happily have one of these”. 

Spoiler alert: were I shopping around for a small-ish EV, I’d have one of these too. Objectively, you get more for your money with a Chinese competitor – the BYD Dolphin Surf or Aion UT, for example – but the Renault feels like more than just basic transport. It looks chic, handles well and has that certain je ne sais quoi that car enthusiasts like to call ‘character’.

What I liked about the Renault 5

For this final long-term test report, I’ve decided to list my likes and dislikes about the Renault 5, based on using HT26 LZF – a 52kWh model in Iconic Five+ spec – as my daily driver since June. Let’s start with the good stuff…

How it looks

To my eyes, the 5 E-Tech’s design owes more to Marcello Gandini’s second-generation Supercinq, launched in 1984, than the Michel Boué original of 1972. Either way, it’s instantly recognisable as a Renault 5, yet somehow avoids looking overtly retro. You’d never mistake it for anything other than a modern car. 

There are also lots of neat details when you look closer, such as the French Tricolore flags within the headlights and 5-shaped charge indicator on the bonnet. And you can also order in the R5 in ‘proper’ paint colours, such as dazzling Pop Yellow and Pop Green, rather than just varying shades of grey. My car is a more subtle Midnight Blue, although I’ve convinced myself it resembles the Renault 5 GT Turbo Raider – an object of my affections in the 1990s.

The 5 is equally stylish inside, where its dark exterior contrasts with yellow recycled denim upholstery and drive mode-dependent ambient lighting. There are further nods to the past in the R5 Turbo-style seats, ribbed dashboard trim and textured rooflining. While many new-car cabins contain little more than an oversized iPad, the Renault does things differently. 

How it drives

It has taken a while, but we’re reaching a point where affordable EVs are genuinely fun to drive. The R5’s closely related cousin, the Alpine A290 hot hatch, was a trailblazer here. And the recently launched Peugeot E-208 GTI is even better. 

The standard 5 isn’t a car you’d set your alarm for on a Sunday morning, but its well-weighted steering, eager turn-in and punchy 150hp e-motor can still raise a smile. Just as importantly, it rides well, smothering speed humps and potholes like a larger, more luxurious car. There isn’t the delicacy of a classic R5, but this remake is in a different league when it comes to build quality – and at least half-a-tonne heavier, too.

I find the car flows better in default Comfort mode than in over-caffeinated Sport. However, the energy-saving Eco mode, which softens throttle response, limits top speed to 70mph and dials down the heating or air-con, is genuinely useful when you want to eke out extra miles without the need for a charging stop. 

A further plus point is the nicely calibrated One Pedal mode, activated by pulling the right paddle behind the steering wheel. This ramps up regenerative braking, helping to recharge the battery and lengthen the car’s range. It also means you can drive around town using – you guessed it – one pedal, which is an engaging, EV-specific skill in itself.

Charging and efficiency

That segues us neatly into talking about batteries, charging, range and other topics that will have petrolheads shrugging their shoulders or rolling their eyes. Bear with me.

Theoretically, this bigger battery 52kWh version of the R5 can deliver 252 miles on a full charge, although recent aerodynamic and battery management upgrades have boosted this to 267 miles. In reality, my car never displayed a range of more than 224 miles with a 100 percent charge, which has decreased to around 200 miles in recent colder weather. 

That doesn’t sound like a lot, but a) the figure is a realistic one, and b) the 5’s small battery can be charged at up to 100kW, so refills en route don’t take long. But the time you’ve been to the bathroom, bought a coffee and caught up with the latest drama on the parents’ WhatsApp group (OK, just me then), it should have added enough juice to get you home.

Throughout my time with the R5, its average efficiency has wavered between 4.3 and 4.4 miles per kWh. That’s not bad, even for a small EV, particularly given that many of those miles were on motorways. 

In truth, I still wouldn’t want to run an electric car without access to a home charger, but the public network is improving all the time. I never had any problems with connecting the Renault to charging points, either – an issue that has cropped up with other EVs. As in all other areas, the 5 has been completely reliable.

What I didn’t like about the Renault 5

This is a shorter section, because I liked the R5 a lot. Given how many awards it has won – European Car of the Year 2025 and UK Car of the Year 2026 among them – that may not come as a surprise. However, testing a car for a few hours, often on great roads, isn’t the same as daily-driving it for months. And to its credit, the Renault’s initial sparkle didn’t fade.

It’s a tight squeeze in the back 

In the 1970s, erudite motoring journalist LJK Setright described the back seat of a Peugeot 104 as ‘no more than a padded parcel shelf’. The Renault’s rear bench isn’t quite so cramped, but legroom is tight for anyone other than small children. My two lanky teenagers complained about it with tedious regularity.

The Renault’s 326-litre boot is also on the small side, partly because of the batteries beneath its floor. There’s no ‘frunk’ under the bonnet to store a charging cable, either. Exclusive economic modelling for City AM assesses whether Manchester City are too big to fail and whether a contagion threat should be factored into any punishment of the club.

You have to go back to 1984 and the US state rescue of Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company to pinpoint the moment that “too big to fail” entered the popular lexicon.

More than two decades later, the label was in widespread use again as governments on both sides of the Atlantic raided the coffers to save banks – most notably in the UK, Royal Bank of Scotland and Lloyds Banking Group – during the financial crash of 2008.

In recent weeks its use has spread to football, and in particular discussions of the impact on the wider game if Manchester City were to be dealt severe sanctions after being found guilty on more than 100 counts of breaking Premier League financial rules.

One argument advanced goes something like this: if City are clobbered with relegation from the top division and massive fines, it could quickly render them insolvent. And because they owe hundreds of millions of pounds in transfer fee instalments to other clubs in England and abroad, it could trigger a domino effect that topples innocent teams and further damages the integrity of the game.

It’s a theory that the independent commission currently mulling City’s punishment – while the club pursues in parallel an appeal against the original findings – will have to consider.

But how credible is the threat of contagion? Is it a genuine risk or a last-ditch ploy from those advocating for leniency towards England’s most successful club of the last 15 years? In short, are Manchester City really too big to fail?

City AM commissioned independent economic modelling in an attempt to shed some light on those questions. The report, compiled by Dr Danny F Hill of sports valuation consultancy Virsolus, considers the financial impact on the club of various scenarios, including one or two seasons outside of the Premier League, the size of any fine which may be imposed and the conditions which might be attached, and access to parachute payments.

The findings, while necessarily limited by the finite variety of scenarios modelled, provide the most meaningful indication yet of how much risk City’s case carries to the rest of football. 

How other clubs may be affected if Man City go into financial shock

Self-evidently, clubs who have recently sold players to Manchester City and for whom a portion of the transfer fee remains unpaid could be affected in the event of default. 

According to the analysis, six clubs account for around 85 per cent of City’s estimated transfer instalments for the next two years, with Chelsea the most exposed following their sale of Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez for £125m in September this year. 

The other five are, in order of most exposed: Lille, due to their sale of Ayyoub Bouaddi for £86m in August; Everton, following their sale of Iliman Ndiaye for £60m in September; Nottingham Forest, who sold Elliot Anderson for £116m in June; Palmeiras, for the sales of Vitor Reis and Allan Elias for a total of £64m since 2025; and Bournemouth, who traded Antoine Semenyo for £62.5m in January.

Were City to become unable to pay their outstanding obligations to any of these clubs, it could cause liquidity problems that mean they, in turn, cannot meet transfer instalments for players they have signed in recent years. 

In the case of Chelsea, for example, who have spent £345m in the last two years on 10 players, that could create difficulties in paying, for example, Aston Villa, for Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martinez.

That could, hypothetically, then impact Villa’s ability to pay clubs they owe, such as Southampton, Atletico Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain and Freiburg. And so on and so forth.

“Liquidity contagion is economically plausible,” the report states. But whether City qualify as too big to fail rests on a more drastic outcome: the club falling into administration and dragging others with them. 

And on that point, the report finds no evidence to justify a doomsday scenario, which also rests on the relative solvency of other clubs. “Systemic insolvency is not demonstrated,” it adds. “These relationships do not establish that the resulting payment disruption would be sufficient to cause widespread club failures.”

How Man City’s revenue may be affected

The most extreme form of contagion would require Manchester City to go bust, a prospect raised if they were to be banished from the Premier League either by a heavy points deduction that ensures relegation or, in a move considered less likely, a vote of other clubs to expel them.

The economic modelling by Dr Hill, a US-based Briton and Assistant Professor of Finance at Providence College, estimates the impact on City’s revenue of spending one and two seasons outside the Premier League. The latter scenario could occur if, for instance, they started next season in the second tier with a large negative points balance.

It estimates that City would suffer a £268m hit to their revenue if relegated, a figure that rises to £330m over two years even if they achieve promotion at the first attempt. Were they to spend two seasons outside the Premier League, revenue could suffer by £566m. 

While these are vast sums, the report concludes that they are not necessarily enough to trigger City’s insolvency as long as the club makes cuts, sells players and their ultimate owner, Sheikh Mansour, continues to support them. The latter consideration appears more likely since the Abu Dhabi royal injected a further £100m into City’s parent company last month.

“Overall, the analysis suggests that Manchester City’s financial interconnectedness does not, by itself, establish that the club is too big to fail,” the report says. 

“The more relevant question is whether any sporting or financial sanction would create a liquidity shortfall City could not absorb or refinance, and whether that shortfall would then exceed other football clubs’ and financial institutions’ capacity to manage their own obligations. The model suggests this outcome is conditional, not inevitable.”

The effect of variable approaches to fines and parachute payments

It has been widely speculated that any punishment handed down to Manchester City would include a financial penalty of some kind, at the very least in the tens of millions of pounds and potentially in the hundreds. 

But it is not just the size of the fine which is important, the report notes. How the fine is collected is equally if not more significant. For instance, a one-off fine of £200m payable now would hurt the club’s liquidity more – and therefore make it more likely to fall over – than a £300m fine payable over five years.

Parachute payments could also be critical. Expulsion from the Premier League via a vote of other clubs might deny City the downside mitigation benefits that flow to clubs relegated from the top flight by on-field performance. The absence of £100m in parachute payments while out of the Premier League would add to the strain on City’s finances.

The biggest single factor in determining how close City come to insolvency, the report concludes, may be Sheikh Mansour – more specifically, whether he sees the value in continuing to support an asset in which he has already invested billions of pounds.

“This leads to a potentially different interpretation of the ‘too big to fail’ argument. City may be too big to fail because of its importance to its own investors,” it says. 

“From an investment perspective, allowing City to enter financial distress could jeopardise considerably more than the immediate cost of meeting outstanding transfer obligations. 

“The consequences could include deterioration in enterprise value, commercial relationships, sporting competitiveness, geopolitical fallout and the wider strategic value associated with the ownership group’s football investments.” 

So are Manchester City too big to fail? And for who?

As the independent commission mulls how severely Manchester City should be punished, then, this analysis suggests there is no evidence to support fears of a catastrophic chain reaction blowing up other clubs.

There may be important considerations to be made regarding the way in which any fine should be collected but the Virsolus report says that City’s future survival rests more in the hands of the club’s ownership than anything else.

“The central finding is that City’s financial interconnectedness creates the potential for contagion, but its strategic importance to its controlling investors may provide a stronger economic incentive to prevent it,” it states. 

“Paradoxically, the ‘too big to fail’ argument may be more compelling to City’s owners than to the wider football community. This does not eliminate systemic risk but suggests that a serious contagion event would more likely require both a substantial financial shock via the fine size, payment schedule, and payee restrictions, and a failure, withdrawal, or constraint of the ownership and financing mechanisms that would ordinarily absorb it. 

“The critical question is who would find its failure economically more unacceptable.”

    John Healey may have opened Pandora’s Box with an increase to the UK bank surcharge. Samuel Norman looks at whether he will resist the temptation to extend it.

    Few things in British politics have proved to be as permanent as a “temporary” tax.

    When the Conservatives introduced the 25 per cent energy profits levy in 2022, it came with a strict December 2025 sunset clause. Six months later, the deadline slipped to 2028. By 2024, under a Labour government, it was extended to 2030 and hiked to 35 per cent. 

    The old Whitehall trick even applies to income tax, which itself arrived in 1842 as an emergency three-year measure, yet survives nearly two centuries later on rolling annual renewals.

    It is little wonder that the City has already switched into defensive mode after Chancellor John Healey’s “time-limited” hike to the banking surcharge.

    While the Budget document insisted there would be legislation for the time-limited period and it would “not be extended,” it has done little to reassure the sector. 

    “We hope this tax rise is limited,” William Chalmers, finance boss of Lloyds Banking Group, said. 

    He added the measure would be “unhelpful” for the government’s growth ambitions.

    Writing in City AM, UK Finance chief David Postings said: “History gives us reason to be cautious. Taxes introduced in response to temporary pressures have a habit of lasting longer than originally intended”.

    He added the government should look to reduce the burden over the long term and not increase it.

    “This is not an abstract concern. International firms decide where to deploy capital and create jobs. A stable and predictable tax regime is one important factor in those decisions.”

    Banks ‘disappointed’ by tax hike

    The increase amounts to a £1.5bn tax grab and will take surcharge receipts to £2.4bn for the 2027-2028 period. This will be up from £1.2bn in the last year. 

    Natwest, Nationwide and Lloyds are set to be the most exposed to the surcharge increase, according to RBC analysis. Meanwhile Jefferies estimates the surcharge costs around 0.5 per cent of market value, due to the temporary basis.

    “If this is genuinely 15-month time-limited, the capital impact at around 0.5 per cent of market value is more relevant,” Jonathan Pierce, analysts at Jefferies, said. 

    “Granted, investors may not believe this is the case.” 

    RBC’s Benjamin Toms added “The market will be sceptical that these changes will be temporary based on experiences elsewhere in Europe such as Spain,” 

    Spain introduced a 4.8 per cent levy on banks’ net interest income and fee revenues for 2023 and 2024, raising highs of €1.7bn. The nation’s government would go on to extend this to 2027 and replace the flat rate with a sliding scale tied to revenue earned. 

    Healey’s changes will give rise to caution for bank investors, who have trodden this path before. But ahead of the Budget the UK’s outsized tax rate for lenders already stood out – as one banking source irately pointed out, the increase marked an “extra tax on top of an extra tax”.

    Another industry source said there was “disappointment” following the tax hike, even if many had “come into the day thinking it could have been worse”.

    John Duncan Edwards, chief executive of transatlantic trade body British American Business, said: “It is surely an act of self-harm to target a sector at which the UK excels.”

    Time limits taken with ‘pinch of salt’

    Healey framed the move as helping to fund an energy support package, including the flagship policy of paying £100 to 20m households to help with bills this winter following the surge in prices from the US-Iran war.

    “I don’t see an obvious linkage between energy prices and bank taxes,” Chalmers said.

    Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot, pointed to the energy windfall tax continuing in operation today, adding “banks will be very wary of this”.

    “This time limit should be taken with a pinch of salt,” he added.

    “The geopolitical situation shows no sign of abating… there will need to be a material change to the conflict in the Middle East for the better in order for the government to feel they can return to the previous levels.”

    Banks had been on the backfoot ahead of the Budget after rumours of a windfall tax ran rampant. Many were bracing for a reversal of Jeremy Hunt’s 2023 bank tax cut, taking the surcharge back to eight per cent.

    But the Trade Union Congress suggested the surcharge could be raised to a 16 per cent in order to capitalise on the booming half-year profits of top lenders. 

    That paved the way for some positive share movement when it was announced the surcharge would move to six per cent for just a temporary period. But stocks moderated through the session and finished only moderately up, when compared to the highs reached in the aftermath of Healey’s announcement.

    “A ‘do no harm’ Budget was our test. It is one that the Chancellor has not quite met,” Miles Celic, chief executive of TheCityUK, told City AM, diplomatically.

    “[The bank tax’s] temporary nature matters, but only if the Chancellor honours his commitment to removing the increase after 15 months.”

    Here are just some of the figures: borrowing forecasts for the next five years have risen £65bn since March. By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn a year on debt interest alone – up £36bn a year. Terrifying.

    Caterham is a small town on the southern tip of the London suburbs, just beyond the ULEZ but within the M25. I moved here about 18 months ago, but have always lived in the area. 

    Google the word ‘Caterham’, though, and you won’t be presented with news about the roadworks on Church Hill or the new coffee shop on Croydon Road. That’s because this town is best known – faintly famous, even – as the birthplace of Caterham Cars.

    The Caterham Cars story begins in 1973, when Graham Nearn bought the rights to carry on building the Lotus Seven – a basic, lightweight two-seater powered by a four-cylinder Ford engine. Seven assembly moved to Dartford in 1987, but a showroom survived next to Caterham station until 2013. I can remember staring through the windows as a child, intrigued by these strange, bug-eyed sports cars.

    Today, I’m getting behind the wheel of a new Caterham Seven. It too is powered by a four-cylinder Ford engine – and its appearance has scarcely changed since 1973 (or indeed 1957, when the original Lotus was launched). But that’s kind of the point; for anyone acquainted with Sevens, driving one always feels familiar. A bit like, well, coming home.

    Derived from the Seven 310

    Caterham has been using Ford’s all-aluminium 1.6-litre Sigma engine since 2006, and stockpiled a batch of them after the Blue Oval halted production in 2020. However, it is now down to the final 25 cars, marking the end to this era with a special edition Seven: the 310 Encore.

    For the uninitiated, Caterham offers a range of outwardly similar sports cars, from the beautifully basic 85hp Seven 170 to the supercar-baiting 314hp Seven 620. There are retro-styled roadsters and full-blooded racing cars in the mix, too.  

    The 154hp Seven 310 was itself a special edition of sorts. It began as an option pack for the middle-ranking 270, with a bit of extra power and a sharper setup. However, Caterham soon acknowledged the 310’s popularity by making it a permanent fixture in the model lineup. 

    Aside from the naturally aspirated Ford engine, the basics are a five-speed manual gearbox, rear-wheel drive and a kerb weight of 540kg. To put that latter figure into context, a Jaecoo 7 SHS, currently the UK’s best-selling car, tips the scales at around 1,800kg. 

    Welcome to the New Order

    You can spot an Encore straight away thanks to its full-length body stripes, which are replicated on the side panels. There’s also an attention-grabbing choice of paint colours, each one named after a famous song: Blue Monday (pictured here), Orange Crush, Goodbye Yellow Brick Road, Green Light, White Noise or Back in Black.

    Further aesthetic mods include a vented, aero-optimised nose cone from the Seven 620, a radiator grille from the 420 Cup, front wings in exposed carbon fibre and anodised black (rather than chrome) trim. Two-piece 13-inch Apollo alloy wheels are shod with semi-slick Toyo R888R tyres.

    Both regular and wide-body ‘SV’ configurations are available – the latter aimed at those who struggle to squeeze into the confines of a standard Seven. Dynamic upgrades run to sports suspension with a wider track, moveable spring platforms and an adjustable rear anti-roll bar. You also get a limited-slip differential and beefier 254mm front brakes with four-piston calipers and a racing-spec master cylinder.

    Mind the side exhaust

    Last but certainly not least, there is the Ford Sigma engine, presented here in its highest state of tune, with spikier dual overhead camshafts, a lightened flywheel and a reprogrammed ECU. A total of 154hp, along with 124lb ft of torque, equates to 0-62mph in 4.8 seconds and a blustery maximum of 127mph.

    It all breathes through a side-mounted exhaust that exits just underneath your right ear – and makes stepping into a Seven while wearing shorts a perilous process. Like me, you will probably scorch your shin once on the hot tailpipe, then never make that mistake again. You can also detach the tiny Momo steering wheel to make access easier. 

    Unlike the hard-shell buckets of Caterham’s racier ‘R’ models, the Encore has softly padded leather seats that I found very accommodating. There’s still the pre-flight faff of four-point harness belts, though, and you won’t find any other concessions to comfort. Still, Radio 4 would be inaudible above the mechanical cacophony, while air conditioning is provided by the great outdoors. 

    Lean and roofless

    Believe it or not, a roof is optional on the 310 Encore (£1,000), but it’s a box that British buyers will need to tick. Removing the tight-fitting fabric top takes about five minutes and involves a lot of metal poppers, but no grazed knuckles or swear words – unlike British sports cars of old. Once rolled up, you can store it in the Seven’s boot, which has just enough space for a few shopping bags. 

    You can also detach the lightweight doors for the full al fresco effect, although there is nowhere to store them within the car. Still, a doorless Seven provides one of the most unique vistas in motoring, with jostling suspension up ahead and the road rushing past inches beneath your elbow.

    The carbon fibre dashboard is a flat panel with simple rocker switches and small, Encore-branded dials. You fumble around beneath the steering wheel to slot in the dainty key, then prod a bright red engine start button. Encore une fois? Don’t mind if I do…

    Driving the Caterham Seven 310 Encore

    Even after so many years (and so many special editions), there is nothing quite like a Seven. This isn’t a car you can drive while thinking about those infuriating tailbacks on Church Hill, or whether you’d prefer oat milk in your latte. Instead, you roll up your sleeves and immerse yourself in the experience. 

    Sitting so far back in the car, right above the rear axle, with the long, louvred bonnet stretching out ahead, feels odd at first. There’s an initial rotational inertia caused by having the engine at one end and the driver/passenger at the other, which encourages you to commit to a corner, aim the inside front wheel at the apex then use the throttle to trim your angle of attack. It sounds difficult – daunting, even – but feels the exact opposite. Even on damp roads and lightly treaded tyres, the Seven doesn’t try to catch you out.

    You feel the car’s lightness through every input and response. From its endlessly chatty steering to its resolute, track-tuned damping, the Encore bubbles with effervescent energy. If you want a car for road trips and weekends away, it’s probably all a bit much. But for a dusk drive on a summer evening, or blasting away the cobwebs on a winter morning, it’s just the tonic. The best Caterham Seven I’ve driven, in fact. 

    A sign-off for the Sigma

    In some Sevens, the engine feels secondary to the chassis, a supporting actor rather than the headline star. That isn’t the case here. The Sigma unit punches hard, revs furiously and barks like classic rally car, with a fusillade of thuds and pops on the over-run. While the 2.0-litre Ford Duratec engine in Caterham’s 360, 420 and 620 models is ultimately more powerful, it isn’t as crisp or charismatic.  

    The manual gearbox comes from a Mazda (the MX-5, presumably) and its wonderfully mechanical, wrist-flick shift helps you to stoke the engine’s enthusiasm. The pedals are well placed for heel-and-toe downshifts, too – provided you have smallish feet. My size eight trainers were fine, but larger folk might need to wear dedicated driving shoes. Or even drive barefooted.

    Not once while blasting around Surrey and Kent did I feel that the Encore needed more urge. A power-to-weight ratio of around 300hp per tonne is plenty on the public road, especially when you don’t have any electronic aids to dilute the drama and/or save you from yourself. How refreshing to drive a new car where job one isn’t figuring out how to switch off all the bleeping assistance systems. Pun very much intended. 

    Besides, in a Seven you don’t need to go fast to have fun. Even ambling around with the doors off is a lovely way to pass the time. Particularly in the Caterham’s home town, where it attracts “nice car” comments every time I clamber out, hopping inelegantly over that hot exhaust. 

    Verdict: Caterham Seven 310 Encore

    The 310 Encore costs £39,995 if you build it yourself, or an additional £2,595 if the Dartford factory does the spannering for you. That seems a lot for a car with no more mod-cons than a skateboard, but consider that a Lotus Emira costs at least £79,500, while the cheapest Porsche 911 is now £105,200. And neither can match the sheer driving joy of a Seven.

    Caterhams are also well known for their very limited depreciation, which should soften the financial blow. Alternatively, you could just buy one and keep it forever, confident in the knowledge that the legislators will eventually figure out a way to ban simple, fun cars like this one.

    There is speculation that a turbocharged 1.3-litre engine from Horse Powertrain – already used in the Caterham Academy race cars – will replace the Sigma soon. In the meantime, the Encore makes for a fitting and rather wonderful finale. You’d better move fast, though; at the time of writing, only a handful of the 25 build slots are left. If you buy one, bring it to Caterham and say hello. 

    Tim Pitt writes for Motoring Research

The UK has the talent, technology and ambition to become a world leader in the industries of tomorrow, but realising that potential will depend on something more fundamental: whether we have the energy infrastructure to support growth.

    Britain is competing internationally for businesses to invest and grow, and electricity that is both reliable and affordable is a core component. Since the end of 2019, the UK has grown by 6.2 per cent compared to 16.3 per cent in the US. If we are to achieve these levels of growth, we need to be decisive and competitive in the upcoming budget. 

    Energy is the often-overlooked foundation of economic growth. When the system works, we barely give it a second thought. But without reliable and affordable electricity, even the most advanced technologies cannot reach their full potential.

    History shows us what is possible when infrastructure keeps pace with innovation. When London’s first electric underground railway opened in 1890, it demonstrated how new technology, supported by the right infrastructure, could transform a city. Today, we take the Tube for granted, rarely considering the energy system working behind the scenes.

    Britain faces a similar challenge today. The technologies may be different, but the principle remains the same: ambition alone is not enough. We need the infrastructure to turn it into reality.

    As electricity demand grows, that challenge is becoming increasingly urgent. Westminster projects that the UK’s electricity demand is likely to double by 2050. 

    For too long, the debate about Britain’s energy future has focused on how much electricity we can generate. What matters just as much is whether we can deliver reliable, affordable electricity to businesses when and where they need it, regardless of the weather or season. Recent scrutiny of the National Energy System Operator (NESO) acts as a clear reminder that delivering energy security requires strong governance and operational resilience to keep our electricity system running. 

    Not just renewables

    A diverse and flexible energy system – one that combines growing renewable generation with energy storage and dispatchable power that can respond when demand rises or when the weather doesn’t cooperate – can deliver that. It also requires stronger grid infrastructure and smarter technologies to manage supply and demand.

    Crucially, we need to make better use of the infrastructure Britain already has.

    Across the country, existing power stations, grid connections and industrial sites represent valuable assets – these can and should be adapted to support emerging industries, alongside continued investment in new infrastructure.

    Nowhere is the importance of getting this right clearer than in artificial intelligence.

    AI has the potential to transform industries from healthcare and financial services to manufacturing and scientific research. But unlocking that potential will depend on Britain having the energy infrastructure to deliver reliable, affordable power at the scale required to support a significant expansion in data centre capacity. AI and data centres alone will account for up to 16 per cent of Britain’s electricity demand within a decade.

    Building that capacity here is critical to strengthening the UK’s AI capabilities and ensuring Britain captures the investment, jobs and economic benefits of the technology that will define the next century.

    Yet delivering the infrastructure is proving challenging. Grid connection delays risk holding back projects at precisely the moment international competition for AI investment is fierce.

    Investors need confidence that Britain can provide not only the skills and technology they need, but reliable, affordable power to support their long-term ambitions.

    This is where making better use of existing energy infrastructure, alongside developing new capacity, could help Britain unlock investment more quickly.

    From the Ukraine War to tensions in the Middle East, the case for a diverse, flexible energy system has never been clearer as an energy security and economic priority.

    Britain cannot control the next global crisis or the pace of international competition, but it can make decisions today that strengthen its resilience and competitiveness. The upcoming budget provides a chance for just that: investing in growth.

    Will Gardiner CEO of Drax

    Which is the Underground’s most haunted Tube station? James Ford offers the definitive countdown of the top three

    When we think about the capital’s best known ghost stories and most haunted locations, we probably all think of the same few suspects: the headless ghost of Anne Boleyn wandering the ramparts at the Tower of London, Jack the Ripper silently stalking the streets of Whitechapel in thick fog and the Highgate Vampire prowling through the cemetery in search of blood. Surely the Undead of the Underground should have their stories told too? 

    Well, rest assured that City AM has got you covered. We have raided the archives – and sifted the seriously scary from the simply spooky – to determine the definitive list of the top three most haunted Tube stations. So, descend with us on an ethereal escalator to take a Tube ride into terror…

    3. Bethnal Green

    Whereas most of Tube’s most stations have one or perhaps two ghosts, Bethnal Green earns its spot here because it has 173, all of them the result of a single tragedy. 

    Bethnal Green’s Central Line platforms are some of the deepest on the network, which made the station a very popular bomb shelter during the Second World War. In March 1943, when the air raid sirens blared and a nearby battery of air defences cranked into action, there was such a rush to get into the station, with hundreds of people pouring into the narrow staircases and walkways, that those at the bottom of the stairs were crushed and suffocated en masse. The fatalities included 84 women and 62 children. 

    The incident is the worst single loss of civilian life in Britain during the war and the deadliest disaster in the history of the London Underground. Worse still, the air raid alert that caused the deaths was just a drill to test fire new rocket-based air defences and no bombs fell. To protect wartime morale, the incident was hushed up for years and an official report was classified. To this day, people claim to hear children sobbing, women crying and panicked screams lasting for over 10 minutes before the sound slowly fades away. 

    2. Bank

    Bank makes it onto this list because its signature ghost has the best name of any spectral entity on the Tube network: the Black Nun of Bank. Better known in her lifetime as Sarah Whitehead, and not a nun but rather a grieving sister: in 1812 her brother, a clerk at the Bank of England, was convicted and hanged for forgery. In response, Sarah had a nervous breakdown and took to dressing in heavy, black mourning dress, visiting the bank daily and asking employees: “Have you seen my brother?” 

    In the end the directors of the bank offered her a financial settlement on the condition that she stop, which she accepted. But, after her death some 20 years later, reports started of sightings of a woman dressed in black and weeping while roaming Threadneedle Street, the halls of the Bank England and the platforms of Bank station, often accompanied by the smell of decay and a sudden cold feeling.

    1. Aldgate 

    Aldgate was probably always going to top our list. Afterall, it was built on a plague pit. And not a small one. This particular plague pit – located behind St Botolph’s church and dating back to 1665 – contained the remains of more than 1,000 victims of the Great Plague. Furthermore, the station’s construction was troubled by a large number of accidents and deaths, including some workmen who were buried alive digging tunnels. Anyone who has seen the film Poltergeist knows that disturbing burial grounds never ends well.

    But it is not just the obvious ghostly foreshadowing that puts Aldgate on this list but its actual haunted history. In 1896 a house located over the road from the station burnt down in a devastating house fire, killing three young girls from the Sullivan family (aged six, three and eighteen months). Ever since passengers at Aldgate have reported hearing disembodied childish laughter, running footsteps and the sounds of children playing on the platforms. Some have even reported feeling their sleeves being tugged, or tiny feet stepping on theirs, all of which has been attributed to the ghosts of the Sullivan girls.

    And the Sullivan girls are not Aldgate’s only ghostly presence. In 2000, a track worker at Aldgate survived a 20,000-volt electrocution after slipping on the electrified rail. A colleague claimed to have seen a translucent elderly woman kneeling and stroking the worker’s hair just after he fell, leading to speculation that either the ghostly entity intervened to save the worker from death or was responsible for pushing him in the first place. The lore has suggested that the ghost – known  as the Spectral Old Lady (or, less poetically, as the ‘Hair Stroker’) – was a woman who fell on the tracks and died whilst sheltering during the Blitz.

    For years urban legend maintained that spooky events and ghoulish sightings at Aldgate were so frequent that staff maintained a written record. However, Transport for London has always denied the existence of the so-called Ghost Logbook. (But, then again, if I was a public transport authority maintaining a private Necronomicon, I’d deny it too!)

    Remember this list next time you are stood on an empty Tube platform late at night. Are the hairs on the back of your neck standing up? If you strain your ears, can you hear children playing? Do you think you can hear distant footsteps? Is someone tugging gently at your sleeve? Or, worse still, is someone stroking your hair? Sweet dreams, dear reader, sweet dreams…

    And an honourable mention:

    The British Museum

    If you thought this list was lacking a Mummy’s Curse, don’t worry. The ghost of a priestess in the service of Amun-Ra, the Egyptian King-God, is said to haunt the tunnels around the old British Museum station wearing a loincloth and headdress and usually seen screaming or wailing. This ghost story is linked to the so-called ‘Unlucky Mummy’, an object (an inner coffin lid, not an actual mummy) in the British Museum’s Egyptology collection. This would have made our top five but, sadly, the British Museum station closed in 1933. 

    James Ford is a former adviser to Mayor of London Boris Johnson

    Manchester United director Edward Glazer has emerged as the leading donor to President Trump’s Republican Party among the Premier League’s sizeable American ownership contingent ahead of the US midterm elections.

    Glazer, whose family owns the majority of Manchester United, has donated over $220,000 to the Republican National Committee in 2026 through his Tampa Bay Buccaneers NFL team, according to declarations collected by City AM from the Federal Election Commission of the United States of America. 

    His $221,502 (£166,000) contribution spans eight separate donations, ranging from four installments of $36,917 in February, March, April and June down to $7,383 in the middle of 2026.

    Manchester United’s total debt is above £1bn, driven by borrowings and credit drawdowns. The wider Glazer family are estimated to have made around £1.3bn during their tenure as Manchester United owners while the club’s on-field fortunes have dwindled.

    Midterms control at stake

    Tuesday’s midterm vote could see both the House of Representatives and Senate fall into Democrat hands, threatening the remainder of Trump’s second term. There are fears he may become a lame duck president, and could be impeached over a number of issues ranging from Iran to historic Capital Building riots and more.

    But Glazer isn’t the biggest political donor out of the increasingly Americanised Premier League ownership group. Crystal Palace co-owner Josh Harris has donated $250,000 to SLF PAC, an independent Republican-aligned lobby group, through his Apollo Global Management firm. His business partner David Blitzer — who alongside Harris owns a stake in the Washington Commanders NFL team who have touted naming their new arena the President Trump Stadium — has donated $63,875 to mostly Democrat runners for Congress and the House of Representatives. Dan Goldman, Donald Norcross, Wesley Bell, Ritchie Torres, Roy Cooper (all Democrat) and Bill Cassidy (Republican) are all Blitzer beneficiaries. 

    Manchester United, Glazer and donations

    Bill Foley, owner of AFC Bournemouth as well as Prem Rugby team Exeter Chiefs through his Black Knight consortium, has donated $201,500 to a mixture of party representatives, including $125,000 to Leadership in Action, a firm that has backed Republican Aaron Flint to the tune of over $200,000 this year.

    Ipswich investor Marc Lasry has donated $7,300 to Democrat causes while Aston Villa co-owner Wes Edens has donated $5,000 to Republican-sympathetic candidate Mike Crapo.

    Former Chelsea owner Todd Boehly has spent $46,200 backing Republican organisations and lobby groups ahead of the midterms.

    But the likes of Arsenal owner Stan Kroenke and Fulham’s Shahid Khan have not yet donated to any political cause, according to the Federal Election Commission of the United States of America register.

    The midterms take place on Tuesday with Trump’s Republican party defending its three-seat lead in the Senate – the Democrats would need four gains to take the house due to any 50-50 tie being broken by Vice President JD Vance – and their one-seat lead in the House of Representatives.
