The post WorldOracle Tests Whether World Models Can Reliably Predict Real-World Executions appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]> Key Takeaways
  • WorldOracle is a benchmark for action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) that scores each model’s predicted rollout against the paired real-world execution, with both starting from the same initial observations and following the same action sequence.
  • Seven representative models were evaluated; arm motion was predicted relatively well, but object positions and movements often deviated from reality, and performance dropped over complete operation sequences.
  • The platform opened to developers on October 16 and accepts both open-weight and closed-source models.

In one WorldOracle case, the robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted a successful pick. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

In one case showcased by WorldOracle, a robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted that the robot had successfully picked up the fruit.

Given the initial frame and action sequence of a real manipulation episode, the model generated a rollout that looked plausible on screen but differed from the actual execution. The success it depicted never happened in reality.

Researchers from Princeton University, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Toronto, NVIDIA and AgiBot have jointly introduced WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) by comparing their predictions with real-world executions that start from the same initial observations and follow the same action sequences.

The team evaluated seven representative models — among them DreamDojo, Cosmos 3, IRASim and GE-Sim 2.0 — and identified two prominent problems. First, while the motion paths of robot arms are predicted relatively well, the positions and movements of manipulated objects can still deviate from reality. Second, models that perform well over short horizons can degrade significantly over complete operation sequences.

On October 16, WorldOracle, an evaluation platform for action-conditioned world models, officially opened to developers. The research team has collected real manipulation episodes in advance, recording both video and actions. Developers use the initial frames and action sequences provided in the evaluation set to generate predicted videos and submit them to the platform, which scores each submission against the corresponding real execution record. The results show whether a model has accurately predicted the consequences of the actions, helping developers pinpoint weaknesses and verify improvements.

Project page: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18826

How Do Seven World Models Perform?
Arm motion is right, but objects don’t always follow

The predicted motion of a robot arm reaching toward a piece of fruit and closing its gripper may closely match its actual motion, yet the model can still incorrectly predict whether the fruit is lifted and where it moves next. To assess the two separately, the research team compared the position and motion of the robot arm and of the manipulated object in each predicted video against the real-world recording, and scored them individually.

Spatial alignment scores for the robot arm and the manipulated object. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

The results show that all five models evaluated on the human-operated AgiBot G2 data scored higher on the arm than on the object. In other words, even when the arm in the generated video follows the given actions well, the position and movement of the object may still depart from reality. IRASim scored 78.8 on the robot arm but only 29.1 on the manipulated object, while Cosmos 3 scored 89.4 and 45.4, respectively. The remaining models showed gaps of varying size.

Accuracy declines as the rollout horizon grows

Time presents a second challenge. Completing a continuous task often requires multiple grasps, placements and adjustments, and the object state left by one interaction becomes the starting point for the next. Whether a model stays close to reality must therefore be tested over the full process.

WorldOracle evaluates both the first 30 seconds of each trajectory and the complete long sequence.

WorldOracle-SV scores of the same models under the two evaluation horizons. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

On the same set of AgiBot G2 teleoperation data, the WorldOracle-SV scores of all five models fell. DreamDojo dropped from 50.56 to 27.08, and Cosmos 3 from 53.99 to 26.60, nearly halving in both cases. GE-Sim 2.0 fell from 73.86 to 63.33; it posted the highest score of the five models at both horizons and the smallest decline over the full sequence.

The relative ranking also shifted. IRASim scored below Ctrl-World, DreamDojo and Cosmos 3 over the first 30 seconds, but above all three over the full sequence.

What Can WorldOracle Measure?

WorldOracle evaluation framework: real actions are recorded, the model predicts what follows, and the result is scored against the real execution. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

Accurately predicting a failure earns a high score

WorldOracle starts from pre-collected records of real manipulation. A model is given the initial frame and the action sequence and generates a predicted video, which is compared with the real execution of the same actions.

What models must predict includes missed grasps, drops and spills. If an operation fails in reality, accurately predicting that failure counts as a correct prediction.

Failed executions therefore serve as an important class of test samples: they reveal whether a model follows the given actions and their consequences, or defaults to a successful version of the task.

The benchmark covers two robot embodiments, AgiBot G2 and YAM, as well as first-person human-hand manipulation. Four tasks (fruit picking, towel hanging, water pouring and drawer pulling) involve interaction with rigid, deformable, fluid and articulated objects, respectively. Task coverage varies by embodiment, as defined in the evaluation set.

The human-hand setting is intended for world models that can accept hand-motion input, testing whether a model can predict subsequent object changes and interaction outcomes from a recorded sequence of hand poses. Models with egocentric world-modeling capabilities are evaluated zero-shot in this setting, without any additional hand-adaptation data provided by the platform.

Real execution footage for the four task types. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

The data come from two sources. The first is human-operated data collection, including robot teleoperation trajectories and human hand-manipulation trajectories. The second is policy rollouts, in which an autonomous policy controls a real robot.

When a robot executes autonomously, it can produce pauses, jitter and motion corrections that differ from human operation. Including such data helps test whether a world model remains accurate when faced with actions from different sources.

The platform offers three tracks:

  • WorldOracle-Core: evaluates predictions over the first 30 seconds of human-operated trajectories.
  • WorldOracle-Policy: evaluates predictions over complete episodes of autonomous policy rollouts on AgiBot G2.
  • WorldOracle-Long: evaluates sustained prediction over complete, human-operated long sequences.

The WorldOracle study compares several embodied world-model benchmarks. Of these, WorldOracle is the only one that simultaneously covers action-sequence input, real-world execution data, failure cases, long-horizon interaction, multiple embodiments, multi-view evaluation and autonomous policy rollouts.

Breaking down prediction error: outcomes and process

The predicted and real robot arm positions may closely match even when the model gets the fruit’s grasp state wrong; two final states may look alike while the paths that led to them differ. A single score can hardly capture such differences.

WorldOracle checks predictions with four complementary metrics:

  • Physical State Correctness: checks whether object positions, grasp states and liquid transfer at the end of each interaction match the real outcome.
  • Interaction Spatial Alignment: checks whether the positions and movement paths of objects, robot arms or human hands are consistent with the real process.
  • Key Interaction Area Fidelity: focuses on regions such as the object, gripper and hand, combining pixel-level, perceptual and semantic similarity to reduce the influence of large background areas on the score.
  • Multi-View Action Coherence: for models that support multi-view output, checks whether robot motion across synchronized camera views is aligned with the real execution.

The first three metrics are averaged with equal weights to form the WorldOracle-SV (single-view) score; for multi-view evaluation, the fourth metric is added and the four are again equally weighted. Sub-scores are also retained, allowing developers to distinguish problems in state prediction, motion trajectories and local detail.

To validate the metrics, the researchers asked 119 participants to compare 128 pairs of predicted videos. The four metrics agreed with human choices on which prediction was better 88.1% to 93.2% of the time.

The researchers also note the benchmark’s limits. It measures how closely a prediction matches a single recorded real execution. For fluids, deformable objects and stochastic contact, the same action can lead to several plausible outcomes, and a single reference cannot fully describe that range.

Training support also differs across embodiments: AgiBot G2 models use a benchmark-specific training set, YAM models use public data, and the human-hand setting is evaluated zero-shot. Scores across the three settings should therefore not be used directly to judge embodiment difficulty or cross-embodiment generalization.

How Can Developers Participate?
Open submissions give model iteration concrete feedback

WorldOracle supports both open-weight and closed-source models. After registration and approval, developers choose a track according to the embodiment or manipulation setting their model supports, generate and upload predicted videos following the submission guide, and view composite scores, sub-scores and comparisons.

For model iteration, this feedback can be tied to specific questions: Did a change make object motion more accurate? Did it reduce incorrect predictions of failed operations? Does the improvement still hold as the prediction horizon grows?

Whether the futures generated by a world model can be relied upon must be tested against real execution. WorldOracle turns that test into a unified set of tasks, data and scoring methods, giving developers a basis for comparing models, identifying errors and verifying improvements.

Project page: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/

Submission guide: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/submission/

Hazardous environments are good use cases for robots, which are expanding into new use cases. ANYbotics AG today launched ANYmal X, which it claimed is “the world’s first legged inspection robot for explosive atmospheres.”

The new quadruped is designed to meet strict safety standards in oil, gas, and chemicals, said the company. ANYmal X uses an advanced industrial AI stack to conduct routine autonomous inspections in environments that are dangerous to people, it said.

“Four years of pioneering engineering with more than 10 patents went into ANYmal X,” stated Péter Fankhauser, co-founder and CEO of ANYbotics. “Many experts thought a legged robot could never be made safe for explosive atmospheres.

“Oil, gas and chemical plants are among the most hazardous and most costly places to operate,” he added. “That makes them the prime case for physical and industrial AI, yet until now, the areas that matter most were off-limits to robots like ours. That changes today.”

Spun out of ETH Zurich in 2016, ANYbotics said its ANYmal robots and the Shift operations platform automate routine inspections in multiple industries, keeping people out of harm’s way and turning inspection data into maintenance action. Backed by more than $150 million from leading European and Silicon Valley investors, ANYbotics has about 200 employees in Zurich, San Francisco, and Barcelona.

Equipment failures in hazardous spaces are costly, says ANYbotics

“Valued at $102 billion, the global oil, gas, and chemical sector is the largest market for autonomous inspection,” noted ANYbotics. “Two major operational costs drive this market value: the expensive skilled labor required for manual inspection, and the downtime caused by preventable equipment failures.”

“Because critical components, like pumps, compressors, valves, and piping, are located in hazardous zones, where standard robots are banned, human operators still need personal protective equipment, handheld gas detectors, and entry permits to inspect these areas on foot,” it said.

Undetected equipment failures cost the world’s 500 largest companies roughly $1.4 trillion each year in preventable downtime, ANYbotics said. In the oil and gas sector alone, a single hour of unplanned downtime can cost up to $500,000 according to Siemens, while U.S. extraction workers face a fatality rate seven times the national average, found NIOSH.

In addition to keeping workers out of harm’s way and minimizing downtime, ANYmal X can provide continuous, repeatable, structured observational data that enhances digital facility planning models, such as digital twins. ANYbotics said this gives them greater contextual detail to be more useful across an entire organization.

Submit your innovation now!

Certifying a robot for hazardous zones is one of the hardest parts of the design process

Every device used in hazardous areas, from radios to flashlights, must be explosion-protected, or “ex-proof,” said ANYbotics. Each unit requires independent certification proving it cannot ignite a flammable atmosphere, even when something fails. ANYbotics built ANYmal X to comply with the ATEX standard in Europe and IECEx globally.

Fixed equipment typically achieves compliance using heavy, explosion-proof enclosures or limiting electrical energy to prevent ignition, the company explained. A legged robot cannot use either approach. It requires high-power motors and a large battery in a frame light enough to climb stairs, exposed cameras and sensors for navigation, and autonomous docking capabilities.

ANYbotics has designed its legged robots for complex environments. Source: ANYbotics

Every one of these components had to be certified ex-proof without sacrificing the autonomous mobile robot’s (AMR) payload capacity, agility, or operating speed, said ANYbotics.

“We asked one question over and over: Which credible event in the life of a walking robot could create an ignition source, and how do we make sure it never does?” said Andrea Corda, chief technology officer of ANYbotics. “Working closely with the certification bodies, we answered that question component by component. The result is a new explosion-protection approach for an entire class of autonomous mobile robots.”

ANYbotics performed a comprehensive ignition-risk assessment for ANYmal X’s service life and implemented safeguards for each potential ignition source. Each of its components has been designed to minimize ignition risk.

The company said the new robot’s AI computer and inspection equipment are enclosed in nitrogen-filled, sealed chambers. Non-metallic shells insulate metallic components, conductive feet provide grounding, and automatic cutoffs monitor temperature. All 12 leg actuators and its battery are protected by flameproof casings. Charging and data transmission use energy barriers, so no connection is exposed to hazardous areas.

ANYmal X’s onboard software monitors the robot’s condition before, during, and after each mission. It also tests durability against shock, vibration, corrosion, solar radiation, and salt mist to ensure that all protective measures function properly in normal use.

ANYmal X ships as a ‘complete system’ proven at industrial scale

“A certified robot is only the entry ticket for inspecting oil, gas, and chemicals facilities,” said Thierry Obédé, chief revenue officer at ANYbotics. “ANYmal X is a complete end-to-end inspection solution built for performance, safety, and security. ANYmal X runs on Shift, which schedules robot missions, organizes findings by asset, and helps maintenance teams track changes over time. To ensure top-tier data protection, the whole system is developed and operated under ISO 27001 information security standards.

“Plants run on process data from their control systems and business data from their ERP,” said Obédé. “The third source, what operators see, hear and measure on their rounds, has always been manual. ANYmal X now captures it autonomously, even inside hazardous areas, and we stand behind the whole chain, from the robot on site to the work order in the maintenance system.”

“Returns are one of the hardest jobs in logistics,” said Gulde. “Returned products almost never arrive in a robot-friendly sequence. Items differ in shape, orientation and packaging, and the mix changes continuously.”

“That is exactly what Cortex is built to handle on the Universal Robots platform,” he said. ”By rapidly reconditioning returned goods for resale, the solution also helps retailers comply with European Union regulations prohibiting the destruction or landfill disposal of returned merchandise.”

NVIDIA plays a role in the collaboration

NVIDIA’s technologies are a key part of the Sereact and Universal Robots demonstration at GTC Berlin. Cortex is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, an open simulation framework, using NVIDIA Cosmos open world models.

It is post-trained with reinforcement learning using NVIDIA Isaac Lab framework and benchmarked on Teradyne Robotics hardware before any model is deployed. In deployment, Cortex runs on NVIDIA Jetson Thor at the cell where inference must happen at line speed and on NVIDIA DGX Spark for site-level development, validation and model updates.

Teradyne Robotics also uses NVIDIA computing in its Universal Robots cobots and Mobile Industrial Robot platforms. The company said it is contributing SimReady OpenUSD robot assets to SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face for both UR and MiR products, helping developers discover and reuse robot models in simulation with less asset preparation.

]]> Talky Labs, a Spanish startup developing AI-powered technology to automate accounting and financial operations, has raised €1.5 million in a pre-Seed funding round to support team expansion, further product development and improvements to the company’s technical infrastructure.

The investment, closed in September 2026, saw participation from venture capital firms HelloWorld, Silence VC, Motive Force, and Aera Capital. Alongside angel investors Sebastián Gunningham; CEO of Remitly, Paul Golbaum; CEO of Lightbase and former CTO of Seedtag, and Javier Morenés, among others.

“Two years ago, I met my co-founder Jorge Beamonte at a networking event. That night, I called my mom and told her: ‘Mom, today is the most important day of my life. Everything is about to change,‘” said Maximilian Letón in a public statement.

Talky’s funding comes amid a series of European investments in AI-powered accounting and financial operations during 2026.

In Belgium, Dytto raised €1.5 million to develop its AI assistant for accountants, while Denmark’s Plinto secured €2.9 million for automated financial controls. Germany’s mika raised €6 million for AI-powered accounting and tax services, and UK-based Zalos obtained €3.1 million for enterprise finance automation.

In Spain, Barcelona-based Dolfin secured €2.1 million for adjacent financial workflows.

Together these rounds amount to approximately €66.8 million, including Talky’s investment.

“Every company has its own way of doing accounting, and it’s almost never written down. Talky learns those criteria, applies them to the hard cases and turns them into information for better decisions,” adds Jorge Beamonte, co-founder and CEO of Talky.

Founded in 2025 by Jorge Beamonte; CEO, and Maximilian Letón (23); COO, Talky aims to help businesses automate financial processes that traditionally depend on accountants’ experience and knowledge of internal company practices. Despite operating with a team of just nine employees, the startup reports having processed more than 1.8 million documents and over €2 billion in client expenditure through its platform.

The company addresses a common challenge in corporate finance departments: accounting decisions often rely on information scattered across enterprise systems, spreadsheets, emails, contracts and individual employees’ knowledge. While conventional automation tools can process standard transactions, unusual invoices or exceptions frequently require manual intervention, creating delays and increasing the risk of errors.

Talky’s platform uses AI to learn from a company’s historical accounting records and the expertise of its financial teams. Rather than relying exclusively on predefined rules, its technology identifies how previous transactions were handled, extracts relevant accounting criteria and applies that knowledge to new financial operations.

When the system encounters an unfamiliar situation or lacks sufficient information to make a decision, it identifies the appropriate employee to consult.

According to the startup, its technology processes between 86% and 93% of accounting documents without human intervention. The platform can read invoices, suggest accounting entries, review tax information and reconcile bank transactions before recording the results in the client’s enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.

The funding comes as Talky looks to expand its presence among large enterprises and financial services providers managing high volumes of transactions. Its founders have identified recruitment as a central priority, with plans to grow the team while continuing to develop the platform alongside existing customers.

]]> PaperFoam, a Dutch company that manufactures sustainable, biodegradable, starch-based packaging, has secured a €2 million loan from Invest International to expand its production facility in the Czech Republic and strengthen working capital for its Malaysian and U.S. plants.

The Hague-based Invest International is a Dutch government-backed organisation that helps Dutch and Dutch-linked businesses overcome barriers by providing financial support, foreign market knowledge, and sector expertise.

Jeroen Plag, Chief Investment Officer at Invest International, said, “PaperFoam is a great example of a Dutch innovator that has travelled a difficult path from promising technology to an internationally scalable company. Our involvement dates back to 2020, when we supported the company during its first expansion into the Czech Republic. 

“With this new investment, we’re helping to enable the next phase of growth at a time when traditional financiers still view it as too risky. For the Netherlands, it’s crucial that we help green leaders in the manufacturing industry scale up. This way, we retain innovation within our own country and demonstrate that sustainability and international competitiveness go hand in hand.”

Founded in 1998, Paperfoam was founded by Vertis Holding, a former Dutch IT company. The Barneveld-based company is a global provider of biodegradable starch-based packaging solutions, with production facilities in the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, the United States, and Malaysia. 

PaperFoam b.v. is owned by PaperFoam Holding b.v. Since March 2023, Nissha Co. Ltd., a Japanese stock-listed company, has owned 30% of PaperFoam Holding b.v. The other 70% is owned by Sustainable Pioneers Holding b.v., a Dutch entity.

PaperFoam states that it develops packaging solutions based on starch and natural fibres as a fully fledged alternative to conventional plastic and paper. Using its patented foaming technology and natural raw materials, the company creates lightweight packaging with an “exceptionally low” carbon footprint. The material is also fully compostable, and the fibres can be easily recycled into paper.

PaperFoam Plus is thicker and stronger than PaperFoam and is designed as a sustainable alternative to EPS (Expanded Polystyrene). It offers protective qualities (drop-tested up to 5 kg), is up to 5 mm thick, and is compostable in both home and industrial composters.

The company serves customers in sectors such as consumer electronics, medical, dry food, and cosmetics.

Willem Derkman, CEO of PaperFoam, said, “Developing an innovative and sustainable alternative to traditional packaging requires time, investment, and partners who are willing to look further ahead. Thanks to the ongoing support from Invest International, we have been able to take important steps in our international growth. This funding helps us further expand our production capacity and efficiently serve new markets and clients.”

According to the company, production machinery from Dutch suppliers Kuyer Metaal in Nijkerk and Shuffle-Mix in Barneveld makes the expansion possible in part.

This will directly support companies across the space supply chain, from component manufacturers and launch technology developers to […]

The post European SpaceTech recieves a €560 million injection to promote European sovereignty appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> A new partnership between Deutsche Bank and the European Investment Bank (EIB) is set to mobilise a €560 million investment towards European SpaceTech, helping businesses scale, bring new tech to market, and strengthen Europe’s independent space capabilities.

This will directly support companies across the space supply chain, from component manufacturers and launch technology developers to satellite applications and in-orbit services.

“This new partnership between the EIB and Deutsche Bank will help unlock investment in Germany and across Europe – backing the companies, supply chains and technologies that will make Europe’s space sector stronger, more competitive and ready to scale,” said Nicola Beer, European Investment Bank Vice-President.

The agreement follows a series of SpaceTech financing announcements across Europe in 2026.

In Germany, Munich-based The Exploration Company secured €387 million, HyImpulse Technologies raised more than €50 million, ATMOS Space Cargo attracted €25.7 million and deltaVision received €10.2 million.

Elsewhere, Finland’s ICEYE raised €450 million in primary funding, Spain’s PLD Space extended its Series C to €288 million and France’s UNIVITY secured €27 million.

Alongside further announcements involving AIRMO, Hydrosat and Arkadia Space, these financings exceeded €1.3 billion, independently of the proposed Deutsche Bank–EIB investment mobilisation.

EU-Startups previously reported on the EIB’s separate €30 million venture-debt loan to PLD Space in April 2026.

“Europe has the engineering talent to lead in space. Our job is to help finance its next stage of growth,” added Marc Mueller, Global Head Trade Finance & Lending at Deutsche Bank. “Working with the EIB, we can offer space businesses the long-term financing they need to invest, expand production and compete internationally.”

Agreed ahead of the European Space Agency (ESA) Space Investor Forum in Munich, this operation also builds on cooperation between the EIB and European Space Agency to address the financing needs of Europe’s space sector. ESA provides market intelligence and sector expertise to support the development of financing solutions that reflect the needs of space SMEs and Mid-Caps and enable the space sector to access finance.

It also helps connect these financing opportunities with the European space ecosystem, raising awareness among eligible companies and facilitating outreach to potential beneficiaries.

The initiative will support investment in technologies including reusable launchers and spacecraft, advanced propulsion systems, satellite manufacturing and Earth observation. These technologies underpin services ranging from communications and navigation to wildfire detection, pollution monitoring and security.

The financing will have a pan-European reach, with around half of investment expected in Germany and the remainder elsewhere in the EU.

“This partnership with Deutsche Bank will help companies across Europe’s space sector invest in the technologies, production capacity and supply chains needed to scale up and compete globally. In doing so, we are strengthening Europe’s capacity to deliver essential space services more autonomously,” said Robert de Groot, European Investment Bank Vice-President.”

Space businesses often face long development cycles, complex technologies and uncertain commercial returns, making conventional bank lending harder to secure. The partnership aims to give Deutsche Bank long-term funding and flexible financing structures to support commercially viable companies investing in their next stage of growth.

The partnership forms part of Space TechEU, the EIB’s dedicated space financing programme launched in November 2025, designed to mobilise an estimated €1.4 billion in investment with commercial banking partners.

The idea is that this will compliment broader EIB Group support through direct investment loans, venture debt, equity investment and advisory services. By combining these instruments with commercial bank lending, the Group aims to help European space companies secure financing at successive stages of development – from innovation to industrial expansion.

“Europe has a growing number of space companies with outstanding technologies that are ready to scale,” said ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher. “The next step is ensuring they have access to the capital they need to grow. This initiative can help open that path, enabling European space companies to scale up, compete and succeed.”

The post European SpaceTech recieves a €560 million injection to promote European sovereignty appeared first on EU-Startups.

The combined entity will span more than 5,000 members and partners across 25 countries on six continents. The network links climate investors, […]

]]> Greentech Alliance (GTA), a Berlin-based global connection network for sustainable technology businesses, has agreed to acquire Intermobility, a Paris-based transport and mobility network connecting more than 1,000 companies, public authorities, and ecosystem players.

The combined entity will span more than 5,000 members and partners across 25 countries on six continents. The network links climate investors, startups, corporates, and policymakers in one of Europe’s most challenging sectors to decarbonise.

“Europe does not have a mobility technology problem, it has a coordination problem. The capital, the startups and the cities are all there, but they rarely meet. Bringing Intermobility into Greentech Alliance puts the people who build, fund and buy mobility solutions in one network, and we are inviting investors and companies who want a seat at that table to join us,” said Charles Newton Price, CEO, Greentech Alliance.

The acquisition, whose financial terms were not disclosed, comes as Europe grapples with transport emissions that have remained stubbornly above 1990 levels and as startup funding continues to decline. According to the European Environment Agency, transport emissions were 25.3% above 1990 levels in 2023 and accounted for around 31% of total EU emissions. 

Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based clean-transport advocacy group, estimates the sector needs €310 billion in annual investment by 2030 to meet climate targets. However, data from Via ID and Dealroom show European mobility startups closed 654 funding rounds in 2025, down from 785 the year before, raising $10.1 billion in total private funding. Greentech Alliance says the acquisition is designed to bridge this gap.

Founded in Berlin in May 2020 by Lubomila Jordanova, Simon Thies, Hannah Kromminga, and Jan-Jaap Verhoeve, Greentech Alliance is a curated global network for ventures, investors, educators and partners building what it describes as a more regenerative economy. The organisation is incorporated as both a Canadian not-for-profit and a German for-profit company.

It currently counts more than 3,000 community members and partners across six continents, including more than 700 investor members, and has facilitated more than 2,000 introductions.

Intermobility was founded in 2022 by François Hoehlinger as a European network of transport and mobility players spanning private companies and public institutions. By bringing Intermobility’s operators, cities and public authorities into the same network as GTA’s climate investors, startups, and corporates, the deal paves the way for a mobility solution to mature from pilot to scale.

For investors, GTA membership will now offer curated access to mobility ventures from both communities, alongside introductions to co-investors, corporates and public buyers. For companies. It opens direct channels to customers, pilots and capital across Europe and beyond.

The two organisations will also explore joint ventures and financing projects, including work linked to GTA’s Climate Zero programmes, subject to separate approval. Hoehlinger will join GTA’s board to help shape the Alliance’s direction as it scales internationally.

“Mobility only changes when founders, investors, operators and public authorities move together. Intermobility built that table in Europe. Greentech Alliance gives it international reach and access to capital, while keeping a grounded European perspective at its heart,” said Hoehlinger, founder, Intermobility.

Since its inception, GTA has successfully connected members on its network and with the acquisition of Intermobility, it has an opportunity to move beyond connection. Using its proven model of trusted introductions and curated membership, the alliance will aim to bridge the gap between climate solutions and funding shortfall.

]]> OPINION: You can’t scale with a startup mindset https://www.eu-startups.com/2026/10/opinion-you-cant-scale-with-a-startup-mindset/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:29:36 +0000 https://www.eu-startups.com/?p=373257 The best advice once your company achieves product-market fit? Don’t get stuck on things that got you there, keep adjusting your architecture and workflow to fit your new realities and sizes. Starting strong is one thing, but the real point is pushing past the growth ceiling without crashing: McKinsey found 78% of products launched successfully […]

The post OPINION: You can’t scale with a startup mindset appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> The best advice once your company achieves product-market fit? Don’t get stuck on things that got you there, keep adjusting your architecture and workflow to fit your new realities and sizes.

Starting strong is one thing, but the real point is pushing past the growth ceiling without crashing: McKinsey found 78% of products launched successfully only to fail later on. Having worked in international expansion, I have seen how the practices that help a startup gain traction can cause troubles as it grows. Here is my top-5 of what’s better to be changed once a company is too big for a startup mode, and what habits are worth keeping in mind.

Money moves faster than decisions

Congratulations, it’s been your big funding round. Having more capital can feel like you have almost unlimited freedom to chase everything at once. This money mostly goes to ideas that already work, more on tests, all at once. In a ten-person startup, the founder knows every ongoing experiment. In a 100-person company, nobody does. Tests overlap, compete for the same target audience, and rarely get switched off. Meanwhile, decision-making slows down as more people have something to say. More money won’t fix messy operations, it just makes the mistakes more expensive.

The Turkish quick-commerce company Getir expanded to nine countries by the end of 2021 and bought Berlin rival Gorillas for €1.13 billon ($1.2 billion) in December 2022. Yet, in a few years the company chose to exit Germany, the UK and the Netherlands to focus back on its core  Turkish business. Having enough money to go global doesn’t automatically mean it’s the right move. Sustainable scaling requires strong research: diving into local consumer behavior, understanding specific market nuances, and adapting your model to what local buyers actually want.

To grow without burning capital, build a fixed and transparent framework of your experiments: a single log where every project has one owner, a set budget, a clear deadline, and kill criteria agreed before launch. Each ongoing test should be backed by a specific hypothesis and (ideally) data. If an experiment went great in one market, don’t hurry to move forward –  assess whether the conditions that made it work still apply in other regions.

Customer behaviour, channel preferences, and acquisition costs vary from country to country, so goals need to be tailored to actual team capacity and adapted market by market.

Hiring and ownership need a system

In a startup mode, team members do everything at once, no matter the difficulty level. Quite often, juniors jump in wherever they’re needed, keep going, and naturally become team leads. Loyalty is important, but management requires a different skillset. Wharton professor Peter Cappelli points out that top individual contributors who get promoted often make the weakest managers. 

The same applies at the executive level. When founders are responsible for each new decision, they’re likely to slow down processes in their own business. Getting advice and seeing fresh perspectives from someone who has their own area of responsibility creates a clear structure with solid boundaries. 

Bringing in senior leadership only works if you fix how responsibility is assigned. As headcount grows, each person assumes someone else is handling it. Psychologists call this diffusion of responsibility. Every project needs one named owner with the authority to execute, and clear processes for who decides and who reports progress. If a project has two owners, in practice, it has none.

AI will not replace everyone

Every company that’s actively growing now feels pressure to automate more and hire less. But implementation itself is a huge project, and for plenty of everyday tasks, a skilled person is still faster, cheaper, and far less painful to manage.

In May 2025, Klarna backtracked their earlier beliefs that AI has a potential to replace human work. A bit more than a year earlier, the company paused hiring customer service agents in favour of their AI assistant. The bot took 75% of the company’s customer chats  in more than 35 languages. It sounded high-potential at first, but then there was: lower quality of support. Klarna began recruiting human agents again, while AI keeps handling simpler requests. 

The point is to define for your business when to use AI, and when human touch is a super power. Everything repetitive and predictable can go to the AI team, and situations that win from empathy and critical thinking, are better left for people. The next step is to start educating your team to make sure they’re staying flexible and are using modern solutions for the new way of living.

AI is way more than just right prompting. Show employees how they can make their own simple tools for their daily workflows – through online courses, internal bootcamps, hackathons, or any other solutions that work best for your business. Developers can then turn the most promising ideas into advanced solutions.

Plan beyond the next quarter

Startups live month-over-month. Meanwhile, scaling needs a longer horizon, with a solid six-month and a year plan, all while maintaining a flexible approach. Your core metrics have to evolve, too. 

A longer perspective also offers you a unique view of which temporary fixes no longer work and need to be redone in favour of a stronger infrastructure. Spreadsheets and manual workarounds are fine at a hundred orders a day, not at a hundred thousand. A McKinsey survey revealed that about 30% of CIOs said more than 20% of their new-product budget is diverted to fixing tech debt.

To keep everything aligned, run a strategy session every six months. On a more routine basis, make it a norm to have bi-weekly leadership syncs to review progress, track unit economics, and adjust tactics before small operational cracks can turn into a real problem.

Growth makes centralisation a necessity

As you grow, your operational architecture has to go through changes, including a call on what stays central and what lives in-market. Having worked in international expansion, I’ve seen how companies hit a ceiling when they try to manage global growth from two extreme ends: either micro-managing every local solution or letting regional teams operate like separate startups.

Core product decisions, CRM, brand guidelines, and customer support standards require consistency, so they are best managed centrally. Where you can really leave room for local teams is in what they know best: local landscape, relationships and competitors, regional traditions, preferences, and behaviors. The real challenge here is finding the right balance. Centralization cuts out messy duplication and keeps your brand cohesive, but excessive control from the top will blindside you to market-specific realities.

Scale up, but keep the best of the startup mindset. Stay adaptable. Keep testing (but make it wisely and don’t waste resources). Count money the way you did when there was very little of it, because the budget is never infinite, no matter how big the last round was.

]]> Easol, a London-based experience commerce platform, has closed a €26.78 million ($30 million) Series A extension round, bringing its total raised to date to €53.57 million ($60 million).

The round comprises €17.85 million ($20 million) in equity and an €8.92 million ($10 million) debt facility. The equity portion was led by Y Combinator, with participation from Tiger Global, Foundation Capital, FMZ Ventures, Notion Capital, and Eight Roads. The debt facility was provided by Viola Credit.

“We built Easol to give experience businesses control over their entire business and bring their technology in-house. AI is now allowing us to do so much more, with rising costs and tighter margins we can now support experience creators in scaling their business growing revenue in ways we couldn’t have imagined when we first launched the platform in 2021,” said Ben Simpson, co-founder and CEO of Easol.

Founded in 2021 by husband and wife duo Ben and Lisa Simpson, co-founders of Rise Festival, who previously managed live experiences drawing two million guests annually across locations from the French Alps to the Sahara Desert. While running Rise Festival, the Simpsons grew frustrated with managing experience businesses across too many disconnected tools that offered no real data ownership.

“The technology and software solutions that experience businesses must stitch together to be able to offer a variety of different booking, payment and activity options develops a working environment for creators that is complex, inflexible, and expensive,” they told EU-Startups.com in 2022.

To overcome this disconnected tools bottleneck, they set out to build a platform that gave experience creators genuine control of their operations. As an all-in-one platform, Easol brings bookings, payments, marketing, customer support and guest data under a single connected system, all hosted on the client’s own domain and kept entirely within the business’s ownership. The company says it has never sold its customers’ data to third parties.

Easol now has offices in London, New York, and Los Angeles, and has powered experiences booked by 2.8 million guests across more than 135 countries so far in 2026. Its client roster includes Coachella, Stagecoach, Defected, Afronation, Rapha, Swingers – The Home of Revelry, Boots in the Park, State of Play Hospitality, Bingo Loco, Snowboxx, The Cube, and Hijingo, among others.

The funding enabled Easol to develop and launch Teammates, its new agentic AI tools built natively inside the platform. Teammates helps experience businesses to create their own AI agents covering sales, support and operations. These agents rely on live business data to identify missed revenue, resolve guest queries, update bookings and surface actionable insights automatically.

Easol says many experience businesses run on lean central teams, leaving significant revenue on the table. In early deployments, one Teammates agent reportedly identified approximately $50,000 in upsell opportunities from guests with no add-ons attached to their bookings, and generated the outreach to pursue them while another client recovered $28,000 in outstanding payments in seconds.

Eve Szlendak, Head of Sales, State of Play Hospitality UK, said, ”I used to spend up to three days building reports to capture every possible scenario. Now, the dashboards give me the information I need instantly.”

Since its earliest days, Easol has argued that digitising the experience economy is not merely a convenience but a commercial necessity. With surging demand for live and in-person experiences, the company sees AI as a competitive advantage to operate, analyse, and take action across whole businesses.

]]> Ares Intelligence, a London-based startup building what it describes as an evidence-based platform for AI transformation, has secured €2.9 million (£2.48 million) in funding.

The round was backed by Creandum and Lakestar, with participation from angels connected to Google DeepMind.

“Enterprise AI today is mostly coding, and that’s only the start. The opportunity across the rest of the business is far bigger and still largely untapped, and we’re at the very beginning of enterprise adoption,” said Richard Keuntje, Vice President, Creandum.

Founded in 2026 by Matt Falconer and 21-year-old Alfie Ranstead, Ares Intelligence was built to solve a problem the founders encountered first-hand while running Instruct, their previous automation company. It says customers ran into the same problem: they wanted to automate parts of their business but had no reliable way of knowing where to begin. Ares Intelligence was to fix this knowledge gap.

The platform deploys an AI interviewer that holds confidential, voice-based conversations with every employee in an organisation, in more than 70 languages. Within weeks, leadership receives a prioritised, evidence-led roadmap identifying where AI can save time and money.

Ares’ platform is GDPR- and SOC 2-compliant, with anonymisation controls that let businesses mask names, redact voices, or strip role metadata before reports reach leadership. Customers can deploy it on their own cloud or use Ares’ infrastructure, in the EU or the US, with data retention windows set by the business.

The founders say the entire process, from training employees on what AI can do to conducting individual interviews, collecting insights and drafting recommendations, takes weeks rather than the months usually taken by a consulting firm.

Ares Intelligence’s approach also flips the script on top-down AI strategy by not relying only on a handful of senior managers to identify AI transformation opportunities. The company’s AI interviewer captures the knowledge of the people closest to the day-to-day work, identifies gaps such as manual workarounds, broken handoffs, and use of unapproved AI tools.

“Businesses across Europe know they need to adopt AI, but many still don’t know where to start. It’s vital that companies begin their AI transformations now to avoid falling behind,” said Falconer, co-founder and CEO, Ares Intelligence.

]]> A friend of mine runs a company that builds software for other companies. He has the same problem in most sales meetings. He shows what the system can do, the prospect leans forward and asks how it works, and my friend, who is not daft, goes slightly vague. If he explains it properly, they might go away and build it themselves.

Some of them go away and build it anyway. About a year later, a fair number rang back and asked for help.

So there is still money in knowing how to make something work. What AI has done is make the gap between a clever demo and a defensible company rather uncomfortable to look at. The tools that let your team build sophisticated software cheaply let a competitor rebuild it cheaply too, and your customers can have a go over a long weekend. The development bill has come down for everyone. That includes the people trying to put you out of business.

Your supplier has a product team too

In my previous article, I asked what would happen to a startup if its model disappeared tomorrow. There is a quieter version of that dependency. The supplier carries on answering your API calls and starts selling what you sell.

On 24 February, Anthropic released finance plugins for Claude covering equity research, investment banking, private equity and wealth management, with workflows that run across Excel and PowerPoint. If you were selling an AI equity research assistant on 23 February, you had a new slide to write for your next board meeting.

Figma had it worse. On 17 February, it announced an integration with Claude Code, letting interfaces built in Claude drop straight onto the Figma canvas. On 17 April, Anthropic launched Claude Design, which produces interface mockups and interactive prototypes. Three days earlier, Anthropic’s chief product officer had stepped down from Figma’s board, which, in hindsight, was something of a hint. Figma’s shares fell 7% on launch day. Presumably the next partnership meeting had a slightly different atmosphere.

You may also be using that provider’s tools to build the product it is about to replace. I wouldn’t hold that against anyone. I would just keep it in mind.

Somebody else’s high street

In February 2025, Chegg, which sells homework help to students, reported that its non-subscriber traffic for January was down 49%, against a decline of 8% in the second quarter of 2024. It blamed Google’s AI Overviews for answering the questions that used to send students to its site, and sued Google that same week. That is Chegg’s account, and Google disputes it. The shape of the problem reaches well beyond homework.

The platform that sends customers to your door can start answering their questions on the doorstep. You still have a website. Fewer people have a reason to visit it.

Before anyone talks about a moat, it is worth checking how much of the surrounding land you actually own.

Six months used to be a moat

A feature that once took six months of engineering may now take a fraction of that. Marvellous, until you realise those six months were most of what kept the competition out.

Customers do the same sum. Some will decide their own developers can rebuild enough of your product in-house. They will underestimate the maintenance and the awkward exceptions, as my friend’s returning clients did. Their attempt still costs him a year of sales, and he doesn’t get the year back when they ring.

So where is the moat?

It starts with knowing how to get a better result. It deepens with the things you learn that a competitor can’t pick up by watching your demo.

Take my own industry. Getting an AI to produce a plausible trade recommendation is easy to show on stage. Getting software to behave inside a broker’s real trading infrastructure is another matter. Permissions have to hold when an instruction is ambiguous; someone has to reconcile the books when a transaction fails halfway through. None of this appears in the sales presentation. It turns up in the third week of production, usually on a Monday.

A competitor can copy your screen without knowing how you handle any of that. A customer can build a prototype without ever finding out why your production version took so long.

Proprietary data helps, provided you actually have the rights to use it. A pile of public documents anyone can download offers rather less protection. Calling it a knowledge base does not make it yours.

The test is simple enough. If someone offered your visible features at half the price, would your customers stay? “We shipped first” is not an answer.

Make sure you can change the engine

Whatever the advantage is, it has to survive a change of model. 

Founders should know what they would run instead of their current provider, and whether it is good enough on their customers’ actual work. Benchmarks are not customers. For some applications, an open-weight model hosted in-house is the sensible answer.

Buying a server does not give you a moat. It does stop a supplier’s product roadmap from closing your company.

If switching providers would strip out everything your customers value, then the valuable part was never yours. You were renting it.

Whose moat does regulation dig?

This is also why I am skeptical of calls for an AI slowdown. A voluntary pause is hard to hold when competitors keep building and customers can leave. The data centres still need paying for.

Regulation can do something a voluntary pause can’t. It can make getting in more expensive.

A large provider spreads the cost of compliance across a business that already exists. A startup has to find that money before it has much revenue. Rules that make independent models prohibitively expensive would leave smaller companies even more dependent on the suppliers already eating into their margins.

There are good reasons to regulate AI. But when the biggest providers ask for more rules, I’d like to know who can afford to follow them. A requirement their legal department absorbs before lunch may be enough to stop a smaller competitor getting funded at all.

Europe’s AI Act makes some allowances for this, including exemptions for certain open-source models. Much depends on the detail. Writing rules that only the largest companies can afford to follow is an excellent way of keeping them the largest companies.

What they were paying for

Founders should assume cheaper development means more competition. The defence has to be something that grows every time you serve a customer and is still standing after the next model release.

Clients came back because copying the idea was easier than delivering the result. AI made their first attempt cheaper. It did not give them the vendor’s experience. They saved on development and spent a year finding out what they had been paying for.

The pattern is familiar. An internal team looks at a vendor’s product and concludes it could be rebuilt in a couple of sprints. Occasionally, it can. More often, the organisation pays for the lesson twice: once in the build, and again in the operational gaps that only appear in production.

]]> Bleu Robotics, a Paris-based startup building AI models for industrial humanoid robots, has raised a €5 million pre-Seed round, to reach its goal of reducing the full humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or shorter.

The round was co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with participation from Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst, and board members at Meta.

Benoît Berkoukchi, co-founder of Bleu Robotics, says, “Humanoid robots in manufacturing are the next automotive sector, with the potential to help Europe and the US reshore production. But most robotics companies are trying to train humanoids with millions of data points and build fully general-purpose models. That approach isn’t suited to manufacturing. There isn’t enough data on factory work, and there won’t be internet-scale data, the kind LLMs were built on, for robots for a long time. Our methodology means we can do more with less.”

The round comes amid continued European investment in robotics software, humanoid systems and Physical AI during 2026.

In France, Paris-based Inbolt raised €11 million to expand its hardware-agnostic robot intelligence platform, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics secured €26 million to develop AI-powered skills for industrial robots.

Elsewhere, Belgium’s Motion raised €1.7 million for humanoid deployment, Spain’s THEKER secured €73 million to scale generalist industrial robotics, and London-based Humanoid raised €133 million for its industrial humanoid platform.

Together with funding rounds for Germany’s Sereact, Switzerland’s Enact Intelligence and Poland’s Nomagic, these financings total €372.7 million in 2026, rising to €377.7 million when including Bleu Robotics’ latest round.

Thomas Poitrineau, Investor at Contrarian Ventures, adds, “We were attracted to Bleu Robotics because of their ambitious choice to rethink how humanoid robotics software should work from first principles. It’s rare to find a company led by two world-class robotics researchers and a manufacturing expert, which is also why their software works differently from their competition. Their goal is far bigger than simply making the best model in a lab. It’s an approach that can already scale, putting robots to work in factories within months rather than years.”

Founded in Paris in 2025 by two INRIA researchers and a former Renault manufacturing manager, Bleu’s abductive learning technology reportedly lets robots learn new tasks from only a handful of operator demonstrations.

Its software runs on any humanoid platform and includes the AI model and training devices needed to teach robots on the factory floor.

According to the International Federation of Robotics, there were 5 million industrial robots operating globally in 2025. However, these robots are built to repeat fixed tasks, and are unable to adapt to the high-mix, low-volume production now common in modern manufacturing, so that work still falls to human workers.

Humanoid robots are needed to automate a wider range of complex tasks. While hardware has advanced significantly in recent years, software development has struggled to keep pace, limiting real-world deployment.

Interact Analysis found that of the 20,000-plus humanoids produced last year, only 10% reached real-world applications. Most of these robots today rely on end-to-end models, which learn everything in a single black box and require massive amounts of data to achieve production-ready reliability.

As a result, deployment remains costly and time-consuming for manufacturers, often requiring hundreds of hours of training data, with no guarantee the robot will perform reliably.

Instead of an end-to-end model, Bleu Robotics’ abductive learning model allows the robot to learn a new task from as few as ten operator demonstrations, while keeping the explainability required for industrial safety and the 99%+ accuracy that production lines demand.

]]>
In Brief 7 min read
  • NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed the 100th US spacewalk from the International Space Station.
  • The astronauts installed and deployed the ISS's seventh roll-out solar array, part of a programme to boost the station's power supply by up to 30%.
  • The mission also offers a closer look at how astronauts train for, prepare for and carry out spacewalks in the vacuum of space.

Two astronauts have completed a seven-hour spacewalk outside the International Space Station (ISS), installing and deploying a new solar array in a mission that marked the 100th US spacewalk from the orbiting laboratory.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent seven hours and 11 minutes working outside the station on 29 October. They returned to the Quest airlock at 3:08 p.m. Eastern Time after successfully installing the seventh of eight planned roll-out solar arrays.

Although it was the 100th US spacewalk conducted from the ISS without a visiting space shuttle docked to it, the mission was the 285th spacewalk overall in support of the station. The larger figure includes 66 spacewalks from the Russian segment and 119 carried out by visiting space shuttle crews.

The new equipment will help provide electricity for the station’s experiments, life-support systems and other operations. NASA says the additional power will also support the ISS’s eventual safe and controlled return to Earth.

The spacewalk was Menon’s fourth but Kutryk’s first. It was also the first by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured outside the station with NASA astronaut Anne McClain.

A seven-hour job outside the space station

Menon and Kutryk began their spacewalk at 7:57 a.m. Eastern Time, leaving the station through its Quest airlock.

Menon wore a spacesuit marked with red stripes, while Kutryk wore an unmarked white suit, allowing mission controllers and television viewers to distinguish between them.

Their principal task was to install an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, known as an IROSA, on the station’s 2A electrical power channel.

The equipment had been delivered earlier in October aboard a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft. It was temporarily stored on a platform outside the ISS until the astronauts could install it.

The solar array weighs approximately 340 kg and measures about three metres long in its packed configuration.

After releasing it from its temporary mounting, Menon attached himself to the end of Canadarm2, the station’s Canadian-built robotic arm. Carrying the folded solar array, he travelled on the arm towards the installation site on the station’s port-side structure.

Kutryk made his way separately along the station’s framework, remaining secured by safety tethers.

Once together at the worksite, the astronauts mounted the equipment and connected it to the station’s electrical system.

Unlike conventional solar panels that require motors to unfold, the new array uses stored energy in flexible carbon-composite supports to unroll itself.

The panel extended to approximately 19 metres in length. It took about just over 11 minutes to deploy fully.

The astronauts also completed additional preparatory work for the next spacewalk, including tasks involving the mounting equipment for the eighth and final roll-out array.

Why the space station needs more electricity

The ISS has relied on large solar panels to generate electricity since its assembly began in orbit.

But the original arrays have exceeded their intended 15-year service life, and their power output has declined with age.

NASA has been adding smaller, more efficient roll-out arrays alongside the older panels rather than replacing the entire original system.

The new panels partly cover the existing arrays while generating additional electricity.

When all eight roll-out arrays are installed, NASA expects the station’s available power to increase by up to 30%, raising its generating capacity from approximately 160 kilowatts to 215 kilowatts.

The extra electricity will support scientific research, station equipment and essential operations during the remaining years of the ISS programme.

It will also help maintain the systems needed for the station’s planned controlled deorbit at the end of its operational life.

Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to conduct another spacewalk on 5 November to install the eighth and final roll-out array on the 3B electrical power channel.

That installation is expected to complete the station’s solar power upgrade programme.

How the astronauts prepared for the spacewalk

The work outside the ISS was the result of several days of preparation by the station’s Expedition 75 crew.

Earlier in the week, Menon and Kutryk rehearsed the movements needed to carry the solar array from its storage platform to the installation site.

Their colleagues, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, practised operating Canadarm2 and reviewed the camera positions and lighting conditions needed to monitor the work.

The two spacewalkers organised their tools inside the Quest airlock and prepared small checklists that could be attached to the cuffs of their spacesuits.

They also checked their suits’ oxygen, cooling, water and communications systems. Their emergency jetpacks were inspected to ensure that the batteries, fuel supplies and thrusters were working.

On Wednesday, the four astronauts held final discussions with specialists on Earth, reviewing the installation procedure and the robotic arm’s movements.

Watkins and Delaney remained inside the station during Thursday’s operation, helping the spacewalkers prepare and supporting the work outside.

What is a spacewalk and how is it done?

A spacewalk is any activity in which an astronaut leaves a spacecraft while in space. NASA calls it an extravehicular activity, or EVA.

Despite the name, astronauts do not actually walk. In the absence of normal gravity, they move by holding onto handrails, pulling themselves along structures or using equipment such as robotic arms.

Spacewalks allow astronauts to repair equipment, install new hardware and carry out experiments that cannot be performed inside a spacecraft.

Before leaving the station, astronauts put on specially designed spacesuits that function much like miniature spacecraft. They provide oxygen for breathing, regulate body temperature, maintain pressure and allow communication with the crew and mission controllers.

Preparation begins several hours before the astronauts go outside.

One important precaution is breathing pure oxygen to remove excess nitrogen from the body. Without this procedure, changes in pressure could cause nitrogen bubbles to form in the bloodstream and tissues, producing a painful condition known as decompression sickness, or the bends. Scuba divers face a similar risk.

Astronauts leave through an airlock, a small chamber with two doors. The inner door is closed before air is removed from the chamber, allowing the outer hatch to open without releasing the station’s atmosphere into space.

Once outside, astronauts remain attached to the station by safety tethers. Their tools are also secured to prevent them from floating away.

They carry an emergency device called SAFER, short for Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue. Worn like a backpack, it uses small thrusters that an astronaut can control with a hand-operated device to return to the station if accidentally separated from it.

A typical ISS spacewalk lasts between five and eight hours, depending on the work involved.

Training for work in the vacuum of space

Long before astronauts attempt these operations in orbit, they practise on Earth.

One of NASA’s main training facilities is the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory near Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

The enormous swimming pool contains approximately 6.2 million gallons of water and allows astronauts wearing training spacesuits to rehearse tasks around submerged replicas of spacecraft structures.

By carefully adjusting their buoyancy, instructors can recreate some of the difficulties of moving and handling equipment in weightlessness.

Astronauts also use virtual reality systems to practise working outside the station. Special headsets and gloves allow them to rehearse movements, become familiar with their surroundings and prepare for complicated operations.

These rehearsals are especially important because even simple tasks can become difficult in bulky, pressurised spacesuits.

From the first spacewalk in 1965 to the ISS’s 100th US excursion

The history of spacewalking began more than six decades ago.

On 18 March 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov became the first person to leave a spacecraft in orbit. His historic spacewalk lasted about ten minutes.

Less than three months later, on 3 June 1965, NASA astronaut Ed White became the first American to conduct a spacewalk during the Gemini 4 mission. He spent approximately 23 minutes outside his spacecraft.

Spacewalking later became essential to human space exploration, particularly during the construction of the ISS.

Astronauts helped assemble the station in orbit, connecting modules, installing equipment and carrying out repairs that could not be completed by robots alone.

The first US spacewalk from the station’s Quest airlock took place on 20 February 2002, when NASA astronauts Carl Walz and Daniel Bursch spent five hours and 47 minutes testing its systems and carrying out maintenance.

The record for the most spacewalks by an individual astronaut belongs to Russian cosmonaut Anatoly Solovyev, who completed 16 excursions totalling more than 82 hours.

In Brief 3 min read
  • NASA's X-59 is designed to make supersonic flight quieter for people on the ground.
  • The aircraft is testing technologies that could influence future aviation regulations.
  • Comparisons with Concorde highlight how supersonic ambitions have evolved over time.

At first glance, NASA‘s X-59 Quesst looks like a modern-day Concorde. Yet the experimental aircraft has been designed with a completely different objective in mind.

Here’s how NASA’s X-59 compares with Concorde across speed, altitude, design and supersonic noise.

X-59 vs Concorde: Which aircraft is faster?

The X-59 has reached Mach 1.53 during flight testing, faster than its planned cruising speed of Mach 1.4. But it still has some way to go to match Concorde.

The iconic Anglo-French airliner cruised at Mach 2.04, approximately 1,354 mph (2,179 km/h), carrying 100 passengers between Europe and the United States in around three and a half hours.

The X-59, developed by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works for NASA, has reached approximately 1,010 mph (1,625 km/h). Its usual operating speed will be around 925 mph (1,490 km/h).

Why sonic booms happen and how NASA’s X-59 Quesst plans to eliminate them Why sonic booms happen and how NASA’s X-59 Quesst plans to eliminate them

How do Concorde and the X-59 compare?

Concorde entered commercial service in 1976 with British Airways and Air France and retired in 2003. It remains the fastest passenger aircraft ever to have flown. 

The X-59, which first flew in October 2025, is an experimental aircraft with room for just one pilot.

Why was Concorde restricted in the United States?

Concorde’s sonic boom was loud enough to disturb people on the ground, which hampered supersonic operations.

The US Federal Aviation Administration introduced restrictions on civilian supersonic flights over land in 1973. Concorde could fly to New York JFK and Washington Dulles, but had to slow below the speed of sound when operating over US territory.

That kept airlines from taking advantage of its full performance on domestic transcontinental routes, limiting Concorde’s commercial appeal.

The X-59’s design prevents shockwaves from combining into the loud boom that Concorde produced. Its long, narrow nose separates the pressure waves generated at the front of the aircraft from those produced by the wings. NASA has also kept the underside of the aircraft smooth and mounted its engine above the fuselage, where the wings help shield the ground from the engine inlet’s shockwaves. 

The space agency expects people on the ground will only hear a quiet thump, more like a car door closing from about 20 feet away.

The noise-dampening design presents a challenge for piloting the aircraft. The X-59’s nose is so long that its pilot cannot see directly forward through a windscreen. Instead, pilots rely on camera images shown on a cockpit display to see what’s ahead.

NASA’s X-59 has already exceeded its target speed

The aircraft first broke the sound barrier on 5 June 2026, reaching approximately Mach 1.1.

A week later, on 12 June, it reached Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet, the conditions NASA has planned for its future noise research flights.

During testing in September, NASA pushed the X-59 to Mach 1.53, its highest reported speed. By the first anniversary of its maiden flight on 28 October, it had completed 40 additional flights and reached altitudes above 56,000 feet.

NASA is now preparing for acoustic testing to measure the aircraft’s actual noise levels. Flights over selected US communities will follow, allowing researchers to record how residents respond.

NASA hopes the findings will give regulators the evidence they need to establish noise limits for future supersonic passenger aircraft. The FAA is already working to replace the longstanding US restrictions with noise-based standards, with rulemaking milestones planned for 2027.

In Brief 4 min read
  • IATA's 2026 Global Passenger Survey found that 43% of travellers were deterred by visa and immigration requirements, up from 33% in 2025.
  • Biometric airport processing continues to grow, with 58% of passengers using biometrics and 84% interested in digital passports.
  • AI travel planning is going mainstream, with 49% of travellers using AI to search flights, find cheaper fares and discover destinations.

Immigration requirements are discouraging many from international travel, even as passengers become more comfortable using artificial intelligence (AI), biometrics and digital passports, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA).

The findings come from an IATA survey of more than 10,000 respondents across over 200 countries, published on 28 October.

Immigration requirements dampen international travel demand 

According to IATA’s 2026 Global Passenger Survey, 43% of respondents said immigration requirements had discouraged them from visiting a destination, compared with 33% in 2025.

Among those deterred by entry requirements, 53% said the complexity of the process was their main concern. Privacy and cost were each cited by 17% of those surveyed.

IATA said governments need to simplify visa and immigration procedures to remove barriers to travel.

“Passengers are embracing technology to make travel easier. AI is becoming a mainstream travel planning tool, while biometrics and digital identity are creating a faster and more seamless airport experience. Yet many travellers continue to face barriers from complex immigration and visa processes,” said Nick Careen, IATA’s Senior Vice President, Operations, Safety and Security.

Passengers want simpler digital immigration procedures

Despite concerns about entry requirements, passengers are increasingly willing to complete immigration formalities digitally before travelling.

The survey found that 86% would be willing to share immigration information electronically before departure to speed up the process, compared with 83% in 2025.

Meanwhile, 45% would prefer to complete immigration procedures before reaching the airport, up from 41% last year.

A clear majority of travellers prefer online visa applications, with around 60% favouring applying online, compared with 25% who would rather visit an embassy or consulate.

IATA said more than 100 countries already issue electronic visas. However, differences in how these digital documents are verified create difficulties for airlines checking passenger documentation.

The association is calling for common standards that would allow airlines and governments to verify digital travel credentials more efficiently.

Biometric identification gains ground at airports

Biometric technology has become a more familiar part of the airport experience.

Some 58% of passengers reported using biometric identification during an airport journey in the previous 12 months, up from 50% in 2025 and 34% in 2022.

Among passengers who had experienced biometric processing, 87% said they were satisfied with it.

The survey also found that 78% would be willing to share biometric information to avoid repeatedly presenting a passport or boarding pass at airport checkpoints.

Interest in digital passports is particularly strong, with 84% of respondents saying they would like to use one for online check-in instead of a physical document.

However, passengers remain concerned about how their personal information is protected.

Data breaches were the leading concern, cited by 59% of respondents, followed by information being shared with other organisations (49%) and uncertainty about how personal data is handled (41%).

Nearly half of passengers use AI to plan travel

AI is also becoming part of how passengers research and arrange their journeys. The IATA survey found that 49% of respondents had used AI for travel planning. 

  • Searching for flights to a particular destination was the most common application, cited by 21% of respondents.
  • 19% used AI to find cheaper flights
  • 17% used AI to identify potential destinations.

IATA said airlines need to consider how their products appear in AI-powered searches and how passengers can move from researching a journey to making a booking.

Europe trails other regions in AI and biometric adoption

The survey revealed considerable differences in passengers’ attitudes towards digital travel technology.

Europe recorded the lowest use of AI for travel planning, at 35%, compared with the global average of 49%. Only 47% of European respondents had experienced biometric identification in the previous year, against 58% globally.

European passengers were also less willing to share biometric data, with 70% supporting its use for airport processes compared with 78% worldwide.

The Middle East recorded the highest AI adoption, at 72%, and the strongest interest in digital passports for online check-in, at 91%.

North America had the highest proportion of passengers who had experienced biometric processing, at 63%, although respondents there also expressed the greatest concern about data breaches.

Africa recorded the highest proportion of passengers discouraged by immigration requirements, at 52%, followed by Asia-Pacific at 49%. Europe’s figure was 38%, and North America had the lowest share, at 35%.

Overall, 87% of respondents said they were satisfied with air travel, although satisfaction in Europe was the lowest of any region, at 84%.

IATA’s 2026 Global Passenger Survey shows clear progress in many parts of the digital journey, but government policy still requires harmonisation before truly seamless travel becomes a reality.

An Italian Army CH-47 Chinook operating with the EU peacekeeping mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina has crashed during a training flight, killing four people and injuring 11 others.

The accident occurred near Gorice in the Brčko district and has renewed attention on military helicopter safety as investigators work to establish the cause.

Italian CH-47 Chinook helicopter crashes in Bosnia with 15 onboard

According to Italy’s defence ministry, four were killed, and 11 were injured, none of whom had life-threatening injuries.

The safety record of the CH-47 Chinook

The CH-47 Chinook is among the world’s most widely operated military helicopters. First entering service in the early 1960s, the twin-rotor aircraft is used by armed forces around the world for heavy-lift transport, troop movements and humanitarian support missions.

More than 1,200 Chinooks have been built, with the type remaining in frontline service across Europe, North America, Asia and the Middle East.

According to Aviation Safety Network data, 61 CH-47 helicopters have been written off worldwide since 2000, including aircraft lost during military operations. Six of those write-offs have occurred since 2020.

In the US Army, the largest operator of the type, Chinooks flew more than 386,000 flight hours between 2019 and 2020, according to Army safety data. Over that period, the fleet recorded six Class A mishaps, seven Class B mishaps and 34 Class C mishaps.
